cynefin.antiPattern: Treating a complex problem as if it were merely complicated—commissioning a detailed master plan that is dead on arrival.
paragraphs: Dave Snowden created it to decide how to act based on the nature of a problem, because each domain demands a different way of working. For Recuenco, a complicated problem is a job for a good consultant, while a complex one calls for a CPS practitioner—though he warns that not everything unknown is chaotic. He considers it an eye-opener for grasping complexity, yet still a simplification of reality.

domains.name: Clear
domains.text: Cause and effect are obvious to anyone; solved by applying known best practices. Previously called "simple."

domains.name: Complicated
domains.text: A relationship between cause and effect exists, but it takes analysis or an expert to uncover it. The domain of a good consultant.

domains.name: Complex
domains.text: Cause and effect can only be understood in hindsight; you must experiment, observe, and adapt. The domain of CPS.

domains.name: Chaotic
domains.text: No link between cause and effect is discernible; you act first to stabilize the situation and only then try to make sense of it.

domains.name: Confused
domains.text: You don't yet know which domain the problem belongs to; the first job is figuring that out. Recuenco links it to aporia.

deepDive.thesis: Cynefin opens your eyes to distinct regimes of causality, but mistaking its neat borders for reality—or calling every gap in your knowledge "chaos"—wrecks strategy.
essay: Dave Snowden's Cynefin framework draws boundaries between distinct realms based on how cause and effect connect, placing structured complexity halfway between rigid order and the pure randomness measured by Kolmogorov entropy. For Recuenco, that map is a turning point because it reveals that each domain requires a radically different mode of intervention. Better still, problems don't stay frozen in one quadrant: under his General Law of complex business systems, controlled experimentation pushes every complex process toward the complicated—and eventually into common sense.

Despite his admiration for Snowden, Recuenco dismantles two widespread misunderstandings. The first is taking the diagram literally: Cynefin illuminates the nature of complexity, yet oversimplifies the reality of a company in crisis, where problems don't live in watertight compartments but in a total entanglement of resources. The second is the alibi of chaos: slapping the "chaotic quadrant" label onto any unfamiliar territory to hand the keys over to mindless trial and error—throwing spaghetti at the wall instead of thinking strategically before running experiments.

In the architecture of CPS, Cynefin serves as a compass for dosing hard thinking alongside targeted experimentation. Taking the leap into the void required by the complex quadrant—Dr. House style—never means abandoning judgment: ten hours of reflection save a hundred hours of blind labor. Today that boundary carries fresh urgency, because the moment a complex process is tamed and crosses deterministically into the complicated, artificial intelligence encapsulates it. Anyone who masters Cynefin knows how to navigate genuine uncertainty instead of wasting talent competing in spaces already ripe for automation.
keyInsights: Cynefin is a formidable eye-opener for grasping complexity, yet inside a real company problems refuse to respect neat boundaries: they operate as a collective entanglement of resources.
Confusing the unknown with the chaotic quadrant breeds an intellectual free-for-all that replaces strategic judgment with brute force and indiscriminate trial and error.
Every complex process tends, through controlled experimentation, to become complicated and then common sense—and that is the exact moment AI models and encapsulates it.
Even while critiquing framework oversimplifications, Recuenco shares Snowden's allergy to gratuitous "quantum" metaphors, which almost always herald a corporate smoke-and-mirrors storm.

threadExamples.title: Spaghetti at the wall, Dilbert, and Dr. House
threadExamples.detail: In his thread on managing the unknown, Recuenco contrasts the urban legend of throwing pasta at the wall—which he first saw in a Dilbert strip—with Dr. House's hypothesis-driven experimentation: the complex domain demands thoughtfully designed probes, not brute-force flailing.

threadExamples.title: Kolmogorov, the first goose barnacle, and AI encapsulation
threadExamples.detail: From Grassberger's nuance on Kolmogorov complexity as a measure of randomness to the joke about the first starving human brave enough to eat a goose barnacle, Recuenco explains how human exploration shifts processes across Cynefin until they turn deterministic and get absorbed by AI.

quote.text: Yet while Cynefin is a total eye-opener in terms of understanding the nature of complexity, in terms of reflecting reality it is a simplification.
quote.sourceTitle: Complexity vs. Randomness: Why Widely Cited Kolmogorov Complexity Is Simply a Measure of Randomness

reflectionQuestions: Are you excusing chaotic, hypothesis-free experiments with "this is complex" when what's really missing is sitting down to think for ten hours?
Are you trying to solve one department's problem in isolation when it is actually entangled with incentives, sales, and operations across the entire company?
Which of your team's processes have already crossed from complex to complicated and will be encapsulated by AI if you keep treating them as your competitive edge?

emergencia.short: Collective behaviors of a system that cannot be deduced from the behavior of any of its individual parts.
emergencia.analogy: A murmuration of starlings painting impossible shapes across the sky: no single bird directs the pattern; it arises from simple rules between neighbors.
emergencia.howToApply: To change a collective outcome (culture, traffic, market), act on the rules of interaction and the environment rather than just barking orders at individuals.
emergencia.antiPattern: Believing you can predict how a living whole will behave simply by adding up the properties of each isolated part.
paragraphs: Recuenco sums it up simply: collective behaviors we cannot extrapolate from individual ones. His favorite example is an organization's culture, which emanates from its dynamic architecture of incentives. That's why you cannot "change the culture" directly—you would have to alter everything that causes it, and in a complex system that is a contradiction in terms.

deepDive.thesis: Emergence produces collective properties irreducible to their parts, making any attempt to change corporate culture by executive decree a systemic contradiction.
essay: Emergence describes collective behaviors and properties of a system that cannot be extrapolated by inspecting its pieces one by one. Recuenco shows that the phenomenon spans everything from subatomic physics to the human mind—no single neuron is conscious, yet their distributed interaction with the body and environment gives rise to consciousness—and operates with equal force inside organizations. Within a company, emergence is born from the constant collision of stimuli, accumulated historical narratives, and a dynamic architecture of incentives that shapes what people actually do every day.

Two monumental blunders stem from ignoring this mechanism, and Recuenco dismantles both mercilessly. The first is corporate voluntarism around "changing the culture": because culture emanates as an emergent property of real incentives and their history, trying to map and directly rewrite every micro-event behind it is a contradictio in terminis. The second blunder swings to the opposite extreme: invoking emergent complexity alongside Gödel or Turing to declare a problem "unsolvable." While genuinely undecidable problems exist, in practice their share is vanishingly small; almost every dead end is declared out of laziness, ego, or incompetence.

Understanding emergence links complexity science directly to incentive engineering—from Charlie Munger to BJ Fogg and Martin & Pear—and to the strategic core of the business. In CPS, accepting that culture cannot be decreed frees energy to pull the levers that actually work: redesigning the stimuli and dynamics that induce desired behaviors at scale. Anyone who grasps this principle stops preaching values on hollow slide decks, spots when a system rewards talking about a problem instead of fixing it, and patiently reshapes the conditions from which different behavior emerges.
keyInsights: Organizational culture is not an independent variable you can edit with speeches, but an emergent property of a dynamic incentive architecture and its accumulated narratives.
Claiming to "change the culture" directly inside a complex system is a contradiction in terms because it assumes control over every micro-event driving emergence.
Even though Gödel, Turing, and physics confirm that truly unsolvable complex problems exist, in business their real share is tiny compared to those abandoned out of laziness, ego, or poor framing.
If an incentive system rewards talking about a problem rather than solving it, the organization will reliably produce pristine analysis and perpetual paralysis as an emergent outcome.

threadExamples.title: Neural consciousness vs. the Gödel and Turing excuse
threadExamples.detail: When asked whether interdependence makes certain complex problems unsolvable, Recuenco explains emergence through the mind—irreducible to isolated neurons—and points out that despite the theoretical limits of Gödel and Turing, almost no corporate problem written off as impossible actually is.

threadExamples.title: Dynamic incentive architectures and rewarded paralysis
threadExamples.detail: Opening his trilogy on incentive engineering—weaving together Charlie Munger, BJ Fogg, Martin & Pear, and Freakonomics—he explains why culture emanates from historical incentives and quotes the wry exchange where a professional admits their system pays them to talk about the problem, not solve it.

quote.text: Aspects as critical as an organization's culture emanate as an emergent phenomenon from its dynamic architecture of incentives. Accepting this reality lets us understand, for instance, why you cannot actually "change" an organization's culture.
quote.sourceTitle: Analyzing the Importance of Incentives in Business and How They Shape Success or Failure

reflectionQuestions: Which unwanted behaviors on your team are you trying to fix with pep talks when they actually emerge straight from what your system rewards or tolerates?
In your current projects, what problem have you labeled "impossible" or "cultural" just to dodge the political and emotional cost of touching the incentives holding it in place?
If an outside observer watched only your company's real actions for a month—ignoring every memo—what culture would they conclude is actually emerging?

sensemaking.short: The process of making sense of an ambiguous or confusing situation before deciding what to do about it.
sensemaking.analogy: Piecing together a muddled scene by talking to witnesses, checking tracks, and sketching a provisional map before deciding whom to chase.
sensemaking.howToApply: Before rushing into execution, bring distinct perspectives together to put shared language to what is actually happening.
sensemaking.antiPattern: Confusing sensemaking with endless, paralyzing analysis—or skipping it altogether under the pressure to "do something right now."
paragraphs: Recuenco draws it chiefly from Karl Weick and treats it as critical in CPS: before you solve anything, you must understand what is going on. It is a demanding, subjective process loaded with identity, often triggering panic and a sense of void. That is why he insists you never argue about sensemaking: denying someone's narrative feels like denying the person. In his eyes, Dave Snowden is the ultimate sensemaker.
sensemaking.origin: Karl E. Weick, Sensemaking in Organizations

deepDive.thesis: Sensemaking is never a cold data-crunching exercise, but a reactive, identity-laden process that harmonizes mental models with empirical reality.
essay: Introduced to organizational theory by Karl E. Weick atop social-psychology roots like Katz and Kahn, sensemaking describes the ongoing construction of plausible mental pictures to bring order to ambiguous or confusing situations. Recuenco distills it into the friction between two primal tensions: our mental models of the world and their empirical verification. He also compares it to phosphorus in nature—an element so reactive it never appears isolated and chemically pure, always bound up with narrative, aesthetics, history, bodily interaction, and everyday decisions.

His threads dismantle two opposite errors when dealing with meaning. The first is the tyranny of big data and scientism—critiqued via Christian Madsbjerg and Daniel N. Robinson—which tries to explain complex human phenomena through quantitative metrics alone while dismissing culture, language, and lived experience. The second error is forgetting Recuenco's first rule of sensemaking: you do not argue about sensemaking. Because the process carries heavy emotional and identity investment—much as loss aversion clouds investing—attacking someone else's narrative triggers visceral self-defense, never clarity.

Inside CPS, sensemaking is the critical antechamber to diagnosis and hypothesis quality: if you misread what is happening, any brilliant solution will solve the wrong problem. Blending Weick's organizational lens with Madsbjerg's humanistic sensibility and enactive approaches—such as sensory profiles in neuroaesthetics—dramatically widens a team's perceptual radar. Anyone who masters sensemaking listens to reality with nuance, resists corporate groupthink, and understands that transforming a system begins with understanding how its members construct their own world.
keyInsights: Sensemaking harmonizes two permanent tensions: what our mental models expect of reality and what empirical verification hands back to us.
Like phosphorus in nature, sensemaking is far too reactive to appear in isolation; it always operates mixed with narrative, culture, the body, technology, and action.
The first rule of sensemaking is that you don't argue about sensemaking: the intense emotional and identity stakes turn any clash of narratives into a personal threat.
Blind devotion to data hides fatal gaps; against pure scientism, breakthrough results come from crossing empirical evidence with deep literacy in culture, language, and history.

threadExamples.title: Reactive phosphorus and the neuroaesthetics of "neurotribes"
threadExamples.detail: Wrapping up his series on sensemaking, Recuenco likens the discipline to phosphorus oxidizing on contact with air and reviews a book on neuroarts and neurodivergence showing how sensory profiles and enactivism expand the ways neurotypical and neurodivergent minds build meaning.

threadExamples.title: George Soros, Bjarke Ingels, and the tyranny of the algorithm
threadExamples.detail: Following Christian Madsbjerg, he contrasts quantitative obsession with sensemaking connoisseurs like investor George Soros and architect Bjarke Ingels—while noting that for grasping internal company dynamics, Karl Weick's classic remains his gold standard.

quote.text: To sum it up, sensemaking tries to harmonize two primal tensions: our mental models of reality and our empirical verification of those very models.
quote.sourceTitle: The Threshold Between Complexity and Serendipity

reflectionQuestions: Are you trying to win a head-on argument over how to interpret a problem without realizing the other person feels you are attacking their identity?
In your high-stakes decisions, what cultural, linguistic, or emotional reality are you filtering out simply because it doesn't fit into your dashboard or metrics?
When was the last time empirical evidence forced you to revise a cherished mental model rather than rationalize what you were already doing?

sistemas-complejos.short: Webs of parts so tightly intertwined that their problems feed on each other and cannot be treated in isolation.
sistemas-complejos.analogy: A plate of spaghetti: tug a single strand on one edge and half the plate shifts in ways impossible to calculate beforehand.
sistemas-complejos.howToApply: Watch interdependencies and test small interventions that give you live signal back before scaling drastic changes.
sistemas-complejos.antiPattern: Slicing a living problem into independent silos and assuming that fixing each piece separately will fix the whole.
paragraphs: Recuenco quotes Snowden's metaphor of bramble bushes in a thicket: you never know where one ends and the next begins. In a troubled company, problems feed one another and refuse to factor cleanly—fix one and three more pop up. That is why he regards human beings as the quintessential complex system, and psychologists as founding parents of CPS. His General Law states that every complex process eventually turns complicated and, in the end, common sense.

deepDive.thesis: A complex system is not a puzzle you can take apart piece by piece, but a tangled thicket whose evolution constantly redraws the frontier of human value against AI.
essay: To capture how a complex system truly behaves, Recuenco reaches for Cynthia Kurtz and Dave Snowden's seminal image: "bramble bushes in a thicket," where it is impossible to tell where one branch begins, where another ends, or what belongs to what. When the subject is human beings—the pinnacle of complex systems—that interdependence multiplies. That is why he counts psychologists among the founding parents of CPS and recalls Scott Adams's confession: the only businesses that ever worked out for him were the ones where he got the underlying psychology right.

The biggest lie surrounding complex systems isn't technical, it's moral: using them as an alibi for inaction. Although Gödel and Turing proved that undecidable problems exist, Recuenco stresses that the share of genuinely unsolvable business crises is minuscule. Most rot simply because it is far easier to blame COVID, China, or the Phantom of the Opera than to face reality like an adult, accept expert help, or quit the classic mistake of tackling alone what is really a ten-lock safe.

Inside CPS, understanding complex systems lets you read their historical arc: under Recuenco's General Law, controlled experimentation turns the complex into the complicated and ultimately into common sense. In today's world, any intellectual process that can be modeled deterministically will end up encapsulated by AI. Anyone who grasps this dynamic neither burns out swimming against the rip current nor tries to suffocate the Leviathan; they let machines absorb what is already domesticated and focus multidisciplinary human intellect on the live frontier of risk, uncertainty, and uncharted challenges.
keyInsights: Like bramble bushes in a thicket, factors inside a complex system feed one another without clean borders, making isolated or solo problem-solving futile.
Psychologists stand among the parents of CPS because they have spent decades working on the ultimate complex system: human beings and their underlying psychology.
Blaming external shocks—a pandemic, a downturn, or "the Phantom of the Opera"—is the easiest way to hide incompetence, laziness, or misplaced ego behind the label "unsolvable."
As experimentation turns complex processes into complicated, deterministic ones, AI encapsulates them; lasting human value lives in solving the next layer of complexity.

threadExamples.title: Bramble bushes in a thicket and the Phantom of the Opera
threadExamples.detail: Addressing whether complex problems can be unsolvable, Recuenco pairs Kurtz and Snowden's metaphor with a scathing critique of organizations that sweep messes under the rug—blaming COVID, the 11-M bombings, China, or the Phantom of the Opera instead of committing to a collective, ten-lock approach.

threadExamples.title: The rip current and the AI Leviathan
threadExamples.detail: Formulating his General Law of complex business systems, he likens AI's momentum to an ocean rip current: swimming head-on against it or trying to choke the Leviathan only exhausts you, whereas riding the flow opens a new golden age for human thought on unsolved problems.

quote.text: Every complex process tends, over time and with controlled experimentation, to become a complicated process, and eventually something belonging to common sense.
quote.sourceTitle: AI Encapsulates Complex Processes and Redefines CPS

reflectionQuestions: What problem in your organization are you trying to unlock alone with a single key when it is really a ten-lock safe requiring multiple disciplines working together?
What external factor are you using as your "Phantom of the Opera" today to avoid admitting blind spots, ego, or capability gaps inside the system?
Are you exhausting your team by swimming against the current on tasks AI can already systematize, instead of moving them to the frontier where the problem remains genuinely complex?

acoplamiento-suelto.short: Parts of an organization connected without rigidity, leaving them room to adapt when the environment shifts.
acoplamiento-suelto.analogy: A train with articulated cars versus one solid rigid beam: if one car hits trouble or the track bends, the rest don't derail.
acoplamiento-suelto.howToApply: Design teams and modules with clear interfaces and local autonomy so a surprise in one area doesn't paralyze the whole company.
acoplamiento-suelto.antiPattern: Centralizing every approval in a single committee in the name of efficiency, making the organization slow and brittle.
paragraphs: A Karl Weick concept that Recuenco pairs with sensemaking and enactment. It describes organizations whose parts are linked together, not bolted down: each retains room to maneuver. That slack provides agility in shifting environments.

deepDive.thesis: Loose coupling prevents a local failure from dragging down the entire organization by preserving slack and cognitive flexibility in the face of the unexpected.
essay: Recuenco draws the concept of loose coupling from the work of Karl E. Weick, a pioneer in studying how organizations operate under extreme pressure and manage the unexpected. The mechanism is as simple as it is demanding: the parts of a system stay connected to one another, but never welded shut in absolute rigidity. That controlled slack stops a shock in one node from triggering a chain-reaction collapse across the structure and gives each unit breathing room to adapt when reality outpaces central protocols.

Common prejudice mistakes tight coupling for efficiency and loose coupling for chaos. In his special thread written during the Valencia DANA floods, Recuenco shows the exact opposite: hyper-rigid, tribal, or badly incentivized structures—where "if you pay peanuts, you get monkeys"—freeze up or suffer cognitive collapse when reality tears up their script, performing intellectual gymnastics rather than admitting what is right in front of their eyes. Against that paralysis, people who keep their cognitive flexibility and autonomous capacity to act on the ground hold the system together when formal chains fail.

Within CPS, loose coupling forms an inseparable tripod with Weick's sensemaking and enactment. Designing organizations built for high-stakes environments means letting go of the fantasy of total control and carving out margins where local judgment can act with real skin in the game. When a company or society grasps this principle, it stops building fragile chains that only work in calm seas and nurtures teams capable of absorbing sudden blows, keeping common sense intact, and responding without waiting for impossible orders.
keyInsights: Loose coupling keeps an organization's parts connected without welding them rigid, enabling local adaptation when the unexpected overwhelms the plan.
Under extreme stress, the brain prioritizes survival over seeing reality; rigid structures amplify that cognitive collapse, while slack preserves flexibility.
Karl Weick's work on managing the unexpected shows that high reliability in risky environments depends as much on coordinated autonomy as on discipline.
When incentives degrade leadership quality ("put children in charge of solving problems and you'll get addition and subtraction"), tight coupling multiplies mediocrity instead of containing it.

threadExamples.title: The Valencia DANA: rigid paralysis vs. cognitive flexibility
threadExamples.detail: In his special edition written live during the Valencia floods, Recuenco contrasts the gridlock and tribal posturing of straitjacketed institutions with the immediate response of citizens and heroic figures who kept their cognitive flexibility instead of waiting for paralyzing permissions.

threadExamples.title: High-reliability organizations in Karl E. Weick
threadExamples.detail: Reviewing the legacy of Weick—author of Managing the Unexpected—Recuenco links loose coupling to high-pressure organizations, where keeping parts connected yet unbolted marks the line between absorbing a crisis and shattering.

quote.text: Another key concept is "loose coupling," which describes how the parts of an organization can be connected without being rigid. That allows flexibility and adaptation in changing environments.
quote.sourceTitle: Cognitive Collapses, Common Sense, and Heroic Figures in Complex Times

reflectionQuestions: If a critical link in your operations broke today or the landscape shifted overnight, how many teams would freeze waiting for instructions from the top?
Where are you mistaking bureaucratic rigidity and central control for reliability, choking off the responsiveness of people closest to reality?
How much real autonomy—and real backing—do your teams have to improvise with sound judgment the moment the playbook stops working?

autopoiesis.short: A system's capacity to produce and sustain itself, renewing its parts without losing its core identity.
autopoiesis.analogy: Your own body: nearly all your cells turn over across the years, yet you remain you because you preserve the pattern that organizes them.
autopoiesis.howToApply: Ask what core identity must endure while you renew products, people, and processes to keep pace with a changing environment.
autopoiesis.antiPattern: Trying to preserve every historical procedure untouched in the name of "protecting our essence," until the organization fossilizes.
paragraphs: A concept coined by biologists Humberto Maturana and Francisco Varela, which Niklas Luhmann extended to social systems: they define themselves through their own internal communications (self-reference) and preserve their identity even while dealing with the outside world (operational closure). Recuenco speaks of corporate autopoiesis to capture the tension between the new and the well-operated. Each camp inside a company pulls in its own direction, and survival depends on manually recalibrating the lost balance.
autopoiesis.origin: Humberto Maturana and Francisco Varela, and Niklas Luhmann for social systems

deepDive.thesis: Corporate autopoiesis explains why a company must renew itself from within to survive without dissolving the identity that holds it together.
essay: The concept originated with Chilean biologists Humberto Maturana and Francisco Varela to describe how a living organism produces itself, regulates itself, and regenerates its parts while preserving its internal organization. German sociologist Niklas Luhmann imported that logic—without the biologists' blessing—into social systems through three traits: self-reference, operational closure, and functional differentiation. Inside a company, this autopoiesis plays out as perpetual tension: the organization reproduces its own internal rules and communications while trying to adapt to a shifting environment without losing its identity or functionality.

The deadliest mirage in corporate life is thinking this tension between the mature and the new can be settled once and for all. Operational closure shields a company from dissolving, yet overdone it breeds comfortable stagnation and milking the cash cow—as Recuenco illustrates with Apple's iPhone 16: flawless operations, captive ecosystem lock-in, and minimal exploratory nerve. At the opposite pole, chasing endless novelty without mature execution destroys the ability to deliver. Neither extreme survives on its own.

Bringing corporate autopoiesis into CPS illuminates the sweeping economic shift Recuenco tracks for investors, Private Equity funds, and M&A deals: moving away from financial engineering and sheer operational efficiency toward reinventing value propositions. Mastering this dynamic means accepting that the complexity bar never stops rising. A truly autopoietic organization doesn't wait for the market to crack it open; it cultivates transformational talent and cognitive orchestration to inject deliberate renewal inside a rock-solid operation.
keyInsights: According to Luhmann, autopoietic social systems run on self-reference and operational closure: they interact with the environment, yet their decisions remain governed by their own internal logic.
The perpetual tug-of-war between what feels safe and well-operated versus what feels uncertain and exploratory isn't a management flaw—it is the survival condition of any living system.
When a mature company over-indexes on operational closure and short-term margins, it mistakes captive ecosystem inertia for genuine innovative vitality.
Value creation is migrating from financial engineering and cosmetic digitization toward real transformation, raising the complexity required just to stay alive.

threadExamples.title: Apple, the iPhone 16, and the comfort of the well-operated
threadExamples.detail: Recuenco opens the thread poking fun at the iPhone 16 launch—mocked online for looking identical to the 14 and 15—and his own family "surrender" to FaceTime, portraying how an entrenched giant leans on mature operations and user lock-in over exploratory risk.

threadExamples.title: Niklas Luhmann's subsystems and the turn in VC, Private Equity, and M&A
threadExamples.detail: The thread links the legal, political, and educational subsystems described by Luhmann to the present challenge for funds and corporations: shifting from squeezing operating efficiencies and cheap money to rebuilding value propositions through transformational talent.

quote.text: Living beings are in a constant process of renewal and adaptation, which implies an ongoing tension between bringing in new elements and preserving their mature, stable structure.
quote.sourceTitle: Autopoiesis and the Tension in Business Evolution

reflectionQuestions: In your company, is operational closure protecting your distinctive edge—or simply filtering out uncomfortable signals from the market?
Is your business still growing thanks to genuine renewal of its value proposition, or coasting on inertia and switching costs from captive customers?
What real weight do voices defending exploration carry in your leadership meetings compared to those measuring only short-term operating efficiency?

corrientes-subterraneas.short: Low-visibility influences that shape a system from underneath long before they register on the surface.
corrientes-subterraneas.analogy: The quiet murmur around the coffee machine that decides whether a project succeeds or gets sabotaged long before it reaches the executive committee.
corrientes-subterraneas.howToApply: Listen to informal conversations, notice which topics people dodge, and catch silent tensions before they erupt into the open.
corrientes-subterraneas.antiPattern: Governing solely off the official org chart and sanitized status reports painted green on their way up the ladder.
paragraphs: Recuenco also calls them "corrientes subterráneas" (undercurrents) and ties them to second-order consequences and signal reading. He illustrates them through modern music, built out of subcultures and movements that never stood in the limelight. In his threads, he applies the idea to civil-society action: you have to orchestrate many unglamorous moving parts because what actually matters rarely sits on the surface.

deepDive.thesis: What reshapes a system rarely happens under the surface spotlight, but in subterranean undercurrents that demand patient signal-reading and orchestration.
essay: Beyond direct causes and even second-order consequences lie what Recuenco calls undercurrents: barely visible influences working from below to reshape an entire system's structure long before anyone spots them on the surface. Inspired by The Wire magazine's book Undercurrents on the hidden wiring of modern music, he shows how fringe movements, weak signals, and seemingly modest projects end up tapping into far larger streams than expected whenever they hit a real, latent tension.

The usual response to social or corporate dysfunction swings between two equally sterile exits: venting in public "jeremiads" soaked in outrage, or daydreaming about Hollywood lone-hero rescues straight out of Erin Brockovich. Recuenco stresses that acting from civil society—or transforming any complex setting—requires the exact opposite: climbing down underground, reading subtle signals, studying how real movements organize, and orchestrating dozens of unglamorous pieces so steady pressure produces tangible change instead of fleeting noise.

In the architecture of CPS, undercurrents link sensemaking and signal reading to collective intelligence and organized action (#DoThings). Understanding them explains why flashy top-down interventions bounce off a brick wall while others, aligned with a deep current, trigger outsized results—like forcing the cancellation of absurd public contracts. Anyone who tunes their ear to the underground stops reacting solely to today's headline and builds patient coalitions capable of shifting a system from its foundations.
keyInsights: Undercurrents operate at an even subtler layer than second-order consequences: they lay down the hidden wiring of a culture or market long before turning visible.
Public outrage on social media amounts to nothing more than a sterile jeremiad unless it translates into organized civic action and patient multi-front orchestration.
Hollywood myths like Erin Brockovich distort how society actually changes; effective leverage looks much more like structured social movements and Amalio Rey's collective intelligence.
When a modestly scoped project strikes a real deep current, it taps into a far greater volume of water than anyone originally planned for.

threadExamples.title: The hidden wiring of modern music in Undercurrents
threadExamples.detail: Recuenco uses The Wire's Undercurrents: The Hidden Wiring of Modern Music to prove how peripheral subcultures and experiments that never made the front page wound up defining the architecture of contemporary music.

threadExamples.title: Ingobernable, metaverse contracts, and real civic action
threadExamples.detail: Following the shock of the Valencia floods and his podcast episode on Ingobernable with Jaime Obregón, he contrasts public spending on metaverses against neglected digital services, pitting the lone-hero myth of Erin Brockovich or A Civil Action against frameworks like Power in Movement and Amalio Rey's collective intelligence.

quote.text: In fact, lately I'm deeply immersed in everything around second-order consequences—and something even subtler, like subterranean influences ("undercurrents").
quote.sourceTitle: Reflections on Hidden Influences, Music, and Civic Action in Spain

reflectionQuestions: In your industry or community, what fringe signals are you brushing off today because they don't make headlines yet—even as they quietly rewire the rules of the game?
How much of your current energy goes into visible venting about symptoms instead of orchestrating the unglamorous pieces that actually alter the problem?
If you wanted to drive real change beyond a single symbolic gesture, what collective intelligence and parallel fronts would you need to coordinate?

enactacion.short: Karl Weick's idea that organizations are created and defined by what their members actually do and how they interact.
enactacion.analogy: A mountain trail that didn't exist on any map until the repeated footsteps of hikers walking it made it real.
enactacion.howToApply: Remember that every daily decision, conversation, and habit is manufacturing your organization's reality far more than its framed values posters.
enactacion.antiPattern: Waiting for a spotless outside analysis while forgetting that your own actions are already reshaping the very environment you're observing.
paragraphs: Recuenco introduces it alongside Weick, whom he calls the never-quite-acknowledged patron saint of many CPS pillars. An organization is not its org chart, but what its members do in practice. Hence his closing advice: to understand what's going on, track each person's actions according to their skin in the game.

deepDive.thesis: An organization is not what its org chart or mission statement proclaims, but the reality its members build live through their actions.
essay: Formulated by Karl E. Weick alongside sensemaking and loose coupling, enactment argues that organizations and their environments do not sit there like passive stage sets that individuals merely adapt to—they are created and defined through the collective actions, interactions, and interpretations of their members. Every decision made under pressure, every tolerated omission, and every everyday habit writes the true constitution of the system, regardless of what its handbooks, bylaws, or official statements claim.

The trap Recuenco lays bare in his DANA thread is judging people or institutions by what they say in comfortable times. The human brain is wired for survival, not truth; when fear or tribalism triggers cognitive collapse, people perform intellectual contortions capable of denying what stands right in front of their eyes. That is why the acid test never lies in the story people tell, but in the moment the tide goes out—when hard facts strip bare who was prepared and which incentives were secretly running the show.

Inside CPS, Recuenco's parting maxim—"Follow the enactment"—joins Karl Weick with skin in the game and incentive engineering into a ruthless diagnostic tool. If you want to understand an organization in crisis, ignore its values slide decks and trace what each actor actually executes given what they personally stand to lose. Anyone who internalizes enactment stops debating stated intentions, watches real behavior under pressure, and accepts that changing a reality starts with changing the concrete actions that reproduce it.
keyInsights: Organizations are not their org charts or slogans: they are created, sustained, and revealed through the real actions and interactions of their members.
Because the brain puts survival ahead of accepting reality, under extreme stress the narrative twists until it denies the obvious; only deeds carry reliable signal.
Enactment gains its sharpest edge when crossed with skin in the game: every actor's real behavior diverges dramatically based on what they personally have at risk.
"Follow the enactment" works as a diagnostic compass in any crisis: tracking concrete actions cuts through rhetorical fog far faster than debating ideological arguments.

threadExamples.title: "Follow the enactment" during the Valencia DANA crisis
threadExamples.detail: In his thread written live during the Valencia floods, Recuenco shows Karl Weick vindicated by events: while polarized factions twist themselves into knots and stall, people with skin in the game and intact common sense define the real response through their deeds.

threadExamples.title: Buffett, Ogilvy, and the low-tide test
threadExamples.detail: Recuenco reinforces enactment by linking Warren Buffett's maxim ("only when the tide goes out do you discover who's been swimming naked") with his riff on David Ogilvy ("if you incentivize peanuts, you get monkeys"), proving incentives reveal themselves in action, never in talk.

quote.text: Weick is being vindicated in the actions of some and others depending on their skin in the game. Follow the enactment.
quote.sourceTitle: Cognitive Collapses, Common Sense, and Heroic Figures in Complex Times

reflectionQuestions: If you muted every speech, email, and values statement in your organization for a month, what priorities would its actual deeds prove?
In which critical decisions of your project are you trusting the words of people who have zero skin in the game for the outcome?
When pressure spikes on your team, what behaviors actually emerge in practice versus what you claim to stand for when things are calm?

homeostasis.short: The ability of an organism—or a company—to keep its internal state steady by offsetting external changes.
homeostasis.analogy: The human body's thermostat, sweating or shivering to hold steady around 98.6 °F (37 °C) whether outside is freezing or scorching.
homeostasis.howToApply: Build buffers (cash reserves, customer diversity, learning capacity) that absorb external shocks without shattering your core.
homeostasis.antiPattern: Mistaking healthy stability for rigid stagnation—or squeezing efficiency so hard that you have zero margin left at the first bump.
paragraphs: In biology, it is the dynamic balance that regulates temperature, fluids, or blood sugar via feedback loops. Recuenco carries it over to business: a company blends biological, social, and systemic dynamics, and its internal equilibrium can break down and turn pathological. Restoring it means manually tuning the sweet spot between opposing forces like innovation and optimization—sometimes the company's survival hangs on that adjustment.

deepDive.thesis: Corporate homeostasis is neither static calm nor a fixed recipe, but the ongoing manual recalibration of a metastable balance that can easily turn pathological.
essay: In biology, homeostasis is the dynamic equilibrium through which an organism keeps vital variables—temperature, pH, fluids, blood sugar—within a livable range via feedback control systems. Recuenco brings this mechanic into business because every company braids together biological, social, and systemic dynamics. Far from a set-and-forget state, corporate equilibrium is metastable—akin to allostasis and what he calls "scien-arts" (cienciartes)—demanding continuous calibration as the organization exchanges energy and information with a shifting environment.

The most destructive mistake is confusing homeostasis with standing still, or hunting for a magic framework to automate balance forever—just as the WEF dropped CPS because it wouldn't fit inside a neat checklist. Recuenco warns that corporate homeostasis can also sicken and lock into pathological patterns: when executives, employees, board members, and investors split into camps to feed only one of the "two wolves"—the well-operated versus the exploratory—the pent-up strain eventually cracks the ship's ribs.

Within CPS, recovering lost homeostasis requires stepping outside the box, climbing upstream to question the frame trapping the team, and manually dialing in the sweet spot on every front of tension. This shifts a leader from framework worship to the living craft of a scien-art: just as Joe Satriani taught Steve Vai and Kirk Hammett to find their own voice instead of minting zealous clones, mastering homeostasis means holding opposing tensions with personal judgment so the company survives and evolves.
keyInsights: A company blends biological, social, and systemic dynamics whose homeostasis can derail into pathological patterns if no one intervenes upstream.
Internal tensions work like the parable of the two wolves: board, investors, executives, and staff each feed their favored camp until the hull buckles unless someone manages the balance.
Disciplines with metastable equilibria are "scien-arts" (cienciartes) combining scientific rigor with inspiration; reducing them to cookbook recipes or rigid frameworks drains them of life.
Finding the sweet spot on each battleground isn't automatic—it demands relentless individual and collective manual tuning.

threadExamples.title: The ship's ribs and the two corporate wolves
threadExamples.detail: In his thread on biomimicry, hormesis, and corporate autopoiesis, Recuenco describes how the clash between the new and the well-operated strains a company's hull while each stakeholder group feeds one of the two wolves, forcing leaders to recalibrate the sweet spot by hand.

threadExamples.title: The WEF pivot and Joe Satriani's teaching
threadExamples.detail: Explaining why the WEF swapped CPS for tidier systems-thinking recipes, he links metastable equilibria to scien-arts (cienciartes) and points to Joe Satriani—mentor to stylistically distinct guitarists like Steve Vai, Kirk Hammett, and Alex Skolnick—as the antidote to rigid orthodoxy worship.

quote.text: In reality, what you have to look for is the sweet spot across each of the different battlegrounds of tension. It is an individual and collective effort to manually adjust a lost homeostasis.
quote.sourceTitle: Autopoiesis and the Tension in Business Evolution

reflectionQuestions: What repetitive pattern in your company are you treating as "just how things are" when it is actually a pathological homeostasis bleeding you from the inside?
Between your organization's two wolves—exploiting what is safe versus exploring what is uncertain—which one are your KPIs, budgets, and promotions actually feeding?
Are you hunting for a closed framework to save you from thinking about your team's balance, or doing the manual tuning this moment demands?

vaca-esferica.short: A model so oversimplified that it works on paper and fails completely in reality. From the classic physicist joke.
vaca-esferica.analogy: The joke about the physicist who promises to boost a dairy farm's milk output starting with: "First, assume a perfectly spherical cow in a vacuum."
vaca-esferica.howToApply: Use simple models only as rough opening drafts, and always ask what real-world friction was scrubbed out to make the math look pretty.
vaca-esferica.antiPattern: Making real-world calls off tidy simulations that erased the very messiness that actually runs the show.
paragraphs: It comes from the joke about the physicist who solves a farm's low milk yield—provided the cows are spherical and in a vacuum. Recuenco applies it to the determinism he was taught in college, which turned out to be a toy simplification, and to textbook approaches like Watanabe's "CPS for kids and spherical cows." According to the Astudillo Test, any spherical cow that ignores Factor X lands flat on its face.

deepDive.thesis: The spherical cow is the mirage of the deterministic model that shines on a whiteboard only because it amputates context, variability, and human passions.
essay: Borrowed from the famous joke about the physicist who solves dairy production by assuming spherical cows in a vacuum, the metaphor flags any comforting simplification that works only if you erase the world's real friction. Recuenco recounts his own disillusionment with the university determinism summed up in Wirth's formula—"Algorithms + Data Structures = Programs": algorithmic mechanics crush closed tasks like computing digits of Pi or beating us at chess, yet crumble the moment high-variability, context-sensitive processes appear that cannot be foreseen in advance.

What wrecks entire organizations isn't using models, but forcing spherical cows systematically onto human realities. When you try to cram a brand-customer relationship, emotionally charged customer support, or a deeply contextual law into a rigid BPMN flowchart or procedural CRM, you spawn what Sylvia Díaz-Montenegro calls "Golem processes." Through the Astudillo Test and his critique of rationalist idealism, Recuenco reminds us that any "hyper-productive" or purely rational scheme that ignores Factor X and human passions degenerates into dehumanized Taylorism and lands teeth-first on the pavement.

Spotting spherical cows is basic hygiene in CPS. It separates simplistic manuals from the living tangle of complex systems, forcing teams to replace classical procedural tools with designs built for high variability—such as Personotecnia, artifact-centric workflows, or procedural abstraction. Better yet, it inoculates against the arrogance of the rationalist who thinks they hold the magic formula: sharp sensemaking matters for an accurate diagnosis, but falling in love with a tidy theory and insisting on being right is usually the exact prologue to a crash.
keyInsights: The algorithmic determinism that calculates infinite digits of Pi is a useless spherical cow when facing high-variability processes loaded with context and human emotion.
Trapping contextual, human workflows inside classical procedural tools like a rigid CRM or BPMN diagram breeds dysfunctional "Golem processes."
Under the Astudillo Test, no spherical cow that ignores Factor X and human passions survives contact with reality without landing teeth-first.
When efficiency obsession invades everything, work loses its humanity and decays into sterile Taylorism that mistakes tidy order for real effectiveness.

threadExamples.title: Golem processes, abortion law, and Wirth's determinism
threadExamples.detail: In his thread on high-variability processes alongside Sylvia Díaz-Montenegro, Recuenco explains why it is impossible to draft a universally satisfying abortion law or run customer relationships on rigid BPMN flows without spawning monstrous "Golem processes."

threadExamples.title: The Astudillo Test, Taylorism, and the Wilbur Mills affair
threadExamples.detail: To prove how pure rationality without Factor X collapses, Recuenco cites the Astudillo Test, Pablo Grueso's warning that efficiency and fun rarely mix, and the true story of US Congressman Wilbur Mills—who read tax law for leisure before ending up in a scandal with Fanne Foxe and in Alcoholics Anonymous.

quote.text: The Astudillo Test states that you cannot put forward any spherical cow that ignores Factor X without landing teeth-first.
quote.sourceTitle: The Impact of Wanting to Be Right Across Multiple Contexts

reflectionQuestions: What nuanced, human process are you forcing into a rigid CRM, form, or script today—churning out constant frustration and Golem-like responses?
If you run the Astudillo Test on your sleekest strategic plan, which Factor X passions, fears, or incentives did you erase just to make the spreadsheet balance?
Where in your business has the obsession with "optimizing" every step killed off humanity, judgment, and the leeway to handle each case in its context?

contexto.short: The concrete circumstances surrounding a problem that decide whether a solution succeeds or fails. For Recuenco, it is almost everything.
contexto.analogy: The same seed that thrives in damp soil dies in the desert: success was never locked inside the seed alone.
contexto.howToApply: Before importing a 'success story' ('this is how Spotify or Amazon does it'), audit which unrepeatable conditions existed there and are missing here.
contexto.antiPattern: Copying best practices as universal recipes while ignoring culture, timing, cash runway, and team maturity.
paragraphs: Recuenco keeps hammering home that context is often more important than the thing itself. In CPS, every solution/context pair works like a key and its lock: it doesn't matter if six pins align if the seventh jams. That is why he distrusts heuristics—which are blind to context—and recipes lifted from someone else's case. We struggle to account for it because it complicates every neat analysis.

deepDive.thesis: In complexity, there are no universal solutions: every problem demands a key cut to its exact lock, where a single mismeasured tooth ruins the entire job.
essay: Recuenco traces our contextual blindness to neurobiology and schoolhouse math. The brain is an energy-saving machine built to crank out heuristics, and heuristics are blind to context. Add to that the bad habit of hunting for 'general solutions'—like solving a differential equation before pinning down its arbitrary constants. Reality, however, is stubbornly particular: a process always rooted in unrepeatable coordinates. Procedures that claim to be environment-independent haven't discovered universal laws; they are just convenient simplifications we invent so complexity doesn't overwhelm us.

From there, Recuenco blows up two sacred cows of the corporate world. The first is the cult of the Success Story: at best, a case study proves only that a solution worked for one specific problem at an unrepeatable moment in time; extrapolating it to another company is pure magical thinking. The second is what he calls the 'dichotomy of death' inherited from Taylorism: believing we are forced to choose between context-sensitive processes and scalable ones. Nor is it just the objective environment that matters—the subjective framing of a situation radically reshapes how we perceive and perform.

In the architecture of CPS, context stops being an inconvenient backdrop and becomes the entire board. It connects directly to Personotecnia—a single person contains multitudes and shifts depending on the role they occupy—to high-variability processes, and to Colonel Thompson Syndrome, because a brilliant idea delivered too early fails just as badly as a terrible one. Mastering context means tearing up the playbook, tuning out the nine reductionist armchair pundits for every serious practitioner, and designing bespoke interventions once you actually know which lock is sitting in front of you.
keyInsights: Every solution/context pair operates like a unique lock and key: even if six of the seven pins fit flawlessly, one misaligned detail keeps the bolt shut.

Traditional consulting needs to believe in replicable general solutions because its business model relies on selling the same template to different clients; CPS assumes by definition that only particular solutions exist.
Context covers more than external or market variables: the mental frame through which a situation is presented fundamentally alters human memory, judgment, and behavior.
When you don't have a sharp read on the problem's current context, betting on a single closed solution is reckless; first, map the ground you are actually standing on.

threadExamples.title: Max Planck and the ultraviolet catastrophe
threadExamples.detail: Newtonian equations worked brilliantly within their domain, yet broke down completely on black-body radiation. Planck could only unlock quantum mechanics once he mentally broke free from the dogma of a single universal law valid across every context.

threadExamples.title: The hotel chain, Mirotele, and the memory experiment
threadExamples.detail: In Personotecnia projects, Recuenco saw the exact same customer act like completely different people depending on whether they traveled for work, as a couple, or with family—and someone with three PhDs happily binge trash TV or put on Serengeti documentaries just to nap. In the Group A/B memory experiment, merely framing the test as a language assessment rather than a memory quiz erased the age gap and the false positives.

quote.text: In CPS, every solution/context combo has a unique lock-and-key mechanism. It doesn't matter if six teeth fit—if the seventh doesn't, the bolt won't turn.
quote.sourceTitle: Decoding Colonel Thompson Syndrome: implications and reflections

reflectionQuestions: Which famous 'success story' or trendy framework are you importing into your team right now without checking whether the seven pins of your context match the original?
Are you assuming your customers or colleagues behave like static personas instead of watching how their behavior shifts with the specific situation they are in?
If your project fails despite crisp technical execution, what variable of timing, framing, or organizational maturity did you leave unmodeled?

elefante-negro.short: A highly probable risk we deliberately choose to ignore—and when it blows up, pretend nobody could have seen coming.
elefante-negro.analogy: A massive elephant sitting in the middle of the living room that nobody mentions so as not to ruin dinner; when it crushes the sofa, everyone gasps, 'What a black swan!'
elefante-negro.howToApply: Keep a recurring list of obvious, uncomfortable risks that everyone on the team acknowledges in private but nobody puts on the agenda.
elefante-negro.antiPattern: Dressing up crises that have been flashing warning lights for years as 'impossible freak accidents.'
paragraphs: Recuenco borrows it from Nassim Nicholas Taleb's snap-back at everyone calling the pandemic a 'black swan': it wasn't unexpected, we had simply chosen to look away. He links it to Richard Rumelt's 'elephant in the elevator'—the thing we refuse to see because admitting it hurts our interests. Any seasoned strategist has watched a company walk blind into a wall standing inches from its nose.

deepDive.thesis: A black elephant isn't a bolt from the blue; it's a disaster foretold that we willfully ignore out of convenience until it detonates and we feign shock.
essay: The term grew out of Nassim Nicholas Taleb's fury at watching half the planet label the 2020 pandemic a 'black swan' without having read even the dust jacket of his books. Recuenco picks up that baton and pairs it with the classic 'elephant in the elevator' popularized by strategists like Richard Rumelt. The root mechanism isn't epistemological, it's political and psychological: we don't fail because the risk is impossible to foresee, we fail because admitting it exists demands costs, sacrifices, or course corrections nobody wants to pay before the crash.

The most comfortable self-deception is rebranding willful negligence as bad luck. Once the black elephant tears down the room, the exact same pathological choreography kicks in: first everyone stares in bewilderment claiming 'nobody could have known'; next, legacy playbooks are slapped onto an unprecedented scenario; frustration builds, a scapegoat is fabricated, and everyone bemoans the fickleness of fortune. Meanwhile, the people who spent years pointing out that the emperor had no clothes were brushed off as inconvenient doomsayers.

Inside CPS, spotting black elephants is the first test of strategic maturity and truth-coping. The corporate obsession with demanding literal prior experience—'have you done this exact thing before?'—exposes how badly organizations are trapped in paint-by-numbers execution. Anyone who internalizes this concept stops hunting for recipes to replay yesterday's game and trains to navigate structurally analogous but novel situations, willingly paying the social price of naming the obvious out loud before the impact forces everyone to improvise in the rubble.
keyInsights: A black swan is unpredictable by definition; a black elephant is highly probable, plain to see for anyone willing to look, and silenced by vested interests.
Calling a foretold risk a 'black swan' works as a moral alibi: it absolves the people who looked the other way and turns negligence into fate.
As societies and companies, we stay locked into paint-by-numbers reflexes; the moment the script breaks, we reach for obsolete procedures before hunting for someone to blame.
Demanding exact prior experience on problems that have never occurred before blocks complex problem solving; what actually travels is hard-won craft built across structurally similar situations.

threadExamples.title: The 2020 pandemic and Taleb's fury
threadExamples.detail: Recuenco notes that pandemic risk had been flagged repeatedly both by uncertainty thinkers like Taleb and utterly mainstream figures like Bill Gates. Even so, when the crisis hit, the world snapped into a collective 'nobody could have known' reflex—proving Illidan Stormrage's 'You are not prepared!' right.

threadExamples.title: Singular Solving and five years of Java experience
threadExamples.detail: At his own complex problem-solving firm, prospective clients endlessly ask whether his team has solved their exact problem before. Recuenco compares it to job postings that demanded five years of Java experience when the language was barely two years old.

quote.text: A highly probable issue that we have decided to ignore at our own risk—and when it blows up right in our faces, we look at each other in astonishment as if to say, 'Nobody could have known.'
quote.sourceTitle: The pandemic is not a black swan

reflectionQuestions: Which obvious, recurring threat in your organization is currently treated as taboo simply because acknowledging it would force unpopular decisions today?
Which uncomfortable voice on your team are you dismissing as a 'doomsayer' when they are actually pointing at the elephant inside the elevator?
When you hire or ask for help on an unprecedented challenge, are you looking for someone who lived through the identical scenario or someone with proven judgment in complexity?

incertidumbre.short: The absence of certainty about what comes next. CPS accepts and manages it—whereas the human brain handles it terribly.
incertidumbre.analogy: Walking through a forest at night with a flashlight that only reaches fifteen feet: you can't see the trail's end, yet you see plenty to take the next safe step.
incertidumbre.howToApply: Replace bogus forecasts with reversible options, early feedback loops, and the agility to pivot as reality unfolds.
incertidumbre.antiPattern: Demanding 100% certainty before moving a muscle, or buying precision forecasts from snake-oil peddlers just to soothe your anxiety.
paragraphs: To Recuenco, CPS is essentially the management of uncertainty. The human brain short-circuits around it, which is why there is always budget for 'uncertainty reducers': prophets, shamans, fortune-tellers, or strategy consultants peddling manufactured certainty. He points out the absurdity that not a single school subject teaches how to handle uncertainty, even though high-uncertainty environments are now the default.

deepDive.thesis: The brain loathes uncertainty so deeply that it will gladly bankroll any illusion of control—from ancient shamans to Taylorism, civil-service cramming, and 'magic platforms.'
essay: Recuenco starts from an uncomfortable fact: human beings are biologically poorly wired to live with the unknown. Faced with a lack of guarantees, we freeze—and as Kahneman and Tversky proved, we calculate risk atrociously. That vulnerability turns uncertainty into an evergreen business. From antiquity, when chance wore the face of Tyche—a blindfolded, merciless, fickle goddess mocking our anthropocentrism—to modern boardrooms, there has always been bottomless funding for 'uncertainty reducers': diviners, prophets, gurus, strategy consultants, and methodologies coated in scientific veneer.

One misunderstanding Javier dismantles with particular relish is the notion that CPS fights chance to eradicate it. Quite the opposite: nobody respects Lady Luck more than a serious complexity practitioner, standing shoulder to shoulder with classic strategists like Mazarin or Napoleon. The mistake isn't failing to know the future; it is buying cognitive painkillers that promise to abolish it: the 'magic platform' inside the enterprise, Taylorism echoing straight into Soviet five-year plans, photocopied fad diets, or the frantic hunt for a 'magic school' to shield one's kids from a volatile world.

In CPS architecture, owning uncertainty reorders both learning and strategy. Recuenco traces our clumsiness back to grade school, where anything irregular is dismissed—painting the Baroque as mere decorative excess—and years of youth are traded memorizing syllabi for civil-service entrance exams in exchange for illusory job security, with zero coursework in lateral thinking or uncertainty management. Mastering this terrain means stopping payments on fake certainty, accepting that complex environments are the baseline, and crafting resilient decisions that factor luck in rather than pretending it doesn't exist.
keyInsights: Uncertainty isn't a temporary glitch waiting for better software or a tighter strategic plan; it is the baseline operating condition of complex systems.
The historical triumph of Taylor, Gantt, and central planning owed nothing to logical rigor and everything to answering the human prayer to feel that the world is predictable and controllable.
Misunderstood technology—the 'magic platform'—is rarely bought to amplify a thought-through strategy; it is bought as an esoteric talisman to outsource the anxiety of deciding.
CPS does not try to conquer chance; it measures how much luck weighs in every outcome so you neither confuse a lucky break with personal genius nor freeze when the wind shifts.

threadExamples.title: From Taylor and Gantt to Soviet five-year plans
threadExamples.detail: Recuenco links the craze for Frederick Taylor's scientific management to Soviet five-year planning and modern workforce segmentation: every one of them sold the exact same irresistible promise of taming uncertainty in 'scientific' robes, despite glaring factual cracks.

threadExamples.title: The 'magic school,' schoolhouse Baroque, and civil-service exams
threadExamples.detail: While reviewing the Baroque period with his daughter for school, Javier spots the Enlightenment's lingering bias against the irregular and complex. That same aversion explains why parents chase a 'magic school' as armor for life, or why people burn years memorizing instantly searchable facts for the illusion of safety in civil-service exams.

quote.text: There is always money for uncertainty reducers—whether prophets, shamans, fortune-tellers, palm readers, or strategy consultants.
quote.sourceTitle: Bullshit Taylorism

reflectionQuestions: What tool, consultancy, or methodology did you bring in recently more to calm executive-committee anxiety than to multiply an actual strategy?
In your last big professional win, have you honestly separated how much came from your own analysis and how much was a passing wink from Lady Luck?
Which critical decisions are you stalling on today while waiting for absolute certainty that the context will never hand you?

niebla-de-guerra.short: The built-in haze around any complex problem: visibility is poor, you move with caution, and you still have to act.
niebla-de-guerra.analogy: Driving down a mountain road in pea-soup fog: you don't kill the engine—you ease off the gas, sharpen your senses, and read each curve as it appears.
niebla-de-guerra.howToApply: Assume reports arrive late and incomplete; design short cycles of field probing and direct verification on the ground.
niebla-de-guerra.antiPattern: Making irreversible bets on a single outdated map as if you had crystal-clear satellite visibility over the whole battlefield.
paragraphs: Recuenco takes the term from Clausewitz and reminds us that fog isn't an anomaly—it is part of war. His nerd translation is the mist in Silent Hill, which cuts sightlines to a few yards and turns a simple walk into unrelenting tension. Under his corollary to the Roca Salvatella Theorem, tackling a discipline more complex than your skillset drops you into a fog that won't stop you from acting, but sharply shrinks your odds of succeeding.

deepDive.thesis: The fog isn't a quirk of the terrain—it is complexity's native habitat: it shrinks visibility to a few feet and forces you to move without clean maps.
essay: Recuenco starts from Carl von Clausewitz's classic fog of war—fog is part of war itself—and translates it into his nerd lexicon through the mist of Silent Hill. What makes that metaphor razor-sharp is that in the original video game, the fog began as a technical hack to hide the console's hardware limits, yet ended up becoming the central character that chokes visibility to a few paces and traps the player in constant tension. That is precisely how real-world complexity operates: you never get to see the whole map before you move.

The grand illusion Javier tears apart is the Popperian arrogance of demanding mathematical precision from human disciplines. Drawing on a TEDxMálaga talk about medicine as an inexact science, he notes that outside narrow corners of pure math, almost no science runs like deterministic clockwork. Better yet, the fog isn't uniform for everyone: under his corollary to the Roca Salvatella Theorem, whenever you confront a problem of complexity n with a skill level below n, the mist thickens—it won't stop you from pulling levers, but it craters your probability of getting them right.

In CPS architecture, accepting the fog of war marks the border between the neat Lutheran world of rigid procedures and what Recuenco calls 'Hispanic CPS.' Once the terrain closes in like Silent Hill, textbook 'spherical cows' stop working; soft sciences, acute reading of the room, and the nerve to advance without panic or paralysis take command. Mastering the fog means respecting the inherent inexactness of human systems, honestly gauging the thickness of your own ignorance, and taking short, clear-eyed steps.
keyInsights: The fog of war has two sources: the irreducible uncertainty of a complex system, plus the extra haze created by any gap between the challenge's complexity and your actual competence.
Poor visibility doesn't physically stop you from acting—and therein lies the trap: you can charge briskly through the mist mistaking motion for progress while torching your odds of success.
Sneering at the 'soft sciences' for not being 100% Popperian misses the point that those are the very disciplines governing messy human reality, where 'spherical cows' don't exist.
Where procedural predictability ends and fog swallows everything, the edge shifts to whoever can improvise with strategic judgment and read subtle cues rather than waiting for clean orders.

threadExamples.title: The mist of Silent Hill and James Sunderland
threadExamples.detail: What started as a rendering workaround to disguise weak console horsepower became the franchise's narrative signature: a thick fog forcing extreme caution that, in Silent Hill 2, also mirrors the mental barriers and buried truths the protagonist only uncovers by walking straight into town.

threadExamples.title: Medicine at TEDxMálaga and phages against superbugs
threadExamples.detail: Sparked by a conversation with Dr. Sari Arponen on medicine's inexactness and the true story of the San Diego researcher who saved her husband from a superbug using bacteriophages (The Perfect Predator), Recuenco holds up medical practice as the primordial example of CPS operating inside the fog.

quote.text: When confronting a discipline of complexity degree n with a qualification lower than n, there is a fog zone of varying thickness that does not prevent action, yet minimizes the chance of success.
quote.sourceTitle: On the inexactness of medicine and scientific complexities at TEDxMálaga

reflectionQuestions: In which high-stakes problem at work are you projecting total confidence when the thickness of your fog actually signals that your capability lags behind the challenge?
Are you demanding hard-science guarantees and spotless metrics in a purely human domain where only prudent judgment under incomplete information applies?
When visibility drops to ten feet, do you freeze waiting for the definitive deck, or step forward carefully while scanning the periphery?

procesos-de-alta-variabilidad.short: Processes with extreme granularity and context sensitivity—almost always involving humans—that refuse to fit inside a standard operating procedure.
procesos-de-alta-variabilidad.analogy: Treating a complex patient or closing a consultative sale versus bottling soda: each case shifts so wildly that a rigid script wrecks it.
procesos-de-alta-variabilidad.howToApply: Stop standardizing work that requires contextual human judgment; equip people with clear principles, real autonomy, and sharp tools.
procesos-de-alta-variabilidad.antiPattern: Shoving processes that demand empathy, nuance, and case-by-case adaptation into a scripted call center.
paragraphs: Processes involving human interaction are almost always HVPs, because humans are the quintessential complex system. Forcing them into a procedural platform—like stuffing a brand-customer relationship into a rigid CRM—is hammering a round peg into a square hole, and in customer service it breeds 'Golem processes.' Recuenco argues that choosing between context sensitivity and scale is a false dichotomy, and that designing HVPs well calls for Personotecnia and a tightly orchestrated team. His go-to examples: incentives and cultural change.

deepDive.thesis: When a process involves people and extreme context sensitivity, trying to cage it in industrial templates or rigid statutes doesn't tame it—it breaks it and spawns monsters.
essay: Inspired by conversations with Sylvia Díaz-Montenegro, Recuenco borrows the idea of variability from the factory floor only to flip it on its head in human territory. On an assembly line or inside franchises like McDonald's and Starbucks, variation is a quality defect to be stamped out so you can replicate and scale. High-variability processes (HVPs), by contrast, handle interactions of extreme granularity where enumerating every edge case in advance is impossible; that is why classical procedural modeling like BPMN buckles the moment it hits the ground.

The most common blunder is treating any contentious or strategic issue as a rule-writing exercise. Recuenco observes—echoing how Wittgenstein dissolved grand philosophical battles into semantic muddles—that blistering debates like abortion, justice, or surrogacy are fundamentally HVPs: processes so intimately bound to context that no blanket law full of carve-outs can resolve them cleanly. Worse still, when lawmakers legislate from ideology or managers impose static five-year-plan incentives, unintended side effects erupt and the opposing camp immediately games the system.

In the machinery of CPS, HVPs form an inseparable triangle with Personotecnia and dynamic incentive architectures. Nearly every HVP is one because it touches humans—the original complex system—with shifting motives and a colossal iceberg of implicit incentives lurking beneath the explicit ones. Mastering HVPs means walking away from the false choice between contextualizing and scaling, ditching universal templates, picking the right tool for the screw in front of you, and building living systems able to absorb human granularity without choking it.
keyInsights: In manufacturing, variability is the enemy of scale; in human processes, variability is the raw material—crushing it under rigid procedures destroys the value of the process.
Many social and corporate standoffs that look unsolvable are actually high-variability processes mishandled with blanket rules, rigid laws, or cookie-cutter frameworks.
Incentive architectures fail whenever they are built statically: assuming every professional chases the same carrot under all conditions ignores the deeply personal nature of HVPs.
Explicit incentives are merely the tip of the iceberg; underneath operates a massive hidden layer of implicit incentives that frequently rewards talking about problems rather than solving them.

threadExamples.title: Legislating abortion, justice, or surrogacy
threadExamples.detail: Riffing on post-Roe v. Wade shifts discussed on the podcast Nada Que Ganar, Recuenco explains why drafting a universally satisfying abortion statute is impossible: beyond acting as a polarizing Rorschach test, it tries to cram a radically contextual process into a blanket rule that gets hacked immediately by the opposing ideology.

threadExamples.title: White-collar incentives vs. McDonald's standardization
threadExamples.detail: Contrasting the repeatable consistency that lets McDonald's or Starbucks scale globally, Javier shows why static bonus plans in tech and knowledge companies (citing cases like Netflix, Facebook, Zynga, and Mattel) misfire unless engineered as dynamic architectures grounded in Personotecnia.

quote.text: High-variability processes (HVPs) are a subset of processes dealing with critical areas of maximum granularity where a basic procedural approach is both unsatisfactory and incomplete.
quote.sourceTitle: High-variability processes

reflectionQuestions: Which critical customer or employee interaction are you forcing through a rigid CRM workflow or step-by-step script when its outcome hinges on case-by-case nuance?
Does your incentive plan assume everyone on the team chases the same reward, or does it account for how real motivations shift across profiles and life stages?
If you pass a strict blanket policy tomorrow to settle a messy debate in your organization, through which predictable loophole will the losing side game it?

aporia.short: A dead end in reasoning: equally solid arguments pull both ways and no clear answer emerges.
aporia.analogy: Two equally accurate maps pointing in opposite directions at the same fork in the road: arguing harder over the maps won't settle the contradiction.
aporia.howToApply: When a debate deadlocks with strong arguments on both sides, step up a level of analysis or run a small real-world probe.
aporia.antiPattern: Trapping yourself in endless meetings waiting for the killer logical argument that will finally convince everyone.
paragraphs: From the Greek for 'no way through.' Recuenco makes peace with it via Cynefin's confused domain, where you don't even know what kind of problem you are looking at yet. In sensemaking, it is that moment when nothing lines up and there is no fresh data left to cross-check. Traditional consulting papers over those cracks with clichés. CPS works them the way kintsugi works broken pottery—and that, to him, is where the art of the craft lives.

deepDive.thesis: Aporia isn't a flaw in reasoning to plaster over with platitudes; it is the threshold where linear logic runs out and the art begins.
essay: Coming from the Greek 'ἀπορία' ('no passage' or 'no way out'), the term names those crossroads where equally compelling arguments pull in opposite directions without yielding a clean verdict. Recuenco traces its lineage from Socratic irony in Plato's dialogues—built to puncture false certainties—through Zeno of Elea's paradoxes like Achilles and the tortoise and Aristotle's Metaphysics, all the way into contemporary complexity thinking via Dave Snowden and the aporetic/confused domain in the Cynefin framework.

What makes Javier's take especially sharp is his candid intellectual U-turn. He openly admits his visceral disdain for how postmodernism has been weaponized, for idealists, and especially for Jacques Derrida. Yet after reconciling with aporia through Cynefin, he grants Derrida a fair-minded concession: far from being a parlor riddle, aporia is an intrinsic condition of thought and language that exposes internal contradictions inside ideas we pretend are rock-solid—like justice, hospitality, or how we relate to the Other.

In CPS architecture, aporetic disorder is the moment of peak strategic clarity: the instant when you don't yet know which domain you are in or how cause and effect connect. Anyone who can't stomach that void bolts straight for their pet playbook, slapping simple-problem tactics onto a complex tangle. Anyone who learns to sit inside aporia checks the urge for premature closure, inspects the fractured assumptions holding up the contradiction, and treats irreducible uncertainty not as an embarrassing flaw, but as creative raw material.
