quote.text: Warning to startups: if you're genuinely trying to reach a blue ocean, you're going to have to go through the early-adopter phase first. Burning 40% of your VC money on Facebook just means you want to get to the cash ASAP, but you can't always take shortcuts.
quote.sourceTitle: Managing self-segmentation

reflectionQuestions: Are you spending cash and energy matching the feature checklists of much larger rivals in a red ocean instead of stripping away barriers that keep non-consumers out?
If you sell a complex or unconventional offering, are you designing self-segmentation paths for early adopters, or trying to force the mass market with ad spend?
Which essential part of your offering are you amputating just to squeeze it quickly into a mass-market pitch?

sidestepping.short: Slipping a head-on collision with a lateral step that leaves your opponent off-balance and opens space of your own.
sidestepping.analogy: A judoka or matador who never meets brute force head-on: one clean sidestep lets the giant's own momentum carry it right past you.
sidestepping.howToApply: When a competitor outguns you in muscle or budget, find the asymmetric angle where their sheer size becomes a liability, and refuse to fight on their turf.
sidestepping.antiPattern: Digging into a frontal war of attrition against someone ten times your size purely out of pride.
paragraphs: Recuenco picked up the concept from Tekken 3, where a fighter who isn't the strongest wins by sidestepping and leaving the enemy's flank wide open. His textbook business case is the Wii: rather than trading horsepower blows with PS3 and Xbox 360, Nintendo bet on motion controls and a brand-new audience. Slipping a punch forces you to rebalance weight and coordinate the entire organization—and he describes his own CPS practice as a sidestep around traditional consulting firms.

deepDive.thesis: Slipping a frontal blow isn't an improvised parlor trick—it's a coordinated shift in your center of gravity that realigns the whole organization to expose your rival's flank.
essay: Javier G. Recuenco imports sidestepping from fighting games—specifically Marshall Law in Tekken 3, a lighter, technically demanding fighter who wins by stepping off-line to leave an opponent exposed on the flank—and translates it into the biomechanics of slipping a punch. When you lean your torso or step laterally, your center of gravity leaves its original axis and your neuromuscular system has to redistribute weight instantaneously so you don't topple. In business, sidestepping radically reframes the angle you compete from whenever squaring up against a giant would send you straight to the canvas.

The deadliest mistake is picturing sidestepping as a clever product gimmick that leaves the rest of the company untouched. Recuenco demolishes that illusion through console generations: after the GameCube flop, Nintendo didn't win with the Wii just by inventing a wand—it nailed nearly every leg of the table in concert: hardware, first- and third-party games, IP, marketing, finance, timing, and Factor X. Furthermore, the boxing analogy has a clear limit: in business, you never finish the slip in the exact stance you started in, because power balances and decision mechanics shift permanently.

Inside the Complex Problem Solving architecture, sidestepping demands two systemic capacities: a sensor chain akin to bodily proprioception and a pre-aligned organization ready to shift weight together. It takes only one key leg—tech, brand, finance, or staff—hesitating for a split second to leave you parked right under the knockout punch or tripping flat on the mat. Recuenco views his own CPS practice as a sidestep around legacy consultancies; anyone who masters this move learns to play Calvinball while still small, shifting their entire structure in harmony before impact lands.
keyInsights: Without a proper sensor chain (proprioception) and coordinated weight redistribution, trying to sidestep leaves you eating the punch or stumbling helplessly to the floor.
A successful corporate sidestep never returns the organization to its starting stance: it inevitably reshapes internal power, priorities, and decision mechanics.
For a lateral step to land, every critical leg—product, marketing, finance, timing, and Factor X—has to move together; if even one hesitates, the maneuver fails.
When you're smaller than your rivals, mimicking their arms race guarantees defeat; sidestepping shifts the axis of combat to expose their flank.

threadExamples.title: Marshall Law in Tekken 3 and the biomechanics of slipping a punch
threadExamples.detail: Recuenco discovered the idea watching his girlfriend's little brother dominate Tekken 3 with a technically demanding character who won on evasion, then rounded it out by studying how the human body shifts its center of gravity to slip a jab without losing balance.

threadExamples.title: Nintendo after GameCube: 21.7 million units vs. PS2's 155 million
threadExamples.detail: Lacking Sony's consumer-electronics scale and Microsoft's war chest to eat software losses, Nintendo dodged the horsepower war with the Wii and executed an end-to-end sidestep rooted in its innovative streak from the NES to the DS touchscreen.

quote.text: You cannot sidestep without a proper sensor chain (proprioception), weight readjustment, and realignment. The alternative is either failing to slip the haymaker or tripping and hitting the floor defenseless.
quote.sourceTitle: Corporate sidestepping: sensors, weight shifts, and coordination to slip the punch

reflectionQuestions: If your company had to take a lateral step tomorrow against a far larger rival, which departments—finance, tech, brand, or middle management—would hesitate and leave you under the punch?
What real sensors do you have wired into the business to spot an incoming punch early, instead of reacting after it has already connected?
Are you trying to change your company's competitive axis without touching the internal power seats and decision rules that propped up the old model?

zugzwang.short: A chess position where every legal move worsens your situation—yet the rules force you to move.
zugzwang.analogy: A moment on the chessboard where you'd give anything to pass your turn and touch nothing, because moving any piece makes things worse.
zugzwang.howToApply: When you see a problem sliding toward zugzwang, move before you run out of squares—or change the rules of the board itself.
zugzwang.antiPattern: Freezing in place hoping your rival blunders miraculously while your few decent options vanish one by one.
paragraphs: Recuenco applies it to sports: the coach forced to move on from the veteran squad that brought him glory without getting lynched by the fanbase. His core thesis is that there is no such thing as corporate zugzwang if you apply CPS properly—even with your back against the wall or in bankruptcy protection, there are always moves in the right direction.

deepDive.thesis: Unlike chess, true zugzwang never exists in a company if you deploy CPS: paralysis almost always stems from emotional attachment or agency problems.
essay: Zugzwang—from the German for move and compulsion—names that cruel chess predicament where every legal move weakens your position, yet the rules forbid passing. Javier G. Recuenco illustrates its classic form in elite sports, answering whether the legend of the Gasol brothers boxed in coach Sergio Scariolo: the near-impossible dilemma of retiring the heroes who won you everything without having fans, press, and locker room at your throat—the same bind faced by Vicente del Bosque or Zinedine Zidane. Yet the moment he crosses into the corporate arena, Recuenco fires back with his sharpest counter-thesis.

In business, true zugzwang does not exist when Complex Problem Solving is wielded well—not even with a company pinned to the ropes or in insolvency proceedings. The mirage of a locked board appears when executives silently accept the narrow rules of a sixty-four-square box and mistake emotional or reputational pain for a lack of exits. Behind that fake helplessness usually lurk two pathologies: paralyzing sentimentality that blocks conscious calls, and agency problems that tempt managers into leaving hidden "serpent's eggs" for the next person in charge.

Woven into the CPS framework, debunking the zugzwang myth forces you to attack a crisis across all four flanks simultaneously—complexity, Factor X, technology, and strategy—rather than boxing yourself into one variable. Linked to Hilbert's Hotel and Norma Desmond's denial in Sunset Boulevard, it reminds us that value propositions expire as a law of life, and refusing to manage the handoff turns a painful but healthy transition into an avoidable demolition. Whoever masters this clarity swaps fatalism for deliberate, clear-eyed choices—unsentimental when required, yet always aimed at opening fresh moves.
keyInsights: There is no corporate zugzwang if you use CPS properly: even in insolvency, there are always moves available in the right direction.
What many executives call "having no options" is usually cowardice before the political cost of retiring past glories—or an agency problem planting ticking serpent's eggs.
Unlike chess's rigid board, CPS breaks the deadlock by acting simultaneously across all four flanks: complexity, Factor X, technology, and strategy.
Accepting the expiration of cycles and leadership eras is a conscious choice: between pragmatic cool-headedness and emotional paralysis, sentimentality always costs far more.

threadExamples.title: Scariolo with the Gasols, Zidane, Del Bosque, and Florentino vs. Bartomeu
threadExamples.detail: Recuenco examines the dilemma of moving on from champions—from Spain's national basketball team to Messi—contrasting Florentino Pérez's learned, deliberate unsentimentality with Josep Maria Bartomeu's emotional management as proof that supposed zugzwang is actually a choice.

threadExamples.title: Norma Desmond in Sunset Boulevard and hidden "serpent's eggs"
threadExamples.detail: The thread ties corporate deadlocks to two opposite yet equally lethal vices: managers who leave buried time bombs rather than make unpopular calls, and companies that—like Norma Desmond—insist they still have plenty left in the tank long after their era has ended.

quote.text: There is no corporate Zugzwang if you use CPS properly. Even if your company is pinned completely against the wall, in bankruptcy protection, in the most dramatic straits... there are always moves to make in the right direction.
quote.sourceTitle: How a classic Zugzwang plays out in sporting triumphs

reflectionQuestions: In which critical business call are you claiming "there's no good way out" when you are really just dodging the emotional or political cost of retiring a past glory?
What "serpent's eggs" is your leadership team leaving un-defused out of fear of upsetting shareholders, veterans, or legacy clients today?
If you stopped staring at your current deadlock from a single financial or political angle and opened all four CPS flanks, what new move would appear off the current board?

arquitectura-de-incentivos.short: The web of explicit and implicit rewards and penalties that shapes what people in an organization actually do.
arquitectura-de-incentivos.analogy: The real slope of a room's floor: no matter which way you paint arrows on the walls, marbles will always roll downhill.
arquitectura-de-incentivos.howToApply: Before demanding a culture shift with an inspiring speech, audit what actually gets rewarded in bonuses, promotions, and Monday-morning pats on the back.
arquitectura-de-incentivos.antiPattern: Expecting cross-functional collaboration while grading and paying people strictly on individual silo targets.
paragraphs: According to Recuenco, an incentive architecture exists for one purpose only: to modify the behavior of an individual or a group. Economic behaviors that look absurd from the outside suddenly make total sense once you uncover the incentives underneath. He devoted an entire trilogy to the subject, warning that designing corporate incentives is "like climbing Everest without oxygen," because it entangles organizational complexity with the complexity of human motivation.

deepDive.thesis: Designing incentives isn't handing out bonuses—it's behavioral-modification engineering under organizational complexity, every bit as unforgiving as climbing Everest without oxygen.
essay: In the trilogy he devotes to the topic, Recuenco starts by stripping away all romanticism: an incentive architecture exists to modify the behavior of an individual or a collective. Nothing more, nothing less. The catch is that this intervention cuts across two tangled systems at once: corporate complexity—bloated by mergers, regulation, bureaucracy, and silos—and human motivation. That is why shaving 15% off a production line's cycle time goes nowhere if it collides with entrenched habits or family routines without attaching a concrete incentive, such as targeted financing or conditional support, backed by tight supervision.

Recuenco dismantles two widespread illusions: believing that political or executive willpower can bend explicit incentives, and treating incentive systems as static reward tables. Analyzing the demographic collapse of the West, he points out that no government can reverse with speeches a set of material rules that reward comfort and penalize having children. The exact same thing happens inside companies under the McNamara fallacy: lazy effort is thrown at a problem that demands real behavioral psychology—from applied analysis to BJ Fogg's Behavior Model, where motivation, ability, and prompts must converge at the exact same moment.

Within the CPS framework, incentive architecture acts as the gearbox linking operational diagnosis to effective execution. You don't need NASA tech or "laser tools" for a process problem to become complex—it's enough that humans with their own habits and agendas are involved. Once a practitioner masters this architecture—combining operational mapping, Factor X dynamics, and behavioral mechanics—they stop drafting flawless plans on paper and start redesigning the terrain so the desired behaviors emerge sustainably, steering clear of the cobra effect and metastatic entropy.
keyInsights: The sole purpose of an incentive architecture is to modify specific behaviors; if an operational change disrupts habits without an attached incentive and close supervision, it will fail even if it saves 15% of production time.

Designing corporate incentives is like "climbing Everest without oxygen" because it merges organizational complexity with human psychology—yet it usually gets the laziest effort in the entire company.
Real behavioral change requires motivation, ability, and a prompt to align simultaneously, as framed in BJ Fogg's Behavior Model, which Recuenco integrates into his practice.
Ideological slogans and executive decrees have minimal leverage against clear incentives laid out on the table: macro trends like demographics are outcomes, not isolated root causes.

threadExamples.title: The 15% improvement stalled by habits and BJ Fogg's model
threadExamples.detail: In the third installment of his trilogy, Recuenco explains that optimizing production time by 15% hits a brick wall if it forces people to upend family dynamics and personal routines; without linked incentives (financing, grants, or direct support), tight oversight, and aligning motivation, ability, and prompts per BJ Fogg's FBM, the initiative is simply ignored.

threadExamples.title: Demographic collapse in the West and Spain vs. political rhetoric
threadExamples.detail: To show how powerless speeches are against clear incentives, he cites Europe's demographic plunge—calling Spain the "seventh circle of hell"—and the Hispanicization of the United States: rising material comfort and perverse incentives drive unstoppable outcomes that no president can talk away with press conferences.

quote.text: A president or a government has very limited room to maneuver against clear incentives sitting right on the table.
quote.sourceTitle: If you're ideologically driven, you don't have to suffer like I do—feel free to unfollow me

reflectionQuestions: Which part of your latest improvement initiative asks the team to change uncomfortable habits without offering a real incentive or a clear prompt?
If you view your organization's most absurd behaviors as rational responses, what invisible rewards and penalties are manufacturing them today?
Are you trying to fix with sermons and town halls a behavior that is actually being bankrolled by a badly designed metric?

decision-makers.short: The people who actually call the shots in a company, regardless of whether their official title says so.
decision-makers.analogy: The person who actually holds the car keys, even if they're sitting in the back seat in the company photo.
decision-makers.howToApply: Map who holds real veto power, who controls the budget, and who truly sways the call before you ever pitch a proposal.
decision-makers.antiPattern: Spending months winning over an enthusiastic middle manager who has zero authority to sign checks or move the real decision makers.
paragraphs: Recuenco insists that CPS is a discipline for CEOs and decision makers: you can't practice it from the shadows—you have to be aligned with whoever decides and backed by the necessary resources. Sometimes the doorway opens through middle management, who have a sharper read on the company's pulse. One of his signature diagnoses is the chasm between decision makers and technologists, which stalls real transformation.

deepDive.thesis: CPS only exists at the table of someone who can make painful trade-offs and put skin in the game; outside the decision maker's orbit, all you're doing is handing out irrelevant advice.
essay: Recuenco repeats until he's hoarse an uncomfortable truth: Complex Problem Solving is a discipline for CEOs and decision makers. The fulcrum of the lever sits with whoever holds the authority to make painful trade-offs, allocate resources, and put skin in the game. When a CPSer sits across from a board of directors or a family ownership group, they are never just debating the saveur du jour—today, artificial intelligence—but the existential future of the business and a silent mountain nobody in the room names aloud: the private agendas of each board member making the call.

Two common fantasies get dismantled in his threads. The first is the clandestine romance of skunkworks: the idea of "being your company's secret CPSer without anyone knowing." Without alignment with decision makers and real resources, that internal guerrilla warfare is sterile. The second is the illusion that technology transforms companies on its own. Tracing the birth of @unconvcps, Recuenco highlights the yawning chasm between technologists and decision makers: far too many digital transformation projects try to stick a limpet onto a rock with Super Glue or a Post-it instead of building real contextual adhesion.

In the CPS architecture, identifying the true decision maker and mapping their meta-incentives is a boss-level challenge—"80s Spanish video game, final boss, and Silent Hill-style fog wrapped in a hellish burrito." Anyone who masters this layer stops being an outside advisor dispensing risk-free tips—"Popeye advice"—and starts holding crucial boardroom conversations while building liminal bridges between tech and business. Only when the decision maker embraces uncertainty and ties their own fate to the transformation does CPS leave the whiteboard and become real leverage where Taylorism has already lost its footing.
keyInsights: You cannot practice CPS in stealth skunkworks mode: it requires explicit alignment with decision makers, sufficient resources, and willingness to make hard choices and give things up.
Every boardroom holds three things at once: today's tech fad (the saveur du jour), the underlying question of the company's future, and the invisible elephant of each member's private agenda.
Digital transformation routinely fails because of the cognitive abyss between technologists and decision makers: without a contextual bridge linking both worlds, technology delivers zero real impact.
A CPS practitioner does not sell sterile, risk-free recommendations; without skin in the game in the boardroom conversation, you're just handing out cheap "Popeye advice."

threadExamples.title: The limpet metaphor and the birth of @unconvcps
threadExamples.detail: Recuenco compares capitalizing on technology to a limpet in a nutrient-rich sea: to feed, it has to grip the rock with muscle, natural adhesive mucus, and contextual fit. @unconvcps was created specifically to serve as that adhesive between technologists and decision makers—versus digital transformation slapped on with Super Glue, Band-Aids, or Post-its.

threadExamples.title: Talking to the board: Silent Hill fog and Popeye advice
threadExamples.detail: Describing the task of mapping meta-incentives inside a boardroom, he likens it to an impossible level of "80s Spanish video game, final boss, and Silent Hill-style fog wrapped in a hellish burrito," concluding that without skin in the game and crucial conversations, a would-be CPSer ends up dispensing useless Popeye advice.

quote.text: You have to make hard decisions. You have to give things up. You have to put skin in the game. The fulcrum of the lever sits with the decision maker.
quote.sourceTitle: Meta-incentives and corporate decisions (on how to talk to the board)

reflectionQuestions: In your current initiative, are you talking to the person who can actually make painful trade-offs and commit resources, or to an intermediary with no decision power?
What unmentionable private agendas are steering your executive committee's decisions beneath the disguise of the latest tech trend?
Are you building a real bridge between technologists and the business, or sticking shiny new tools onto untouched structures with a Post-it?

falacia-de-mcnamara.short: Making decisions based solely on what is easy to measure and assuming that whatever doesn't fit in the metric doesn't exist or doesn't matter.
falacia-de-mcnamara.analogy: Judging the health of a marriage strictly by counting how many WhatsApp messages a couple sends each day because affection doesn't fit in a spreadsheet.
falacia-de-mcnamara.howToApply: Pair hard metrics with direct qualitative observation on the ground; always ask: "What is vital here that we are NOT measuring?"
falacia-de-mcnamara.antiPattern: Managing strictly by dashboards and optimizing easy-to-track indicators while what truly matters rots underneath.
paragraphs: Coined by Daniel Yankelovich after Robert McNamara's handling of the Vietnam War: counting enemy casualties was easy, while measuring political will and cultural context was hard—so the decisive factor was ignored.

In the corporate world it shows up every day disguised as spotless dashboards: green KPIs across the board while the company bleeds out through broken culture, lost customer trust, or an expiring value proposition.
falacia-de-mcnamara.origin: Daniel Yankelovich (1972), frequently cited in Recuenco's long-form threads (turras) on metrics, Excel, and Lutheran corporate culture.

deepDive.thesis: Measuring only what is easy and discarding the unquantifiable turns executive dashboards into factories of strategic blindness and corporate self-deception.
essay: When Recuenco dissects the Corporate Game—the real playbook for climbing the greasy pole of corporate life—he places the McNamara fallacy as one of its twin pillars alongside the absence of skin in the game. The trap looks deceptively rational: faced with a complex system, a decision maker clings to easily quantifiable variables because they radiate rigor and objectivity, while dismissing qualitative factors that carry far more weight. As Recuenco says until he's blue in the face in his threads, eighty percent of the data that actually matters isn't in any dashboard and never will be.

The crucial nuance in this turra is that the fallacy doesn't stem from stupidity, but from quantitative arrogance fused with short-termism. In Vietnam, the Pentagon reduced a political and cultural conflict to arithmetic subtraction—enemy body counts versus friendly losses; inside large corporations, that same mindset produces pristine scorecards that mask steady business erosion. Shrinking success down to a clean metric—like being number one or number two in market share at any cost—encourages executives to defer strategic investments and despise anything that doesn't yet fit in a spreadsheet.

In the CPS universe, spotting the McNamara fallacy separates people navigating a bureaucratic map from those reading the living territory. Anyone who escapes this trap understands that quantitative data is only a partial footprint, never the full reality, and learns to weave in contextual judgment, weak signals, and incentive reading before deciding. By stopping the habit of erasing with a pencil eraser whatever refuses to be measured, leaders break free from the mirage of control, defuse damaging long-term policies, and avoid building lazy incentive architectures that eventually blow up the organization.
keyInsights: Roughly 80% of the relevant data needed for a complex decision is neither available nor ever going to arrive neatly packaged in a quantitative table.
The McNamara fallacy doesn't just cause technical missteps—it pushes decision makers toward short-termism, compounding the structural problems they set out to solve.
In the Corporate Game, easy metrics serve as an objective alibi that lets leaders ignore cultural friction, competitive erosion, and strategic risks that can't be boiled down to a number.
When this fallacy infects corporate incentive design, it breeds lazy frameworks that reward what's measurable while destroying real value.

threadExamples.title: Robert McNamara in Vietnam and the eraser over Lansdale's notes
threadExamples.detail: The bias takes its name from McNamara reducing the Vietnam War to a mathematical model built on estimated enemy body counts; when Edward Lansdale warned him about unquantifiable qualitative factors—guerrilla dynamics and local resistance—McNamara jotted it down in pencil, erased it, and declared that if it couldn't be measured, it couldn't be important.

threadExamples.title: General Electric under Jack Welch and the blindness of simple targets
threadExamples.detail: Recuenco brings the fallacy into business through 1980s GE: the simplistic mandate to be #1 or #2 in every market locked management into short-term quantitative wins that blinded them to long-term potential and left their high-tech investments late and sluggish.

quote.text: This reliance on quantitative data can lead to a flawed decision built on false assumptions and inaccurate figures. I'm blue in the face from saying that 80% of the relevant data simply isn't there and isn't coming.
quote.sourceTitle: The McNamara fallacy: a hazard for decision-making in the Corporate Game

reflectionQuestions: What decisive variable for your business's survival are you ignoring today simply because it doesn't fit on your dashboard?
How many green metrics in your department are hiding eroding customer trust, internal burnout, or medium-term technological lag?
When someone brings an uncomfortable qualitative signal to a meeting, do you investigate it—or erase it because it 'isn't backed by data'?

incentivo-perverso.short: An incentive that pushes people to do the exact opposite of what its designer intended.
incentivo-perverso.analogy: Paying a bounty for every dead cobra to wipe out an infestation, only to discover people have started breeding cobras at home to collect more cash.
incentivo-perverso.howToApply: Before rolling out any bonus or KPI, spend ten minutes playing: "If I wanted to game this rule for easy money, what would I do?"
incentivo-perverso.antiPattern: Acting shocked by employees' "lack of ethics" when they are doing literally what your reward system pays them to do.
paragraphs: Recuenco ties this directly to the cobra effect—the unintended consequences of an incentive. In business he gives concrete examples: rewarding sales reps solely on revenue pushes them to deceive customers, while rewarding speed tanks quality. He warns that every partial fix spawns unforeseen problems and perverse incentives, and points them out in corporate boards too—right alongside snake eggs.

deepDive.thesis: Weak corporate incentive models aren't harmless—they're lethal, unleashing the cobra effect and spreading entropy like a cancer.
essay: In the second installment of his incentives trilogy, Recuenco explains why perverse incentives are almost the norm rather than the exception inside companies. They emerge at the intersection of two corrosive forces: agency problems—where each actor optimizes their own private gain—and the cobra effect, the unintended fallout of any poorly bounded reward. Pay salespeople strictly on top-line revenue and they will fudge contracts or mislead customers; tie bonuses to the quarter and you kill innovation; reward production speed and you shred quality and attention to detail.

Recuenco dismantles two dangerous mirages. The first is trusting our gut instincts about what motivates people—a compass he calls flat-out useless, backed by Dan Ariely ("Predictably Irrational") and Alfie Kohn ("Punished by Rewards"). The second is forcing procedural playbooks onto high-variability processes loaded with emotional nuance, like customer service: far from taming them, they spawn rigid, counterproductive "Golem processes." Worse still, every partial patch breeds fresh side effects while entropy, like a cancer, metastasizes and steadily gets worse.

Within the CPS architecture, understanding perverse incentives forces you to ditch linear rewards and treat the system as a razor-sensitive house of cards. When skin in the game is missing, misproportioned, or aimed at the wrong attitudes, the entire model turns lethal. Practitioners who master this stop blaming employees' "lack of ethics" and audit the rules of the game instead: they model each high-variability process on its own terms, anticipate second-order adaptive responses, and align incentives with the company's real value.
keyInsights: Every temporary patch slapped onto a complex problem tends to trigger unintended consequences, perverse incentives, and the cobra effect—accelerating an entropy that metastasizes unless you fix the underlying architecture.
Our intuition about human motivation fails miserably: simply paying more or rewarding a single metric routinely erodes quality, ethics, and long-term thinking.

Applying rigid procedural controls and blunt incentives to emotionally charged, high-variability human processes—such as customer service—creates "Golem processes" that defeat the very outcome you wanted.
Recuenco sharpens the classic aphorism about models into an executive warning: all models are wrong, weak models are wildly wrong, and weak corporate incentive models are lethal.

threadExamples.title: The cobra-effect triptych: revenue, quarterly bonuses, and speed
threadExamples.detail: Recuenco grounds the corporate cobra effect in three everyday cases: sales incentives tied purely to revenue that push reps to mislead clients and doctor contracts; short-term quarterly bonuses that starve innovation investment; and production-speed bonuses that cause quality to collapse.

threadExamples.title: Golem processes in customer service and the cracks exposed by Ariely and Kohn
threadExamples.detail: Citing Dan Ariely's "Predictably Irrational" and Alfie Kohn's "Punished by Rewards," he points out that trying to govern emotionally volatile, high-variability processes—like customer service—with rigid procedural rules gives birth to "Golem processes" that degrade service instead of elevating it.

quote.text: Incentives belong to an architecture that is usually a house of cards. And to top it off, there is rarely any skin in the game; when there is, it's in the wrong proportions; and when it's there, it rewards the wrong attitudes.
quote.sourceTitle: Continuing the incentives trilogy: impact on corporate dynamics

reflectionQuestions: If someone wanted to game your current bonus system for maximum payout with minimum real effort, how would they inadvertently sabotage the company?
In which high-variability human processes are you enforcing rigid speed or volume metrics that are already creating 'Golem processes'?
What recent patch did you apply to cover up a symptom that is now sprouting fresh cobra effects in another department?

skin-in-the-game.short: Having something of your own on the line in the outcome of what you decide or recommend, so you win or lose alongside it.
skin-in-the-game.analogy: The chef who eats in their own restaurant every night, or the engineer who walks across the bridge they just designed.
skin-in-the-game.howToApply: Distrust advice from anyone who bears zero pain if it goes wrong, and structure deals where everyone shares both risk and upside.
skin-in-the-game.antiPattern: Listening to bold plans from pundits, consultants, or executives who get paid the exact same whether they nail it or sink the ship.
paragraphs: Recuenco borrows the concept from Nassim Nicholas Taleb and considers it the vaccine against agency problems. That is how Singular Solving operates—through revenue share, equity, or joint ventures, mostly with family-owned businesses. His rule of thumb: distrust decisions where nobody has anything at stake, and walk away from anyone selling you strategy without aligned incentives.
skin-in-the-game.origin: Nassim Nicholas Taleb, "Skin in the Game"

deepDive.thesis: Without something personal riding on the outcome, every strategy decays into an agency problem and every piece of advice follows the path of least resistance.
essay: Taken straight from Nassim Nicholas Taleb, skin in the game is, for Recuenco, the premier vaccine against the cancer of agency problems inside organizations. Its logic is almost hydraulic: water always finds the path of least resistance, and whenever an executive or advisor doesn't absorb the consequences of their calls, their private interests end up overriding the company's. That is why Singular Solving enforces a non-negotiable rule: the top decision maker's stake in the company must be equal to or greater than their stake in themselves.

Far from treating it as a moralistic slogan, Recuenco spells out its practical boundaries and trade-offs. Operating via revenue share, equity, or joint ventures leads them to work mainly with family businesses up to roughly €150 million in turnover—acting almost like venture builders—while closing the door to government agencies and many large corporations that refuse to share risk. He also draws a crisp line between bounded execution and strategy: you can pay by the hour to wallpaper your bedroom or fix a pipe, never to design your competitive future.

In the CPS architecture, skin in the game isn't an exotic billing trick—it's the structural mechanism that builds trust and filters out corporate smoke. Demanding corrected asymmetry transforms the entire nature of an engagement: comfortable slide decks vanish, uncertainty is openly accepted as an essential ingredient, and every proposal passes the acid test of whether its author would put their own neck on the line for it. Once this principle takes hold, strategy stops being a theater of free opinions and becomes a shared commitment to reality.
keyInsights: Skin in the game is the strongest vaccine against agency problems because it removes temptation before appealing to goodwill: water always follows the path of least resistance.
There is a clear hiring boundary: bounded, predictable jobs (like wallpapering a room or plumbing) are paid by the hour; strategy and CPS demand aligned incentives.
Requiring revenue share, equity, or joint-venture structures naturally filters the market toward family businesses and shuts out large corporations and public agencies unwilling to share risk.
Without accepting real uncertainty—and without the top decision maker putting the company's fate ahead of their personal agenda—genuine CPS is impossible.

threadExamples.title: Taleb's trader vs. the banker and the Singular Solving model
threadExamples.detail: Leaning on Nassim Nicholas Taleb's contrast—the trader risks their own neck while the banker operates without putting it on the line—Recuenco details how Singular Solving partners with family-owned firms up to ~€150M through revenue share, equity, or joint ventures, operating much like a venture builder.

threadExamples.title: The spin-off for impossible problems and Gunpei Yokoi's lateral thinking
threadExamples.detail: Because their skin-in-the-game requirement excluded public bodies and big corporates stuck with deadlocked challenges, Recuenco describes launching a separate vehicle for radical solutions, pairing massive problems with Gunpei Yokoi's "lateral thinking with withered technology" rather than chasing Diamandis-style Moonshot leaps.

quote.text: Pay by the hour to wallpaper your bedroom or pay your plumber, but make sure incentives are aligned when you're looking for strategy.
quote.sourceTitle: Snake eggs. Not the literal kind—which is fascinating in its own right—but the metaphorical kind (a latent problem an executive leaves for their successor)

reflectionQuestions: What exactly do the advisors or executives pushing your most expensive strategic bet lose if it blows up two years from now?
In your C-suite, is the real interest in the company's long-term survival greater than or equal to each executive's interest in their own career?
Which critical strategy engagements are you paying for by the hour today—as if they were plumbing—with zero link to actual results?

blitzscaling.short: Hyper-aggressive growth that sacrifices efficiency for speed in order to fatten up a company and flip it as fast as possible.
blitzscaling.analogy: Jumping out of an airplane and stitching the parachute on the way down, betting that burning cash faster than everyone else will leave you alone in the market.
blitzscaling.howToApply: Use it only when a brutal winner-take-all network effect exists and you have the capital lungs to survive the burn.
blitzscaling.antiPattern: Copying the blitzscaling playbook in a traditional business with no network effects, torching margins, culture, and quality with no real moat to show for it.
paragraphs: Reid Hoffman and Chris Yeh coined the term for the aggressive, breakneck scaling of startups. Recuenco talks about the "blitzscaler mindset": exporting private-equity logic to every kind of business—zero commitment to the long term or to the company's soul, just rapid fattening and selling off the shell. There's plenty of money in it, he grants, but no epic and no soul.

deepDive.thesis: The blitzscaler mindset imports the private-equity extraction machine into every business: it speeds up the fattening and the flip of the shell, while ripping out its soul.
essay: Starting from Hermès artistic director Pierre-Alexis Dumas's observation—"speed is the structuring value of the 20th century"—Recuenco examines blitzscaling as coined by Reid Hoffman and Chris Yeh: growing with extreme aggression, sacrificing efficiency and swallowing losses to capture critical mass before anyone else. What makes his diagnosis sharp is tracing the fuel that normalized this behavior: it isn't just startup bravado, it's the spread of the Private Equity gaze across the entire economy, geared toward quickly pumping an asset, squeezing it dry, and flipping the shell at the highest possible multiple.

Recuenco tears apart the survivorship bias that only recites glamorous winners like Airbnb, Uber, LinkedIn, Facebook, or Zoom. Swept under the rug lies a graveyard of multimillion-dollar flameouts where burned capital never bought viability, such as Quibi or Jawbone. Yet the deeper paradox is second-order: funds buy companies precisely because they have soul, and the moment they put them through the rapid-fattening playbook, they extract that very soul. There's tons of money in blitzscaling, Recuenco concedes, but no epic, no long-term commitment, and no lasting meaning.

In CPS's strategic view of the 21st century, this pattern sets up a sharp bifurcation accelerated by AI. Artificial intelligence will send throughput, launch speed, and the median quality of anything replicable and scalable through the roof; for that very reason, it will raise the scarcity—and turn into "human luxury"—everything that resists industrialization: judgment, creative heterodoxy, and lateral thinking. Those who grasp the ceiling of blitzscaling stop racing on hollow speed—"McKinsey decks written on the plane by ChatGPT"—and build offerings with soul, an infinite-game horizon, and an unclonable cognitive edge.
keyInsights: The "blitzscaler mindset" translates Private Equity's extractive logic into everyday operations: prioritizing rapid fattening and flipping the shell over durability and meaning.
Survivorship bias hides the model's corpses: raising massive war chests and running faster than anyone else didn't save high-profile flameouts like Quibi or Jawbone.
A second-order extractive contradiction drives the model: capital buys companies that are valuable precisely because they have soul, then strips it away through mechanical scaling.
As AI commoditizes speed and volume, human lateral thinking and CPS move into the realm of genuine, unscalable "human luxury."

threadExamples.title: The graveyard under the rug: Quibi and Jawbone vs. Uber or Airbnb
threadExamples.detail: Against the usual showcase from Hoffman and Yeh's book (Airbnb, Uber, LinkedIn, Facebook, Zoom), Recuenco drags out blitzscaling's "Hall of Fame" of failures: Quibi, shut down after barely six months despite massive funding in short-form video, and Jawbone, bankrupt after raising huge rounds without holding off larger rivals.

threadExamples.title: Hermès and 'Ford vs. Ferrari': heterodoxy and soul against the Lutheran steamroller
threadExamples.detail: Connecting Pierre-Alexis Dumas's line on speed with the story of "Ford vs. Ferrari," Recuenco notes that Ford only wins back its honor—and earns Enzo Ferrari's respect—when it breaks its own rigid Lutheran playbook and embraces Latin heterodoxy: the exact divide between a brand with epic soul and soulless fattening.

quote.text: The blitzscaler mindset is the transfer of the Private Equity mindset into the wider business world. We're not committed to the long term or the company's purpose—only to squeezing every last drop out via rapid fattening and trying to sell the shell for top dollar.
quote.sourceTitle: The impact of blitzscaling and the future of human luxury

reflectionQuestions: What elements of soul, craft, or customer relationship are you sacrificing today in the name of breakneck growth nobody asked for over the long haul?
If AI matches your production speed and median quality tomorrow, what genuinely human, unscalable edge will still set you apart?
Are you building a company engineered to last for decades, or fattening up a shell to offload onto the next buyer?

consultoria.short: A service that advises companies and defines solutions. Recuenco critiques selling it for problems it isn't built to solve.
consultoria.analogy: Paying someone to read your own watch to tell you the time, hand you a gorgeous PowerPoint, and leave before checking whether you actually catch the train.
consultoria.howToApply: Demand honest diagnosis, capability transfer, and shared risk; hire outside help to think sharper, not to buy political cover.
consultoria.antiPattern: Hiring a marquee firm strictly as career insurance in front of the board ("if it tanks, nobody fires me for hiring this brand").
paragraphs: Recuenco distinguishes professional services, which implement solutions, from consulting, which defines them—and strategy consulting at the top of that stack. He doesn't think consulting is useless: he calls it a "violin" discipline that nails canon projects—problems that have already been solved before. His critique targets miscasting (throwing junior talent at problems that demand deep seniority) and double asymmetry: the client can't judge the expert and often doesn't even know what repertoire to ask for. To paper over that uncertainty, firms sell success stories and justification tokens.

deepDive.thesis: Consulting isn't useless: it's a violin discipline built to nail the canon—ruined by miscasting, double asymmetry, and egos writing checks they can't cash.
essay: Contrary to the caricature that he simply hates consulting, Recuenco offers a far sharper dissection. First he maps the terms: professional services implement and maintain solutions; consulting advises and defines them; strategy consulting does so at the highest level. For decades, these firms have acted as on-demand taps of qualified talent—without locking in fixed headcount—and as reputational insurance for executives hiring prestigious logos. Where they genuinely shine is on canon projects: well-trodden territory where the repertoire already exists and the team knows every note on the score.

His critique aims at two structural pathologies. The first is the double asymmetry of a "violin discipline": anyone can tell a bad violinist within five seconds, yet a client cannot tell whether an AI, Big Data, or Agile consultant is merely two slide decks and ten hours ahead of them—nor do they know what repertoire to request when they just want to sound modern. The second is miscasting: putting bright people into roles that don't fit because their egos write checks their talent can't cash. To soothe the resulting anxiety, firms peddle sugar-coated Success Stories and hygiene-level credential tokens.

Grasping this anatomy draws the exact border where traditional consulting ends and CPS begins. While a consultant sells a packaged solution and pushes to close the deal on the back of past case studies, a CPSer works in unmapped terrain where no prior story guarantees the outcome. That is why commercial outreach in CPS cannot rely on hard-selling: it requires buying time for ideas to sink in and building real trust tokens—a genuine leap of faith earned through demonstrated competence and senior judgment—restoring the deep technical rigor the craft had at its origin with Arthur D. Little.
keyInsights: Consulting nails canon projects—problems solved a hundred times before—but breaks down when miscast into complex, uncharted challenges.
Unlike the violin, where a missed note hits your ear immediately, consulting enjoys double asymmetry: the client can neither evaluate the expert nor specify a clear repertoire.
Success Stories serve a precise psychological role: calming the brain's aversion to uncertainty with spotless tales where everything worked out.
Hard-selling packaged solutions doesn't work in CPS: credentials are mere hygiene tokens, and what actually closes the gap are trust tokens built patiently with senior practitioners.

threadExamples.title: Joe Pesci in 'Thor: Ragnarok' and the theory of miscasting
threadExamples.detail: To prove his critique isn't contempt but role fit, Recuenco cites Joe Pesci: a towering actor who owns "Goodfellas" or "Home Alone," yet would be absurd cast as Thor in "Thor: Ragnarok." That is precisely what happens when methodologies or consulting firms step outside their range and "their egos write checks their talent can't cash."

threadExamples.title: The double asymmetry of the violin vs. Arthur D. Little's origins
threadExamples.detail: Recuenco contrasts modern consulting—where a client can't spot someone running "two slide decks and ten hours ahead" in AI or Big Data—with its 1886 founding by chemical engineer Arthur D. Little, father of unit operations and pioneer of a craft rooted in deep technical mastery.

quote.text: People get me wrong when they think I pick on consulting because I think it's a deeply useless discipline. No—what happens is that it's a 'violin' discipline, like so many others.
quote.sourceTitle: The psychology behind commercial outreach

reflectionQuestions: Is the problem you're about to outsource truly a 'canon project' solved a thousand times before, or are you miscasting traditional consulting into a complex challenge?
When you hire a marquee firm, are you buying genuine problem-solving capability—or a reputational insurance policy to cover yourself in front of the board?
Could you tell today whether the expert pitching you AI or transformation is actually only 'two slide decks and ten hours ahead' of your own team?

huevos-de-serpiente.short: A latent problem a top executive leaves behind for their successor that hatches once they are already out the door.
huevos-de-serpiente.analogy: Sweeping the trash under the rug so the house gleams on showing day, knowing full well it will reek once you no longer live there.
huevos-de-serpiente.howToApply: Audit what technical, cultural, or commercial debt is quietly piling up just to dress up this quarter's numbers.
huevos-de-serpiente.antiPattern: Rewarding short-term results for rotating executives who collect their bonus and jump ship before the problem hatches.
paragraphs: Recuenco pulls the idea from "Lights Out," the chronicle of General Electric's fall: Jack Welch left Jeff Immelt the mess of dismantling GE Capital right into the post-Lehman Brothers era. Variations range from timing the company to hold together just until your retirement to selling off assets to window-dress the books on your way out. At the root there is almost always an agency problem—and the vaccine is skin in the game.

deepDive.thesis: Spotless quarterly earnings often incubate ticking time bombs that an executive bequeaths to their successor so they can cash out today and exit before the blast.
essay: Inspired by "Lights Out," the chronicle of General Electric's collapse, Recuenco coins the term "snake eggs" for latent problems a top executive leaves incubating—consciously or not—to blow up in their successor's face once they've already cashed their chips and walked away. The mechanism feeds on an accounting mirage: people treat corporate performance like a still photograph. Yet quarterly financials lie with ease; a corporation can flaunt dazzling profits and seemingly bulletproof solvency while hurtling full speed toward the end of the road.

Recuenco's sharpest point is that these implosions are rarely caused by an isolated blunder, but by systemic agency problems fused with collective denial—a "Factor X carnival" where nobody wants to point at the elephant in the elevator. When executive incentives pay handsomely for juicing today's number with zero accountability for tomorrow, burying the company's future becomes extraordinarily lucrative. As he reminds readers in his incentives trilogy, these dynamics can't be fixed with a static plan or by "changing the culture" by decree, because culture is an emergent property woven from stories and dynamic incentives.

In CPS practice, hunting snake eggs requires shifting your time horizon and watching the whole movie instead of the quarterly freeze-frame. Anyone who masters this concept audits the gaps between an executive's personal agenda and the firm's intergenerational health, insists on skin in the game as the primary vaccine against moral hazard, and builds dynamic incentive architectures that evolve over time. That breaks the cynical loop where the system itself rewards professionals for diagnosing problems out loud instead of actually solving them.
keyInsights: Corporate performance is never a still photograph: dazzling quarterly numbers can coexist with snake eggs poised to blow the company sky-high right in front of everyone.
The usual root of a snake egg is an agency problem: executives whose private incentives reward them for mortgaging the company's future before heading for the exit.
Major corporate collapses combine warped incentives with collective denial of reality—that blend of cynicism or dissonance that stops anyone from naming the elephant in the elevator.
Defusing these risks demands dynamic incentive architectures and skin in the game, not static plans or naive attempts to 'change the culture' by memo.

threadExamples.title: Jack Welch, Jeff Immelt, and the collapse of General Electric ('Lights Out')
threadExamples.detail: The founding case for the concept: drawing on "Lights Out," Recuenco traces how Jack Welch pocketed fortunes and wrote bestselling books like "Winning" while burying GE's future inside a colossal snake egg that detonated in the hands of his successor, Jeff Immelt.

threadExamples.title: Enron, the dot-com busts, and the 'codfish' of corporate dissonance
threadExamples.detail: As a companion gallery of "nuclear corporate wipeouts," he cites Enron ("The Smartest Guys in the Room") and the nineties dot-com bubble ("F'd Companies")—which he likens to crypto euphoria—summing up corporate denial through an old Mensa joke: holding up a codfish (COD: Cynicism or Dissonance).

quote.text: A company's performance is not a still photograph. Quarterly results deceive. It is entirely possible to watch a company with spectacular earnings and supposedly bulletproof solvency blow up right before your eyes.
quote.sourceTitle: Snake eggs. Not the literal kind—which is fascinating in its own right—but the metaphorical kind (a latent problem an executive leaves for their successor)

reflectionQuestions: Which cuts to maintenance, talent, technical debt, or customer goodwill are dressing up your numbers this year at the cost of a future explosion?
If you personally had to inherit five years from now the exact consequences of the decisions you're approving today, which ones would you kill this week?
In your organization, does the incentive system reward fixing latent problems—or simply talking about them while kicking the can to the next leadership handover?

private-equity.short: Funds that buy companies with heavy debt, strip and optimize them hard, and flip them to maximize the exit.
private-equity.analogy: Remodeling a house with a massive mortgage to slap on a glossy makeover and flip it in five years to the highest bidder.
private-equity.howToApply: When dealing with funds, read their financial clock, exit pressure, and EBITDA obsession so you can tell real value creation apart from financial engineering.
private-equity.antiPattern: Slashing talent, R&D, and maintenance to inflate short-term margins while hollowing out the company's future capacity.
paragraphs: Recuenco distills their classic playbook into eight steps, including loading the business with all the debt its cash flow can carry, selling off non-core assets, bringing in operators paid on target, and clamping down ruthlessly on costs. He argues the industry lives off deal-making and can't survive in the open market, meaning it needs a new incentive architecture and a new value proposition. He dedicated the Post Private Equity arc to this shift.

deepDive.thesis: Private equity assumed it was immune to the obsolescence of its own value proposition; once financial engineering runs out of road, reinventing its incentives is its only way out.
essay: Recuenco compresses the classic Private Equity manual—born in the 1970s and 1980s with KKR's LBOs and Michael Milken's junk bonds—into a tight choreography: load the target with as much debt as its cash flow can bear, sweep excess cash out to shareholders, liquidate non-core assets and outsource aggressively, hire managers on target-linked pay, enforce ironclad cost control, and invest hard to scale the platform. Back when bloated firms just needed cheap money and operational discipline, that machine worked with surgical precision.

The blind spot Recuenco exposes in his Post Private Equity arc is both historical and structural: the industry thought itself exempt from lifecycle laws and the Hilbert's Hotel metaphor, where every value proposition eventually goes stale. Worse, its financial engineering systematically destroys value in businesses built on human subtleties or grassroots communities. Once the cheap-debt party ends—the "The Party is Over" era—funds accumulate "corpses in their portfolios," managed with masked pain and corporate embalming while hindsight prophets recite the obvious after the fact.

From a CPS perspective, the way forward isn't demonizing capital—it's redesigning its incentive architecture and sector value proposition. The Post Private Equity cure shifts value creation away from financial leverage toward genuine operational excellence—maximizing NOPAT and organic growth—while slashing management fees and handing operators real skin in the game on the exit. Anyone who masters this pivot stops speculating with debt and builds living companies with executives styled like "an American waiter at scale," aligned around multiplying the real business.
keyInsights: The classic PE playbook—maxed-out leverage, cash sweeps, asset sales, and iron cost control—worked in the nineties, but its value proposition has drifted into obsolescence.
Private capital obeys the exact same lifecycle as any other industry: ignoring that expiration date has packed portfolios with zombie assets kept upright by financial "embalming."
The traditional manual destroys value in companies whose edge depends on human nuance, living culture, or grassroots communities that cannot survive extractive standardization.
Reinventing Post Private Equity requires cutting management fees and pivoting to organic operational creation with managers holding genuine skin in the game at exit.

threadExamples.title: From KKR and Michael Milken to a Spanish flagship hospital turned profitable in a year
threadExamples.detail: In his financial genealogy, Recuenco links Henry Kravis's LBOs (KKR, 1976) funded with Michael Milken's junk bonds—LBO debt surging 262% between 1980 and 1984 ahead of the 1987 crash—with the effective side of the model: a landmark Spanish hospital that posted a profit in year one after a fund stepped in following a decade of losses.

threadExamples.title: Portfolio embalming and the 'American-waiter-style' executive
threadExamples.detail: Against portfolios stuffed with "corpses digested via embalming," he proposes the Post Private Equity antidote: drastically lower management fees and tie operators to NOPAT and organic growth under the "American waiter at scale" model—living on tips today to walk away with 20–30% once you've built 500 coffee shops.

quote.text: Private Equity, M&As... believed themselves immune to the ailment that hits every company sooner or later: the obsolescence of their own value proposition.
quote.sourceTitle: The shift in value creation from money and operations to value propositions

reflectionQuestions: How much of your business's recent profitability comes from financial engineering or one-off cuts versus genuine organic growth?
If your fee or compensation structure guarantees fat paychecks regardless of how the business performs, what real incentive exists to take risks for operational value creation?
Which parts of your company that carry real soul or rely on human nuance would die if you ran the classic cost-cutting and outsourcing playbook on them?

sindrome-del-coronel-thompson.short: Solving a problem brilliantly and still failing miserably because you ignored the context or showed up at the wrong time.
sindrome-del-coronel-thompson.analogy: Engineering the perfect weapon for a war that ended yesterday: flawless technical execution, zero real-world impact.
sindrome-del-coronel-thompson.howToApply: Alongside technical design, validate market timing, human adoption readiness, and who wins or loses if your solution succeeds.
sindrome-del-coronel-thompson.antiPattern: Falling so deeply in love with the internal elegance of your solution that you forget to check whether the world still needs it.
paragraphs: Named after the colonel who invented the Thompson submachine gun, whose story Recuenco invokes often to drive home that "people are ready when they're ready, and not a minute sooner." You build something that solves the problem cleanly and elegantly—maybe even spawn a whole new industry—and still eat dirt. It happens because every solution only works inside a context: each solution/context pair operates like a key and its lock.

deepDive.thesis: Solving a problem brilliantly in the abstract and flopping in reality isn't bad luck—it's forgetting that solution and context are a single indivisible unit.
essay: One of the most counterintuitive and maddening truths Recuenco hammers into his students is that you can do technically brilliant work, solve a problem cleanly, even pioneer a brand-new industry—and still "eat a turd with chocolate sprinkles." The syndrome honors Colonel John Taliaferro Thompson, inventor of the legendary Tommy Gun. The mechanism behind the tragedy is both cognitive and mathematical: our brains adore context-free heuristics, yet any solution works like the general solution to a differential equation, packed with arbitrary constants that only take shape once boundary conditions are pinned down.

Recuenco blows up naive proverbs like "the early bird catches the worm" or the myth that superior quality sells itself. Expecting people to recognize the obvious is a one-way ticket to disappointment, because "people are ready when they're ready, and not a minute sooner." The syndrome strikes whenever four unforgiving forces are overlooked: timing, the Zone of Proximal Development, agency problems, and Factor X. Besides, "the obvious" is always an ex-post illusion: everything looks self-evident only after you already know the problem, its outcome, and its full context.

This distinction draws a hard line between traditional consulting and CPS. A consultant can walk away proud after delivering an elegant design that charts the unknown; in Complex Problem Solving, if that solution fails on deployment because the full context wasn't captured, CPS has flat-out failed. Internalizing this lesson transforms the practitioner: they stop falling in love with abstract solutions and spend just as much energy mapping the terrain, calibrating timing, and pacing the counterpart's readiness as designing the technical answer.
keyInsights: "People are ready when they're ready, and not a minute sooner": outrunning timing or assuming the market will spot what's obvious leads straight to failure.
A brilliant technical solution is like the general solution of a differential equation: until you pin down the specific constants of the context, it solves nothing in practice.
In CPS there is no alibi along the lines of 'the design was perfect, the client just didn't execute it': if you missed context, ZPD, agency, and Factor X, the project failed.
Obviousness is always an ex-post property: nobody clearly sees in advance what hindsight prophets later declare was inevitable.

threadExamples.title: John Taliaferro Thompson and the paradox of the Tommy Gun
threadExamples.detail: Drawing on the book "Tommy: The Gun That Changed America," Recuenco traces Colonel Thompson's wild saga: he conceived a groundbreaking weapon that brilliantly solved a real problem and birthed an entire category, only to crash headfirst into the unforgiving wall of adoption timing and context.

threadExamples.title: High-school differential equations and the boundary with consulting
threadExamples.detail: To break our brain's addiction to context-free heuristics, Recuenco compares an abstract idea to the general solution of a differential equation: until you determine its particular constants—timing, ZPD, agency, and Factor X—what makes a consultant proud is an "Olympic-grade screw-up" in CPS.

quote.text: Did CPS fail in that case? Yes, because accounting for context is a core part of CPS analysis. What leaves a consultant who likes going above and beyond and navigating the unknown completely satisfied can be an Olympic-grade screw-up in CPS.
quote.sourceTitle: Decoding Colonel Thompson Syndrome: implications and reflections

reflectionQuestions: Is your brilliant solution failing because people 'don't get it'—or because you blew past their Zone of Proximal Development and real timing?
How much time did you spend polishing the technical answer in the abstract versus mapping the particular constants of the context where it has to live?
If deployment failed tomorrow, would you blame the organization's clumsiness—or own up to an incomplete diagnosis of the context?

emulsificador-de-equipo.short: Someone who gets incompatible people to work together, giving meaning and purpose to an otherwise unstable mix.
emulsificador-de-equipo.analogy: Egg yolk in mayonnaise: without it, oil and water naturally repel each other; with it, they bind into a stable, delicious emulsion.
emulsificador-de-equipo.howToApply: When you bring together radically different profiles (hardcore engineers, creatives, business people), assign someone with moral authority and empathy to translate across worlds.
emulsificador-de-equipo.antiPattern: Locking extreme talents in the same room with no translator and no shared purpose, expecting magic to just happen.
paragraphs: Like an emulsifier binding oil and water, their work often goes unnoticed until they are gone: pull them off the board and the mayonnaise splits. They are not a mediator—who merely links opposing sides without necessarily expanding what they can do—but someone who unlocks a new state for the group. Recuenco's go-to example is Andy Fletcher, who, without towering musical virtuosity, held Depeche Mode together.

deepDive.thesis: A complex team is not the sum of its talents; it is an unstable mixture that collapses the moment you expel the invisible agent holding it together.
essay: Recuenco borrows a surgical metaphor from physical chemistry: no matter how hard you shake oil and water, the two liquids separate the instant external energy stops. To stabilize the dispersion, you need a surfactant—an emulsifier—with one hydrophilic end and one lipophilic end capable of linking phases that repel each other. Applied to collective work, a team emulsifier is the person who gets incompatible personalities cooperating under a shared purpose, turning a potentially explosive mix into a coherent operating system whose stability rests on emergent dynamics, never on simply stacking résumés.

Javier dismantles two widespread misconceptions. The first equates the emulsifier with a mediator: whereas a mediator brokers truces and builds bridges between rival factions without necessarily raising their ceiling, the emulsifier lets the group transcend its theoretical capacity by taking on unglamorous work so others can shine at what they do best. The second misconception assumes they have no ego or are expendable; on the contrary, they do have an ego, but keep it under tight control in service of the collective goal. Their tragedy is invisibility: just like pulling Makélélé off the board, you only find out what they were doing the moment the mayonnaise splits.

Within CPS architecture, the emulsifier functions as a true "Anti-Apollo." Against the fantasy of PlayStation teams—where piling up superstars guarantees victory—and against the collapse of the Apollo teams described by Belbin, the emulsifying function enables genuine cognitive orchestration. Once you grasp this, you stop designing teams purely around individual sparkle in performance reviews and start protecting the amphiphilic profiles that sustain internal chemistry. Recognizing that role before you lose it lets an apparently limited group blow past its theoretical ceiling.
keyInsights: A team does not perform as the linear sum of its members: internal dynamics generate emergent properties that can either multiply or annihilate available talent.
The emulsifier is neither a mediator nor an emotional-rational counterweight: they do not settle for preventing clashes, but expand collective performance by sacrificing personal spotlight.
Keeping your ego in check does not mean lacking ego; it means seeing with crystal clarity what role you play on the board and executing it without demanding the limelight.
The emulsifying function usually stays invisible to leadership until the exact instant it is removed and the entire structure falls apart.

threadExamples.title: The Makélélé effect and invisible cohesion in elite sports
threadExamples.detail: Javier cites Claude Makélélé—alongside references like Al Horford or the Pirlo-Gattuso pairing—to illustrate the player who looks replaceable on paper because he doesn't hog flashy stats, yet whose departure breaks the side's balance and "splits the mayonnaise."

threadExamples.title: Andy Fletcher in Depeche Mode vs. PlayStation teams
threadExamples.detail: Without being the band's musical virtuoso, Fletcher acted for decades as a surfactant molecule binding incompatible egos and temperaments, proving why real group chemistry never obeys the logic of stacking stars on a video-game console.

quote.text: Often their work is only noticed when it disappears. When you take them off the board, it looks as if you're removing a part that adds little and is easily replaced—and then suddenly the mayonnaise splits and spoils.
quote.sourceTitle: Team emulsifiers: the process of mixing two liquids that are hard to mix

reflectionQuestions: Who on your team currently absorbs silent friction and translates between incompatible profiles—and what would happen if they vanished from the org chart tomorrow?
Do your promotion and review criteria reward individual showboating exclusively, or can they actually spot and protect your emulsifiers?
Are you confusing a mediator who smooths over isolated conflicts with someone who genuinely raises the group's operational ceiling?

equipo-apolo.short: A team packed with highly talented people that performs far below expectations.
equipo-apolo.analogy: A soccer team full of Ballon d'Or winners where nobody tracks back to defend, everyone fights to take the free kicks, and they lose to a modest, tight-knit side.
equipo-apolo.howToApply: Balance stars with connectors, executors, and complementary profiles; prioritize healthy friction over shiny individual résumés.
equipo-apolo.antiPattern: Signing only the most ego-driven "number ones" on the assumption that individual talent adds up in a straight line.
paragraphs: Talent brings supersized egos, people who insist on doing things their way, and arguments to the point of exhaustion. That's why Recuenco calls them ticking time bombs: without a cognitive orchestrator they implode, just like Van Halen. He learned the concept from Elena Sanz, former president of Mensa.

deepDive.thesis: Assembling extreme talent without cognitive orchestration doesn't multiply output—it builds a ticking time bomb that self-destructs through ego and friction.
essay: Drawing on the Apollo syndrome formulated by Meredith Belbin—which reached Recuenco via Elena Sanz, former president of Mensa—Javier dismantles one of modern management's dearest fantasies: the belief that throwing brilliant minds together automatically produces unbeatable teams. The evidence points the opposite way. Exceptional talent rarely travels alone; it arrives packaged with colossal egos, insecurities, obsessions, personal grudges, and a fierce urge to impose one's own view. Without an external force channeling that energy, the group burns its horsepower on mutual sabotage and endless debates.

The misunderstanding feeds on cinematic tropes that confuse narrative plausibility with operational reality. Javier puts Dr. House under the microscope: what's unrealistic about the character isn't his intellect or misanthropy—there's plenty of both in Mensa—but the idea that the entire solution hatches solo inside his head while highly competent doctors are reduced to lab technicians. The myth of the "all-powerful Super Saiyan" ignores two uncomfortable truths: nobody solves a truly complex problem alone, and most people would rather live in peace than endure the daily friction of extreme talent.

In CPS architecture, the Apollo team proves that cognitive orchestration is no administrative ornament, but a strategic discipline in its own right—as hard as it is invisible to pop culture. Like a conductor whose baton looks superfluous from the cheap seats, the orchestrator keeps geniuses from devouring one another. Once you get this, you stop hiring stars by the pound and start designing the governance architecture that lets them coexist; otherwise, the team's own members will oust the very person holding them together, convinced they can shine brighter on their own.
keyInsights: Hyper-talented teams tend to wildly underperform because extreme talent comes bundled with egos, insecurities, and turf wars over judgment that stall execution.
The lone-wolf archetype—the self-sufficient genius along the lines of Dr. House—is a storytelling mirage incompatible with genuinely complex problems.
Cognitive orchestration is a demanding, autonomous discipline that tends to be undervalued precisely when it works best, because nobody sees the disasters it prevents.
Absent strong orchestration, Apollo team members routinely perceive the orchestrator as a threat rather than recognizing they are being saved from their own excesses.

threadExamples.title: Van Halen and the collapse after Noel Monk's exit
threadExamples.detail: The band had the textbook A-Team—Eddie as the vulnerable technical genius, David Lee Roth as the runaway-ego showman, and Alex as the reliable backbone—yet only avoided implosion while manager Noel Monk acted as cognitive orchestrator; the moment Alex and DLR saw him as a threat and pushed him out, the whole thing fell apart.

threadExamples.title: The Dr. House mirage vs. real teamwork
threadExamples.detail: Recuenco notes that the show works dramatically but betrays CPS reality by turning an entire medical team into mere errand-runners for a solitary genius, reinforcing the "all-powerful Super Saiyan" myth against the real maxim: "you can't do it alone, with friends you can."

quote.text: The main point is that CPS teams without cognitive orchestration tend toward self-destruction. And very often, the orchestration work goes unappreciated, with every member of the CPS team thinking they could do it better on their own.
quote.sourceTitle: How Van Halen falls apart as a band for lack of a cognitive orchestrator

reflectionQuestions: If you've assembled brilliant people who are performing below their potential, are you short on talent—or short on a cognitive orchestrator with real authority?
Is there a "Dr. House" in your organization whose individual brilliance is smothering the collective intelligence of the rest of the team?
Are you protecting the person who frames the work and reins in the group's excesses, or are their peers already starting to treat them as dead weight?

factor-x.short: The pillar of CPS that studies human behavior in complex environments, assuming it can be modeled—even if never completely.
factor-x.analogy: Physics explains a ball's trajectory, but if the ball has fears, pride, envy, and ambition, you need another layer of reading.
factor-x.howToApply: Always factor in emotions, status, fears, hidden incentives, and personal prestige when designing any change or product.
factor-x.antiPattern: Designing solutions that are spotless on paper and blow up on day one because they assume humans are rational calculators.
paragraphs: It is one of the four macro-disciplines in Recuenco's CPS framework and brings together psychology and other behavioral sciences. It differs from the "human factor" in that it refuses to write human behavior off as chaotic and unmanageable: it tries to model and manage it as part of the solution, knowing full well that all models are wrong. It starts from the premise that human beings are the primordial complex system—hence his maxim "there is no CPS without Factor X management," which almost always forces you to have "the conversation," the hard one nobody wants to have. Ignoring it, he says, guarantees catastrophe, no matter how brilliant the strategy.

deepDive.thesis: No viable strategy can ignore human behavior: Factor X does not surrender to chaos—it models and manages human complexity.
essay: Javier defines Factor X through a surgical distinction against the classic "human factor." Whereas the latter takes for granted that human behavior is unpredictable, chaotic, and beyond reach—a classy excuse to drop it from the equation—Factor X accepts the principle that "all models are wrong" yet refuses to throw up its hands. It starts from the fact that a human being is the primordial complex system and that human interaction generates complex systems of complex systems; it therefore demands an operational thesis on how people will react and treats it as a central piece of the solution.

From that premise, Recuenco dismantles two very lucrative delusions. The first is the sterile neatness of the spreadsheet and Classic Economics 101, which engineers spotless solutions under unrealistic lab conditions of temperature and pressure and then acts shocked when human reality shreds them. The second is the myth that being a "clever operator" or a psychopathic executive confers a lasting edge: drawing on Kevin Dutton and Igor Galynker, Javier shows that while such profiles climb fast on coldness and charisma, their empathy deficit blinds them to Factor X and social Tit for Tat—turning cynicism into slow-motion suicide.

As one of the four macro-disciplines of the CPS framework, Factor X runs through all of strategy, cognitive orchestration, and high-variability Personotecnia processes—to the point of folding neuroscience and clinical psychology into business diagnosis. Mastering it radically changes management practice: instead of hiding problems inside antiseptic plans, it forces you down into the mud to hold "the conversation," the uncomfortable talk nobody wants to open. Because in any environment with humans, ignoring grievances, emotional incentives, and mental models does not simplify the problem—it guarantees a brilliant strategy gets blown up from the inside.
keyInsights: Unlike the "human factor," which dismisses behavior as uncontrollable noise, Factor X tries to model it while knowing every model is imperfect yet indispensable.
A human being is the primordial complex system; any business problem involving people entails complex systems of complex systems that cannot be trapped in a spreadsheet.
Psychopathic or "too-clever" bosses may rise quickly, yet lose in the long run because their lack of empathy blinds them to Factor X and triggers Tit-for-Tat retaliation.
There is no real Factor X management without facing "the conversation" and acknowledging the organization's psychological reality before designing the strategy.

threadExamples.title: The Banco Río heist in Acassuso and the wreck of the European Super League
threadExamples.detail: Recuenco pairs Argentina's "heist of the century"—a clockwork job undone by a spurned wife—with the instant collapse of football's European Super League to prove that even technically brilliant plans disintegrate when they misread other people's mental models and emotions.

threadExamples.title: McChrystal's Afghanistan slide and psychopathic bosses
threadExamples.detail: McChrystal's infamous slide popularized the inseparable overlap between strategy and Factor X, while research by Kevin Dutton and Igor Galynker helps Javier explain why not being an asshole isn't preachy moralizing—it's pure strategic self-preservation.
