quote.text: Factor X differs from the human factor in that it does not accept human behavior as utterly chaotic, and tries as far as possible to model expected behavior and manage it.
quote.sourceTitle: The human factor and its connection to CPS

reflectionQuestions: What uncomfortable "conversation" are you putting off on your team today while trying to fix a human deadlock by tweaking processes or KPIs?
In your latest strategic plan, did you explicitly model the real fears, egos, and incentives of the people involved—or assume they'd behave like rational spreadsheet agents?
Where are you mistaking short-term toughness or cleverness for strategic effectiveness, piling up grievances that will eventually detonate your project?

personotecnia.short: The discipline of crafting relevant messages and value propositions for a specific person in a specific context—even at scale.
personotecnia.analogy: The neighborhood greengrocer who knows you're in a rush today and want ripe fruit for tonight—applied thoughtfully and with technology to thousands of people.
personotecnia.howToApply: Understand each person's actual moment, need, and context so you offer something genuinely useful and relevant, not a form email with their first name pasted in.
personotecnia.antiPattern: Slapping "Hi, {{first_name}}" onto an identical mass email blast and calling it personalization.
paragraphs: Recuenco formulated it in his book "Personalización" (2004) in response to marketing's fake personalization: the archetype is the neighborhood greengrocer who knows what you like, and the challenge is pulling that off at scale. He defines it as the body of methodologies and know-how for building relevant messages for a specific recipient in a specific context, governed by three rules. Every profiling shortcut is paid for in accuracy. The more intimate the data, the more reciprocal the relationship must be. And context is singular, because people are not static segments. It is horizontal and touches the entire value chain—not just marketing or sales—and some of its followers describe it as "the CPS of Factor X."

deepDive.thesis: Personotecnia is not marketing with extra data: it is the horizontal discipline that rewires the entire company to earn attention in a singular context.
essay: Formulated by Recuenco from his 2004 book "Personalización" through his contemporary synthesis in Personotecnia '26, this discipline brings together methodologies and technical know-how to build relevant messages and propositions for a specific recipient in a specific context. It rests on three iron rules: every profiling shortcut is paid for in lost accuracy; the more intimate the data, the more personal and reciprocal the exchange must be so it doesn't turn into extraction; and context is singular, because people are not static segments or rigid buyer personas, but shifting bundles of situations.

Javier thus exposes the great con of the past two decades: calling it "personalization" when you hoover up random data to resell it to the ad-tech machine. Drawing on Sperber and Wilson's relevance theory—the brain allocates attention according to the ratio of cognitive effect to processing effort—he explains the perverse equilibrium that follows: overproducing messages that pretend to address us drives up processing costs, recipients build defensive immunity as mental hygiene, and brands respond by cranking up the volume until 99.99% of impressions are discarded and trust is torched.

Within the CPS ecosystem, Personotecnia acts as the non-predatory flip side of the attention economy and demands something most legacy companies cannot stomach: a complete rewiring. It is neither a department nor a campaign, but a horizontal discipline cutting across Porter's entire value chain. Whoever takes it seriously stops mass-manufacturing in the hope that distribution will work miracles, and learns to scale the neighborhood greengrocer's intuition without sliding into opaque surveillance—winning attention back by delivering real cognitive value.
keyInsights: Personotecnia's three rules are non-negotiable: shortcuts degrade accuracy, intimacy demands reciprocity, and context is always singular and fluid.
Today's fragmented attention is not mere novelty addiction, but defensive hygiene against an environment saturated with targeted noise faking relevance.
When a stimulus delivers high cognitive effects for justifiable effort, attention returns: the only sustainable way to ask for it is to deserve it.
Implementing real Personotecnia makes the timbers of mass-production companies groan because it hits Porter's entire value chain, not just marketing.

threadExamples.title: The neighborhood greengrocer vs. the Fortnite model and ad noise
threadExamples.detail: Against an industry that wastes 99.99% of its impressions on opaque surveillance, the greengrocer knows the customer's history and moment by craft; at digital scale, Fortnite proves the power of individualization by giving away the base game and monetizing massively through skins and customization.

threadExamples.title: Fender's lag and Saint Laurent's leap to prêt-à-porter
threadExamples.detail: Just as the great sixties couturiers abandoned the exclusivity of dressing twelve marchionesses because it couldn't sustain a business, Javier explains the twenty-year lag in D2C initiatives like Fender through the sheer difficulty of redesigning top-to-bottom a firm built to mass-produce and delegate to distributors.

quote.text: Personotecnia, in this sense, is not a fancier marketing handbook. It is the necessary flip side of the attention economy.
quote.sourceTitle: Personotecnia and the attention economy: relevance, context, and immunity

reflectionQuestions: When you ask customers for intimate data, what genuine exchange of value do you give back so your approach doesn't feel like extraction?
Are you still operating with static "buyer persona" archetypes that ignore the recipient's changing context and feed their defensive immunity?
If you decided tomorrow to truly personalize your offering at scale, which links in your value chain—outside marketing—would immediately crack under the strain?

test-astudillo.short: Tests whether a business proposition actually accounts for Factor X or only balances in Excel.
test-astudillo.analogy: Asking "would a tired normal person on a Tuesday afternoon actually do this?" before signing off on a gorgeous spreadsheet plan.
test-astudillo.howToApply: Put every spreadsheet and business model through the acid test of real human behavior: laziness, status, distrust, and habit.
test-astudillo.antiPattern: Greenlighting multimillion-dollar projects because the assumed conversion rates in cell G14 make the hockey-stick chart look lovely.
paragraphs: Recuenco named it after a line from César Astudillo about business models and value propositions: "That wouldn't pass Sociology 101." A proposition that pleases the spreadsheet yet fails to grasp psychology or the Zeitgeist ends up crashing: no spherical cow that ignores Factor X lands safely. Recuenco puts it on par with the Bechdel test.
test-astudillo.origin: Javier G. Recuenco, from a remark by César Astudillo

deepDive.thesis: Any business model that only works in Excel and flunks Sociology 101 is doomed to smash into human reality.
essay: Named by Recuenco after a devastating verdict from César Astudillo—"that wouldn't pass Sociology 101"—and placed on the same cultural pedestal as the Bechdel test, the Test Astudillo operates as a reality filter for business models and value propositions. Its thesis is brutally direct: you cannot launch any "spherical cow" that leaves out Factor X without landing face-first on your teeth. When you eject human behavior from an equation because it feels volatile or inconvenient, the model gains mathematical neatness at the cost of losing all contact with the real world.

Javier links this test to several modern pathologies he takes apart without mercy. On one side, the chronic allergy of Excel Warriors and Private Equity toward businesses driven by human unpredictability—where, as Taleb reminds us, money as a proxy for efficiency eventually invades everything until it drains the humanity out of an activity and degrades it into "shitty Taylorism." On the other, the naivety of rationalist idealism that thinks it can tame human passions by decree, forgetting that hyper-productive empires and organizations often implode precisely because they excise their psychological and cultural bedrock.

Inside CPS, the Test Astudillo champions the organizational "corpus callosum": the impossibility of solving complex problems when a chasm divides left and right hemispheres—finance and creativity, or strategy and execution. Healing a company isn't about balancing spreadsheets; it's about closing the psychological and cultural wounds of the people inside it. Mastering this test sharpens your own judgment too: it forces you to hone your sensemaking to diagnose social reality better, and drop the sterile obsession with trying to convince everyone else that you're right.
keyInsights: Stripping Factor X out of a model because it feels messy or volatile leads straight into the McNamara fallacy and "shitty Taylorism."
When efficiency and money colonize a social or creative domain, they strip out its humanity and destroy the very engine that gave it value.
No viable CPS exists without a "corpus callosum": divorcing finance and operations from sociology, anthropology, and creativity guarantees disaster.
Good sensemaking aims to sharpen the quality of your diagnosis and hypotheses; obsessing over proving to others that you are right is wildly overrated.

threadExamples.title: Barça, Goldman Sachs, and Private Equity's terror of Factor X
threadExamples.detail: The concept takes off when Javier examines the risk of an anthropological and sociological phenomenon like FC Barcelona ending up in the hands of Goldman Sachs, illustrating why financiers and Private Equity loathe businesses dependent on human unpredictability.

threadExamples.title: Wilbur Mills and the self-destruction of hyper-productive models
threadExamples.detail: To prove that pure reason never cancels human passions—much like the hyper-productive models straining societies like South Korea—Recuenco invokes Congressman Wilbur Mills, who read tax codes for fun and ended up embroiled in a scandal involving Fanne Foxe and Alcoholics Anonymous.

quote.text: The Astudillo test captures the rule that you cannot propose any spherical cow that ignores Factor X without landing face-first on your teeth.
quote.sourceTitle: The impact of the urge to be right across multiple contexts

reflectionQuestions: If you put your current business plan through "Sociology 101," what real-world behaviors from customers or staff would blow it sky-high?
Where are you optimizing a process until it becomes technically spotless yet culturally dead or unbearable for the people inside it?
At your leadership table, is there a real bridge between financial minds and creative minds—or does each hemisphere inhabit a different planet?

asertividad.short: The ability to defend your judgment firmly and candidly, without aggression and without losing respect for the other person.
asertividad.analogy: Speaking with the firmness of a stone wall and the calm of a lake: you say "this doesn't work" without shouting or apologizing for existing.
asertividad.howToApply: Separate the problem from the person: state facts, stance, and boundaries clearly, listening without surrendering your principles just to be liked.
asertividad.antiPattern: Confusing assertiveness with passive-aggressiveness—or being a pleasant "yes-person" to dodge short-term conflict.
paragraphs: Recuenco considers it indispensable in CPS, because whoever diagnoses has to tell leadership uncomfortable truths—whether they come from MIT or INSEAD. Since assertiveness breeds conflict and almost everyone avoids it, flattery often takes its place, degrading strategy in the process. It only works alongside an almost obsessive self-control that reins in "abrasive pyrotechnics."

deepDive.thesis: Without assertiveness there is no real strategy, yet defending uncomfortable truths requires curbing abrasive pyrotechnics and acting decisively from within uncertainty.
essay: Recuenco places assertiveness at the spine of CPS because he agrees with Richard Rumelt that strategy is relentless Problem Solving: it rearranges chairs, ruffles vested interests, and requires looking the owner in the eye to deliver hard home truths with skin in the game. Assertiveness means voicing judgment, boundaries, and needs with firmness, fairness, and empathy—keeping your composure without trampling on anyone else's rights. Because telling the truth creates friction and almost nobody short of a sociopath enjoys conflict, organizations routinely swap it for "buttery strategy": smooth flattery that destroys diagnostic capacity.

Javier defuses two lethal misunderstandings around the concept. The first confuses assertiveness with aggression: the aggressor only cares about winning and intimidating regardless of the other party—and being an asshole is never free—whereas true assertiveness demands a "fierce restraint on abrasive pyrotechnics," an almost obsessive self-control to stop candor from blowing up the room. The second misunderstanding equates firmness with absolute certainty; in practice, CPS requires holding an uncomfortable paradox: being highly assertive and operational precisely from a place of not knowing, information asymmetry, and doubt.

Once this skill is genuinely woven into CPS practice, it transforms both leadership and client relationships. An assertive practitioner neither peddles snake oil to keep a retainer—they will even hand over McKinsey's phone number when someone else is a better fit—nor freezes under impostor syndrome or the Denia dilemma. Instead, they pair brutal honesty with emotional steadiness, earning lasting moral authority and trust. Anyone who masters that midpoint between cowardly passivity and scorched-earth aggression guides teams through critical crises without self-deception.
keyInsights: Real strategy demands assertiveness because it means confronting power with uncomfortable truths; dodging conflict for comfort breeds "buttery strategy."
The border between assertiveness and aggression is held by iron self-control that stops "abrasive pyrotechnics" before they blow up the relationship.
Being operational and assertive does not require omniscience: the paradoxical core of CPS is accepting that you feel incompetent without stopping bold decisions.
An assertive leader gets things done with fairness and respect, building legitimate authority that intimidation never achieves.

threadExamples.title: Hospital ERs, intensive care medicine, and the Denia dilemma
threadExamples.detail: To illustrate that operational assertiveness is possible amid ignorance and extreme stress, Javier turns to emergency rooms, intensive care, and officiating—arenas where paralyzing fear cannot stall decisions under asymmetric information.

threadExamples.title: "Buttery strategy" vs. candor with skin in the game
threadExamples.detail: Against consultants who replace real diagnosis with flattering pats on the back to avoid conflict, Recuenco champions the candor of looking the owner in the eye—even handing them McKinsey's number when they're the better option—and the everyday example of setting clear holiday boundaries with your boss without slipping into passivity or hostility.

quote.text: Assertiveness, if it wants to be effective, has to come with a fierce restraint on abrasive pyrotechnics—an almost obsessive self-control to keep everything from blowing sky-high.
quote.sourceTitle: Impostor syndrome in healthcare professionals and how it affects decision-making in critical situations

reflectionQuestions: What uncomfortable truth about your project are you sugarcoating today with "buttery strategy" just to spare yourself an immediate clash?
When you defend your judgment under pressure, are you practicing controlled assertiveness—or letting loose abrasive pyrotechnics that shut the other person down?
Do you stall key decisions waiting for absolute certainty instead of training yourself to act firmly in the middle of uncertainty?

autosegmentacion.short: When someone encountering a message not aimed directly at them identifies themselves as interested through their own behavior.
autosegmentacion.analogy: Putting an honest sign on the door of a jazz workshop: you don't chase anyone down the street, yet everyone who loves jazz walks right in.
autosegmentacion.howToApply: Put out signals, content, and offers so crisp and principled that the right customer raises their hand on their own.
autosegmentacion.antiPattern: Writing lukewarm "for everyone" messaging and then burning a fortune chasing people with ads who couldn't care less about you.
paragraphs: Recuenco sees it as the right mechanism for launching complex ideas or non-mainstream products. He himself puts out messages that aren't sales pitches, yet cause the exact people he could do business with to self-select. If you pressure yourself to reach a broader crowd, you water down the wine. And a client who hasn't self-segmented has slim odds of success, even if they desperately need CPS.

deepDive.thesis: When you sell complex, unorthodox solutions, chasing clients doesn't work: you need pure signals that filter for whoever is already ready to see.
essay: Self-segmentation happens when someone encounters a deliberately non-Personotecnia message and reveals on their own, through their behavior, that they are receptive to the premise. In conventional marketing it is usually limited to price skimming or used as a lazy fallback when you don't know who you're selling to. Recuenco flips it completely: for unorthodox, counterintuitive propositions aimed at a connoisseur minority—not by luxury or price tag, but by degree of complexity—it is the most efficient demand-generation engine in a post-Google, post-Facebook world where cold outreach guarantees doors slammed in your face.

At first glance it looks paradoxical that a Personotecnia specialist defends an apparently random discovery mechanism. The nuance lies in the root-level cognitive dissonance baked into CPS: you can stand someone right in front of the fourteen-meter Hollywood sign and, if their mental architecture isn't ready, they will tell you in total honesty they can't see it. That is why Javier dismantles the volume and "total addressable potential" trap: diluting the message to widen the funnel ruins the product, and a client who hasn't self-segmented has near-zero odds of success even when they desperately need the intervention.

In Singular Solving's commercial architecture, self-segmentation replaces traditional sales teams altogether. Both public threads and the CPS training strategy serve as high-fidelity beacons communicating bluntly how they operate—skin in the game, unknown problems, zero muzzles—to attract exclusively counterparts with high agency and cognitive affinity. Whoever masters this mechanism stops burning energy evangelizing impervious boards and builds relationships where the client already shows up mentally ready for the hard work.
keyInsights: Self-segmentation shines on offers for complexity minorities, where cold calling and mass marketing are doomed to rejection.
People are ready when they're ready, and some never will be: a non-self-segmented client's probability of success in CPS is close to zero even if they urgently need help.
Publishing deep, uncompromising content—paired with a rigorous training strategy—acts as a filter for mental architecture and high agency.
Lowering the bar of your message to reach a wider crowd ("watering down the wine") breaks the filter and pulls in clients incapable of handling a real intervention.

threadExamples.title: The rooster-and-hen farm vs. Singular Solving's zero-salesperson model
threadExamples.detail: Javier contrasts the classic pricing case—a farm placing feed at different heights so roosters and hens sort themselves by size—with Singular Solving's method, which ditches salespeople and uses threads and training to filter for cognitive affinity.

threadExamples.title: Giant Hollywood letters and the publishing rejections of John Kennedy Toole
threadExamples.detail: Recuenco recalls the rejections that broke John Kennedy Toole to illustrate what happens to the unorthodox on cold calls, and caps it with his image of the fourteen-meter Hollywood letters: anyone without the right mental frame won't see them even standing right in front of them.

quote.text: So the odds of success for a client who hasn't self-segmented—even if they need us like oxygen—are close to zero.
quote.sourceTitle: Upcoming flagship CPS strategies and training

reflectionQuestions: How much time are you burning right now trying to persuade clients or bosses who objectively need your solution yet aren't cognitively ready to swallow it?
Do your public messages show unfiltered how you actually work—or are you watering down the wine to please more people at the cost of attracting bad projects?
What clear signals and concrete behaviors could confirm a prospective ally has self-segmented before you commit resources to them?

man-on-a-mission.short: Someone devoted to a mission that fuels them with tremendous energy, while carrying the risk of tunnel vision.
man-on-a-mission.analogy: A nuclear icebreaker: it carves a path where nobody else dares go, yet if nobody corrects its heading it can ram straight through the entire harbor.
man-on-a-mission.howToApply: Channel that unstoppable drive into a worthy challenge, and surround them with people who have real authority to call out their blind spots.
man-on-a-mission.antiPattern: Snuffing out their fire with absurd bureaucracy—or, conversely, leaving them unchecked until tunnel vision steamrolls the whole team.
paragraphs: Recuenco openly recognizes himself as a man on a mission on several fronts. The upsides: you run as if doped, your honesty disarms people, and you steamroll the competition. The risks: tunnel vision, emotional entanglement, and a loss of objectivity and peripheral vision. Real danger strikes when three things converge: having a mission, failing to find its sweet spot, and gaining access to some form of power.

deepDive.thesis: Mission-driven conviction dopes you to steamroll competitors, yet without a sweet spot and peripheral vision it turns idealism into destructive pompismo.
essay: Recuenco examines the "man on a mission" archetype—to which he openly admits belonging on several fronts—as a psychological force of tremendous asymmetric potency. Inspired by the obsession with excellence of extreme competitors and Queensrÿche's album "Operation: Mindcrime," the mechanism is clear: when you embrace a cause as a transcendent mission, you enter an almost doped state. Your stamina outlasts any rational calculation, your honesty disarms the lukewarm, and your conviction knocks down opposition like bowling pins, leaving cold pragmatism—which rarely sparks emotional allegiance—at a stark disadvantage.

Yet in closing his trilogy on pompismo, Javier reveals the lethal flip side of that seemingly noble, aspirational drive. A sense of mission is a multidimensional variable that demands finding its sweet spot: poorly calibrated, it induces tunnel vision, emotional overload, and total loss of objectivity and peripheral vision. Drawing on Leon Festinger ("When Prophecy Fails") and Ramón Nogueras ("Por qué creemos en mierdas"), he dismantles naivety toward "angelic idealists": when a prophet collides with reality, they tend to armor-plate their faith even harder—and if they also reach real power, pompismo stops being funny and turns dangerous.

In CPS practice, this concept forces you to walk a high-precision tightrope. Solving complex problems requires the tenacity and inner fire of someone on a mission, yet just as urgently requires external reality checks, teams willing to push back, and constant calibration against facts. Mastering this tension means harnessing mission fuel without handing the steering wheel to fanaticism—surrounding yourself with counterweights and good traveling companions capable of restoring your peripheral vision before you drive off a cliff.
keyInsights: A mission mindset creates an asymmetric competitive edge because it supplies overflowing energy and an authenticity that disarms bureaucratic pragmatism.
The very fire that makes you unstoppable destroys peripheral vision, clouds objectivity, and feeds self-deception whenever reality contradicts your story.
Unchecked idealism is not harmless: when it meets a missing sweet spot and access to real power, it curdles into pompismo with destructive consequences.
Being on a mission requires deliberately engineering counterweights and external calibration so you never cross the line from obsessive excellence into cultish dogma.

threadExamples.title: Queensrÿche ("Operation: Mindcrime") and the Pablo Iglesias vs. Errejón duel
threadExamples.detail: Recuenco pulls Queensrÿche's "The Mission"—alongside the obsessive excellence of Kobe Bryant or Eddie Van Halen—to capture the executor's transcendence, and shows its political punch by recalling how Pablo Iglesias's man-on-a-mission charisma steamrolled Íñigo Errejón's cooler pragmatism.

threadExamples.title: From "When Prophecy Fails" to Hitler's quote on pure idealism
threadExamples.detail: To prove the hidden lethality of unbridled idealism, Javier links Leon Festinger's study of cults doubling down on faith when prophecy fails with internal party purges—such as Vox's crisis in the Balearic Islands—and a chilling quote from Adolf Hitler extolling pure idealism.

quote.text: Even though I have the associated problems clearly mapped out: tunnel vision, emotional involvement, lack of objectivity and peripheral vision. I am equally clear on the upsides: you run doped up, you plow through the competition, your honesty disarms, you knock down your opposition like bowling pins.
quote.sourceTitle: Third and final part on pompismo: the danger of idealism and obsession

reflectionQuestions: In what current project do you feel "on a mission," and which people with real authority currently have permission to call out your blind spots?
When the data contradicts your favorite thesis, are you adjusting course—or acting like the true believers in "When Prophecy Fails"?
Where are you mistaking an idealist's emotional intensity for the strategic soundness of a viable proposition?

man-out-of-time.short: A visionary ahead of their era, whose talent is only recognized and put to use after they are dead.
man-out-of-time.analogy: A surfer who paddles into a wave ten seconds too early: even with world-class technique, the swell hasn't built yet and wipes them out.
man-out-of-time.howToApply: Pair visionary ideas with a reading of the zeitgeist and pragmatic bridges back to the present so society can digest them today.
man-out-of-time.antiPattern: Confusing being right in the abstract with winning in the market: showing up too early looks remarkably like being wrong.
paragraphs: Recuenco describes them as "flesh-and-blood OOPArts" and admires their courage above all. His favorite examples are Nikola Tesla—far less adapted to his era than Edison—and adman Howard Gossage, who had the talent to become a 20th-century icon and whose ideas later generations enjoyed. The name comes from "Tesla: Man Out of Time," the 1981 biography.

deepDive.thesis: True visionaries are artifacts out of their time: uncomfortable while alive, misunderstood by the market, and vindicated once they can no longer cash the check.
essay: Recuenco describes men out of time as "flesh-and-blood OOPArts": human artifacts appearing decades before the world is ready to absorb them. The term echoes the 1981 biography of Nikola Tesla and distills a structural tension of progress—the yawning gap between having a brilliant vision and managing to execute and monetize it in your own era. Anyone trying to sell ideas without established precedents—unlike someone selling physical goods or standard expertise—runs into a market incapable of valuing what it doesn't yet have mental categories to hold.

Javier dismantles the modern cheapening of the word "visionary," whose dictionary definition already spans both brilliant foresight and feverish delusion. Today we hand the "visionary" medal to the successful executive who capitalized on their moment—like Edison or Bill Gates—whereas a genuine visionary tends to be grating: they don't flatter your biases, they point at what you ignore, and they end up ostracized. At the same time, Recuenco avoids romanticizing their practical failure: even while declaring himself "Team Tesla forever" and admiring the provocative nerve of figures like William Blake, he acknowledges that disdain for the mundane and failing to surround oneself well usually condemn them to collect their dividends posthumously.

Within CPS, the man out of time delivers a decisive practical warning: strategic lucidity without market viability is an avoidable tragedy. Being right sixty years before everyone else won't keep a company afloat if you don't build a bridge between your ideas and an audience able to fund and use them. Whoever absorbs this lesson keeps the audacity to think outside their era's taboos, yet pairs it with practical sense, complementary alliances, and deliberate commercial design so the vision lands while they're still alive.
keyInsights: We usually call the well-adapted, successful businessman of his era a "visionary," when real visionaries tend to be uncomfortable and suffer ostracism from their contemporaries.
Selling ideas without established precedents is radically more fraught than selling physical products or labor: you can have razor-sharp insight and authenticity with zero market viability.
Ahead-of-its-time genius doesn't make up for scorning the mundane or choosing allies poorly: without execution and practical partnerships, later generations harvest the fruit.
Turning advanced thinking into real impact means deliberately building both the intellectual proposition and the audience capable of sustaining it financially.

threadExamples.title: Nikola Tesla vs. Thomas Edison in the War of the Currents
threadExamples.detail: Edison—inventor of the industrial lab and owner of a huge street whose last direct-current power station closed in 2007—embodied adaptation to his era, while Tesla, to whom humanity owes more, died in near-poverty because of his disdain for practicalities and inability to surround himself well.

threadExamples.title: Howard Luck Gossage, the forgotten first practitioner of CPS
threadExamples.detail: An adman sixty years ahead of his time—author of lines like "nobody reads advertising; people read what interests them"—and the first to build a firm resembling CPS before it had a name, Gossage never matched Ogilvy's or Bernbach's fame in life, and his books aren't even available in digital format.

quote.text: Humanity owes more to Tesla than to Edison. Some people get paid after they're dead.
quote.sourceTitle: Edison vs. Tesla: the clash of two worldviews in the War of the Currents

reflectionQuestions: If your idea isn't taking off today, are you genuinely ahead of your time—or simply missing an "Edison" to translate your vision into execution and commercial viability?
What practical compromises or partnerships are you avoiding out of disdain for "the mundane," putting a brilliant proposition's survival at risk?
Are you building an audience capable of understanding and paying for your ideas right now, or naively trusting the market to recognize their merit on its own?

recoger-cable.short: Admitting an error, processing it, and changing your mind without clinging to ego. In exploratory work like CPS, it is indispensable.
recoger-cable.analogy: A sailor who sees the wind shift and trims the sails without shame: the goal is making port, not proving your first guess was flawless.
recoger-cable.howToApply: Normalize saying aloud "given the new data, I'm changing my mind"; reward people who course-correct early instead of mocking them.
recoger-cable.antiPattern: Clinging to a bad call for months just to protect your ego and avoid admitting you got it wrong.
paragraphs: Recuenco points to Antonio Escohotado as the model, who walked away from communism because of evidence rather than pressure: disappointment, assimilation, internalization, and finally taking responsibility. Because CPS is exploratory and hypothesis-driven, being wrong and course-correcting is built into the method—even when the client mistakes it for incompetence. He sums it up with a Singular Solving line: "every screw-up is fine as long as it's a new one."

deepDive.thesis: In a complex environment, changing your mind in the face of evidence is neither weakness nor spinelessness: it is the core muscle of strategic recalibration.
essay: Recuenco elevates the colloquial Spanish phrase "recoger cable"—reeling the cable back in—to essential mental architecture for working in complexity. His favorite benchmark is Antonio Escohotado and how he explained leaving radical communism behind: not as a sudden Damascus-road conversion or the result of external intimidation, but as inevitable surrender to the evidence despite personal pain. Javier breaks that mechanics down into four crisp steps—disappointment, assimilation, internalization, and taking responsibility followed by action—proving that course-correcting with grace doesn't shatter identity; it refines it.

The real roadblock isn't intellectual, it's identity: the "ego investments" that push us to defend dead hypotheses just so we don't look incompetent. Javier dismantles two widespread falsehoods here. First, that recalibrating equals lacking conviction: he draws a razor-sharp line between "having no armored ideology" and "having no foundational ideas or principles." Second, that getting things wrong betrays amateurism; in tune with Jorge Wagensberg's "pardon of error"—science as the system best protected from its creator's ideology—and Adam Grant's "Think Again," honest error is the natural toll of exploring uncharted terrain.

Within CPS, reeling in the cable stops being a humiliating walk-back and becomes the operating engine of the hypothesis-test-adapt loop. At Singular Solving they capture it in a crystal-clear maxim: "every screw-up is fine as long as it's a new one." Like beer, learning to enjoy reeling in the cable and the learning attached to it is an acquired taste that takes deliberate practice. Whoever separates themselves from their ego investments gains recalibration speed, spots their biases earlier, and becomes an infinitely more reliable professional the moment the map stops matching the territory.
keyInsights: Truly reeling in the cable follows an upright sequence: disappointment, assimilation, internalization, and taking responsibility through concrete action.
Dropping rigid ideology in light of evidence does not mean lacking principles or core convictions—it means refusing to let ego hijack learning.
In exploratory, hypothesis-driven work, error is not incompetence so long as it is new and serves to recalibrate the model against reality.
Enjoying recalibration and owning your misses is an acquired taste trained deliberately until it becomes a cognitive edge.

threadExamples.title: Antonio Escohotado's mental architecture in the face of evidence
threadExamples.detail: In one of the videos Recuenco cites most often, Escohotado recounts leaving hardline communism with no outside pressure or melodrama, walking lucidly through disappointment, assimilation, internalization, and responsibility to emerge with greater integrity.

threadExamples.title: Wagensberg's "pardon of error" and Adam Grant's "Think Again"
threadExamples.detail: Javier connects Jorge Wagensberg's insight—science as a method built to protect itself against its creator's ideology—with Adam Grant's "Think Again" to contrast corporate rigidity against Singular Solving's exploratory culture, where only repeating old mistakes carries a penalty.

quote.text: Enjoying the walk-backs—reeling in the cable—and the learning process that comes with it is an acquired taste, like beer. You just have to stick with it to enjoy something that will make you a better person and a better professional.
quote.sourceTitle: The importance of recalibration in CPS scenarios, reeling in the cable, ego investments, and Antonio Escohotado's mental architecture

reflectionQuestions: What decision or professional belief are you still defending today more out of past "ego investment" than current evidence?
When someone on your team owns up to an exploratory mistake and corrects course in time, do you reward it as valuable learning or punish it as incompetence?
When was the last time you publicly changed your stance on stronger evidence, following the whole process through to new actions?

altas-capacidades.short: Intellectual capacity well above average. Recuenco considers it invaluable in CPS—and systematically wasted by the system.
altas-capacidades.analogy: A Formula 1 engine stuck in city traffic in first gear: if you never give it a track, it overheats and looks broken.
altas-capacidades.howToApply: Offer real complex problems, autonomy, and mentors up to the task instead of rewarding only obedience and rote repetition.
altas-capacidades.antiPattern: Confusing giftedness with "effortlessly getting straight As" or isolating people as if they were oddities devoid of social skills.
paragraphs: Recuenco argues that bringing gifted individuals into CPS processes—especially during sensemaking—is a major asset because of how effortlessly they spot novel connections. He makes clear that high ability guarantees nothing ("AACC ≠ the right stuff") and that gifted people are just as fallible as anyone else. He also calls out how Spain wastes this talent and how gifted students suffer school bullying at far higher rates than average.

deepDive.thesis: High cognitive ability is irreplaceable fuel for complex sensemaking, yet it confers neither moral superiority nor guaranteed judgment.
essay: Recuenco does not pair giftedness with Complex Problem Solving out of autobiographical whim, but after distilling what enables certain teams to crack problems that paralyze everyone else. Drawing on Lewis Terman, Dean Keith Simonton, and the Cambridge Handbook of Expertise, he points out that gifted individuals contribute disproportionately to scientific and technological progress by forging novel connections. CPS acts as the systematization of that intellectual brute force and uncanny intuition through which great problem solvers have historically operated. That is why their presence multiplies the odds of success in sensemaking.

The major misunderstanding he dismantles across his threads cuts in two opposite directions. On one side, he attacks naive elitism: scoring above 130 on an IQ test or holding a Mensa card merely marks a baseline, never guaranteeing sound judgment or immunity to polarization and bias. Anyone who thinks otherwise falls into the "no true Scotsman" fallacy to expel whoever disagrees. On the other side, he denounces institutional blindness: against an estimated prevalence of 2% to 10%, Spain identifies barely 0.84% of students, condemning thousands of minds to academic failure, bullying, and chronic underutilization.

Integrating giftedness into the architecture of CPS requires abandoning both the fetish of the lone genius and the egalitarianism that flattens talent. High cognitive ability is not a uniform badge—it spans simple talent, complex talent, and profound giftedness—and its real power only emerges when paired with intense dedication, method, and emotional grounding. Anyone who grasps this stops hunting for infallible "heroes" and designs hybrid teams where the associative speed of gifted minds locks into the discipline of the CPS process. That is how cognitive energy normally squandered or bruised by the environment becomes a concrete strategic edge.
keyInsights: "AACC ≠ the right stuff": a high IQ or Mensa membership sets a minimum threshold of raw capacity, never infallibility or automatic discernment.
Segmenting a population by intelligence yields a group completely heterogeneous in values and politics—just as vulnerable to polarization and the no-true-Scotsman fallacy.
Spain's underdiagnosis (0.84% identified versus a real 2–10%) is not merely an educational failure, but a systemic squandering of innovative capacity and employability.
Gifted minds perform at their peak in the sensemaking phase of CPS because the method itself distills the breakthroughs historically achieved by people able to connect distant dots.

threadExamples.title: Mensa Spain's AGM in Gandía and the "no true Scotsman"
threadExamples.detail: Gathering more than 300 gifted people in a hotel, Recuenco shows that their ideological map mirrors the polarization of the Spanish parliament—and that each extreme falls into Antony Flew's fallacy by proclaiming that "the real Mensa" would never stand on the opposing side.

threadExamples.title: Terman and Simonton's studies versus Spain's 0.84%
threadExamples.detail: Against the longitudinal evidence from Lewis Terman (1925–1959) and Dean Keith Simonton (1984) on the disproportionate impact of giftedness in science and leadership, Spanish Ministry of Education figures reveal massive underdiagnosis that wastes that potential from primary school onward.

quote.text: In reality, CPS here is nothing less than what it always is: the systematization and distillation of all prior breakthroughs achieved via the intellectual brute force and uncanny intuition of the heroes of knowledge.
quote.sourceTitle: CPS and Giftedness: the new alliance for innovation

reflectionQuestions: Are you wasting people with strong associative speed on your team because you measure them by process compliance instead of bringing them into diagnosis and sensemaking?
Do you ever confuse intellectual brilliance with infallibility, or assume a fast mind is vaccinated against ego and tribal bias?
What real mechanisms does your organization have to spot and harness complex talent without first demanding that it disguise its difference?

disonancia-cognitiva.short: The discomfort triggered when reality contradicts what we believe—which we usually relieve by doubling down on the belief.
disonancia-cognitiva.analogy: The fox in the fable who, unable to reach the grapes, convinces himself they were sour anyway just to avoid frustration.
disonancia-cognitiva.howToApply: When you feel instant irritation at a fact that contradicts your thesis, pause: it is usually a sign your ego is defending an expired belief.
disonancia-cognitiva.antiPattern: Seeking out only reports and advisors that confirm what you already decided, dismissing every warning sign as "negativity."
paragraphs: Leon Festinger studied it from the inside by infiltrating a cult that predicted the end of the world for December 21, 1954: when the prophecy failed, most members did not abandon their faith—they rationalized it. Recuenco uses it to explain why a group gangs up against whoever brings reality into the room. He also argues that we live in the era of pantomime and collective cognitive dissonance, linking it directly to what he calls truth coping.
disonancia-cognitiva.origin: Leon Festinger, theory of cognitive dissonance ("When Prophecy Fails")

deepDive.thesis: When reality disproves a belief in which we have invested status or identity, we rarely course-correct: we rationalize the failure and attack the messenger.
essay: Starting from the classic study by Leon Festinger, Henry Riecken, and Stanley Schachter in When Prophecy Fails, Recuenco explains cognitive dissonance as the unbearable psychological tension that erupts when facts collide head-on with what we believe and the sacrifices we have already made. The heavier the emotional, reputational, or material investment in a thesis, the less willing a person is to admit error. Instead of updating the mental map, the brain manufactures ad hoc explanations, shields self-deception, and recruits outside accomplices to validate the fantasy and dilute the fear of looking foolish.

The sharpest nuance Javier highlights is that cognitive dissonance is not just an individual quirk, but a tribal glue with violent effects inside organizations. In every corporate paradigm shift, a fault line opens between those who examine the new landscape with curiosity and those who see their standing threatened. The latter do not debate the data calmly: they form coalitions, practice gaslighting, and coerce the exact person introducing the most dissonance into the room—for the crime of walking in with reality under their arm. Even self-deception serves adaptive functions, such as projecting confidence or cushioning guilt, making it all the harder to disarm.

Within the architecture of CPS, understanding cognitive dissonance completely reshapes the solver's craft. Surgical diagnosis is not enough; you have to recognize that dumping the raw truth unfiltered can wreck specific individuals and trigger defensive coalitions that sabotage the solution. Here Recuenco lays out an uncomfortable yet realistic ethic: in very precise tactical moments you must dose the truth or manage the narrative, without ever crossing into accepting something you radically disagree with. Mastering this mechanism teaches you to be assertive without naivety, to course-correct without trauma, and to absorb predictable backlash whenever you shatter a comfortable consensus.
keyInsights: When a prophecy or strategy fails after heavy sacrifices, groups typically ramp up proselytizing: recruiting new believers eases dissonance and dulls the sting of humiliation.
Organizational coercion and gaslighting often stem from a spontaneous coalition of people who refuse to see reality ganging up on the professional who puts it on the table.
Self-deception is not mere clumsiness: it acts as an emotional shield and a generator of perceived confidence, so hammering it head-on usually makes it stronger.
Accepting a premise you know is false just to keep the peace always comes back to bite you; CPS assertiveness means holding firm to the diagnosis without losing tact or the humility to revise.

threadExamples.title: Dorothy Martin's Seekers and the planet Clarion (1954)
threadExamples.detail: In Festinger's infiltrated Chicago study, cult members sold off their possessions awaiting a flying saucer on December 21, 1954; when the prophecy flopped, an alleged automatic-writing message reinterpreted the fiasco and the group flipped from secrecy to enthusiastic media proselytizing.

threadExamples.title: Watchmen and the common enemy in the executive committee
threadExamples.detail: Recuenco invokes Watchmen to illustrate how rival factions bury the hatchet against a greater shared threat: inside a company, those dodging a shift in value proposition band together against whoever brings reality into the room.

quote.text: One of the fundamental reasons people resort to coercion is that those who refuse to perceive the truth band together against the person who introduces the most cognitive dissonance into the room by walking in with reality under their arm.
quote.sourceTitle: Self-deception: the two faces of truth in decision-making

reflectionQuestions: In which company project are you "proselytizing" internally or externally to justify a bet that facts have already disproven?
When an uncomfortable voice challenges a sacred cow in a meeting, do you weigh the evidence they bring or join the group reflex to attack their tone?
What truth are you keeping quiet today to avoid conflict—or blurting out with zero tactical tact—that will come back multiplied six months from now?

neurodivergencia.short: A brain wired differently from the typical norm (autism, ADHD, dyslexia, giftedness) that educational and workplace systems usually fail to handle.
neurodivergencia.analogy: Different operating systems: a Mac is not a broken Windows PC—it simply processes differently and shines with the right tools.
neurodivergencia.howToApply: Design flexible ways of working and learning that harness hyperfocus, pattern detection, and non-linear thinking.
neurodivergencia.antiPattern: Trying to force-fit everyone into one standard mold when their difference is precisely their greatest source of value.
paragraphs: Recuenco uses an X-Men metaphor: against the "Magneto" stance of Peter Thiel and Alex Karp—who view neurodivergence as an edge to dominate the future—he places himself in the "Xavier" camp of educational reform and coexistence. He criticizes companies for demanding "culture fit" that forces neurodivergent people to amputate parts of their identity. That conviction drives his educational projects aimed at early detection and proper support.

deepDive.thesis: Neurodivergence is the defining mutant issue of the 21st century: a decisive asset in the age of AI that companies crush by demanding social camouflage.
essay: Recuenco treats neurodivergence—autism, ADHD, dyslexia, giftedness, and their twice- or thrice-exceptional combinations—not as a marginal clinical label, but as a structural collision with industrial-standard society. Cookie-cutter schools and offices engineered for the statistical average breed stigma, isolation, and trauma because they treat cognitive difference as a defect to fix. In a non-linear 2026 where nobody can guarantee employability five years out and any repetitive task will be swallowed by a script or an AI agent, that clone factory has become both obsolete and dangerous.

The sharpest punch in his long-form threads (turras) dismantles the corporate mantra of "talent shortage." According to Javier, talent is plentiful; what is scarce is executive courage and organizational intelligence to manage human complexity. Many HR departments act like 20th-century customs checkpoints obsessed with "culture fit"—a polite euphemism for not asking awkward questions or challenging inefficiencies. By demanding that neurodivergent professionals amputate pieces of their identity to seem normal, firms sentence them to masking: burning 80% of their daily CPU on social camouflage, leaving just 20% for solving problems until they end up broken, medicated, or depressed.

Inside the CPS ecosystem, neurodivergence occupies a pivotal spot because solving complex problems demands minds free from social-imitation reflexes and capable of reading non-linear systems. Against the confrontational path of figures like Peter Thiel or Alex Karp, Recuenco proposes a constructive, "off-road" alternative: early detection—as natural as steering the tallest kid toward basketball—and new environments like CPS Academy or Colegio Balder acting as Hermes Psychopompos, building bridges between worlds. Leaders who learn to manage without demanding clones unlock the rarest cognitive asset on the market.
keyInsights: Companies do not suffer from a talent shortage; they suffer from a lack of intellectual capacity and executive spine to manage profiles that don't fit the neurotypical mold.
"Culture fit" often operates as a gatekeeper forcing neurodivergent people to burn 80% of their energy on masking, shrinking their real problem-solving capacity to 20%.
In the AI era, operating like an obedient clone guarantees replacement by a script or an agent; strategic advantage shifts toward non-linear minds with independent judgment.
Identifying and supporting neurodivergence from childhood is neither elitism nor social Darwinism—it prevents avoidable trauma and stops grinding down a country's finest intellectual asset.

threadExamples.title: The 80% CPU tax of corporate masking
threadExamples.detail: Recuenco describes how the pressure to laugh at inside jokes and avoid tough questions turns the office into a grinding machine: neurodivergent professionals spend four-fifths of their daily energy faking normality and wind up depressed or pushed out of the system.

threadExamples.title: The tallest kid in class, Colegio Balder, and Hermes Psychopompos
threadExamples.detail: While the tallest student is immediately invited to try basketball or volleyball, nobody knows what to do with an atypical brain; in response, Javier champions the Colegio Balder model and launches CPS Academy as an "off-road" path moving between worlds without selling out.

quote.text: An atypical brain spends 80% of its daily CPU on "masking" (social camouflage) just to seem normal at the office. That leaves 20% to solve problems.
quote.sourceTitle: Education, neurodivergence, and AI: developing talent for a non-linear world

reflectionQuestions: When your company rejects a candidate for lacking "culture fit," are you protecting real values or filtering out someone who would ask uncomfortable questions?
How much daily energy are your sharpest minds wasting on social theater, filler meetings, and unspoken rules instead of tackling complex problems?
Which tasks on your team still reward acting like an obedient clone at the exact moment an AI agent can run them faster and cheaper?

sesgo.short: A systematic deviation in judgment that the brain produces to save energy, distorting the decisions we make.
sesgo.analogy: An automatic mental shortcut: brilliant for not spending ten minutes debating whether a shadow is a tiger, treacherous when investing or hiring.
sesgo.howToApply: Build processes that offset your biases (pre-mortems, independent second opinions, written decisions before group debate).
sesgo.antiPattern: Believing that memorizing a list of biases makes you immune to them; other people's biases are always far easier to spot than your own.
paragraphs: Recuenco leans on Kahneman and Tversky to argue that humans are terrible at assessing risk: we shy away from risk when facing potential losses yet take reckless gambles just to avoid locking in a loss. He explains biases as energy-saving shortcuts in the brain—useful across evolution, yet clouding judgment over the long run. They show up everywhere: in pricing, inside supposedly "data-driven" companies, and in our habit of surrounding ourselves with people just like us.

deepDive.thesis: Our evolutionary brain is wired to conserve energy rather than calculate risk or price value, turning every gut decision into a systematic trap.
essay: Building on the revolution sparked by Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman—and successors like Matthew Rabin—Recuenco starts from a humbling reality: humans are abysmal at evaluating risk. Loss aversion makes losing a hundred euros sting far more than winning a hundred feels good, warping our choices in opposite directions depending on how a problem is framed. The exact same scenario triggers cautious behavior when framed as "lives saved" and reckless bets when framed as "lives lost." These biases are not random glitches, but evolutionary energy-saving shortcuts that routinely cloud modern judgment.

His threads cut deepest when he takes biases out of the psychology lab and drops them into the marketplace of ideas and pricing. While price is concrete, value is purely perceived; the instant we let the brain appraise something, biases like Price-Value Bias charge right in. That is why organizations happily pay for "cognitive fluff": three-hundred-page books that should have been an article, or consulting decks stuffed with workshops and seventy slides. As he reminds us, quoting Mark Ritson, people distrust a brilliant strategy written on half a page because they want to see sweat on your brow rather than pay for pure thought.

Inside CPS, accepting the ubiquity of bias dismantles both naive gut instinct and the mirage of "data-driven" firms that imagine they have outgrown human distortion. Poorly framed data or the illusion of job security—a recurring target in his critique of corporate pomposity (Pompismo)—are just as vulnerable to distortion as any hunch. Anyone who internalizes this lesson builds structural counterweights: reframing problems before deciding, separating sheer volume of work from real value created, and insisting on skin in the game so bad calls carry real consequences and correct cognitive myopia.
keyInsights: Loss aversion makes us absurdly conservative when chasing potential gains and dangerously reckless when trying to dodge an already visible loss.
Framing effects prove that swapping the emotional label on the exact same statistic completely flips our risk tolerance even though reality hasn't budged.
Cognitive fluff in business books and consulting exists thanks to a value-attribution bias: the market would rather pay for visible hours of sweat than for sharp ideas condensed onto half a page.
Absolute job security is an illusion fed by our lousy risk assessment and by corporate environments that warp our perception of our own capabilities.

threadExamples.title: Kahneman and Tversky's dilemma of the general and the soldiers
threadExamples.detail: Presenting identical odds in terms of "lives saved" induces cautious choices, whereas wording them as "lives lost" pushes decision-makers toward extreme gambles—proving how thoroughly framing hijacks judgment.

threadExamples.title: The 70-slide deck versus the half-page strategy
threadExamples.detail: Recuenco revives Mark Ritson's famous quip alongside Price-Value Bias to explain why a mediocre strategy needs a workshop and 70 slides to look expensive, while a great strategy forged over months of thought fits on half a page—and is hard to sell.

quote.text: The fundamental problem is that value is perceived, while price is concrete. The moment we let the brain do the appraising, biases come charging in on horseback.
quote.sourceTitle: Problems around managing vehicles for transmitting ideas, cognitive fluff, and value-attribution mechanisms

reflectionQuestions: What risky bet are you making today solely to avoid admitting a loss that already happened months ago?
If you rewrote your core strategic proposal by flipping the frame—from what you gain to what you stand to lose—would you still make the same call?
Are you rewarding your team or vendors for visible piles of deliverables and slide decks instead of clarity and outcomes backed by skin in the game?

truth-coping.short: The psychological, emotional, or cognitive mechanisms people use to absorb, process, or dodge an uncomfortable truth.
truth-coping.analogy: The defense mechanisms we trigger stepping onto the scale after the holidays: denying the number, blaming the scale, or swearing we'll start in September.
truth-coping.howToApply: When you have to deliver a harsh truth to a team or client, plan how to pace and support it so they can digest it and act rather than freeze up.
truth-coping.antiPattern: Blurting out brutal truths without gauging whether the listener is ready to process them, sparking immediate defensive pushback.
paragraphs: Recuenco acknowledges the term is not established in academic literature and coined it himself. CPS is "a machine for putting people into truth-coping situations": "What do you mean we have no brand?", "What do you mean my company is worth zero?" Managing the emotional reaction of whoever is staring down reality is therefore part of the CPSer's job. He illustrates it with the cult Festinger studied, whose members rationalized their failed prophecy rather than give up their faith.

deepDive.thesis: Because the brain prioritizes survival over reality, exposing an uncomfortable truth without managing its emotional fallout wrecks both the team and the diagnosis.
essay: Recuenco coins and defines truth coping to name the psychological, emotional, and cognitive repertoire we deploy when colliding with a painful or threatening reality. His starting premise is biological and blunt: the brain is committed to survival, not to reality. When CPS strips a company bare with lines like "we have no brand" or "your business is worth zero," the listener scrambles to preserve internal equilibrium—ranging from active acceptance and behavioral change to anger, compulsive distraction, rationalization, or flat-out denial, all shaped by cultural context.

The central insight of these threads is that two dangerous boundaries are routinely overlooked. First, there is honest truth coping—the legitimate grieving someone needs to digest bad news—and dishonest truth coping, which spins the narrative to evade accountability, separated by a razor-thin line. Second, being right does not absolve you of clumsiness. Analyzing his own misstep in a tweet about the private equity sector, Javier shows you can keep a contrarian thesis completely intact while still apologizing when you lay it on unfairly.

In real-world CPS practice, truth coping turns emotional management into a first-tier technical skill, not soft decoration. A CPSer works inside "a machine for putting people into truth-coping situations," and forgetting how the other person processes truth amounts to repeating the Spartans' blunder with Ephialtes: being dead right and losing the battle because you humiliated someone with the power to sink you. Mastering this layer lets you deliver unflinching diagnoses without torching the goodwill required to execute the transformation.
keyInsights: CPS is a factory of truth-coping moments because it forces executives and founders to look straight at truths they spent years cushioning.
Honest and dishonest truth coping share outward symptoms—anger, paralysis, rationalization—yet one aims to digest reality while the other tries to armor up against it.
"Nothing in life is more overrated than being right": winning the technical argument by humiliating the other person usually ruins practical implementation.
Standing firmly behind a contrarian thesis is fully compatible with owning up to an unfair tone without walking back the substance.

threadExamples.title: The raw collision of CPS: "What do you mean my company is worth zero?"
threadExamples.detail: Recuenco catalogues the recurring scenes of his craft—discovering there is no real brand, that a key executive isn't up to the job, or that the business is worth zero—where clients swing between active acceptance and defensive theatrics to protect their emotional balance.

threadExamples.title: Ephialtes at Thermopylae and the arc on the end of private equity
threadExamples.detail: After firing off an overly harsh tweet that splashed Crescenta amid his thesis on private equity's exhaustion, Javier invokes Ephialtes guiding the Persians to remind us that being technically right never justifies burning goodwill or being unfair.

quote.text: The goal of truth coping is to maintain emotional and cognitive equilibrium in the face of these realities. Because, remember: the brain is committed to survival, not to reality.
quote.sourceTitle: Truth coping: how to survive uncomfortable truths in companies and people

reflectionQuestions: When you deliver a tough diagnosis to a client or colleague, do you also design space for them to process the truth, or are you just trying to prove you're right?
Facing the latest piece of bad news about your own project, are you practicing honest truth coping to absorb it—or crafting clever excuses to dodge it?
Where have you mistaken intellectual firmness for needless cruelty, burning the goodwill of people you actually needed on board?

bothism.short: When faced with two opposing approaches, getting the strengths of both to coexist instead of picking only one side.
bothism.analogy: Instead of arguing whether a car needs a gas pedal or a brake, you realize driving requires using both at the right moment.
bothism.howToApply: When handed a false dichotomy ("quality or speed," "art or science"), look for how to harness the productive tension between both poles.
bothism.antiPattern: Falling into binary tribal warfare or settling for a lukewarm middle ground that waters down the strengths of both positions.
paragraphs: Recuenco borrows the term from Mark Ritson, who coined it for marketing's tired feud between creativity and strategy. It is not a naive compromise: discarding either side leaves part of the solution on the table, which fits the nature of complexity. Recuenco applies it to himself—trusting both data and intuition at once—and warns that anyone who embraces bothism takes punches from every camp.
bothism.origin: Mark Ritson, column in Marketing Week (2020)

deepDive.thesis: Complexity rarely yields to picking a tribe: bothism fuses seemingly opposing strengths and accepts that non-tribal thinking always draws fire.
essay: Recuenco imports the term bothism from Mark Ritson's column on marketing's sterile war between creativity and strategy, linking it to Jim Collins's "tyranny of the OR" and Binet and Field's synthesis of short-term versus long-term thinking. Its logic is strictly pragmatic: when two approaches look antagonistic, throwing one overboard to embrace the other exclusively means forfeiting part of the solution. That is why he applies the rule to his own career: despite serving as a Data Manager back in 1995 alongside Bill Inmon, he pairs data-centric rigor with deep respect for trained intuition.

The most common mistake is confusing bothism with spineless fence-sitting or Pollyanna nice-guyism. Recuenco makes clear it is never about handing out participation trophies to avoid conflict—Ritson himself champions bothism without hesitating to land a verbal slap when warranted—but about refusing to "buy the whole pig when you only want pork chops." He also punctures the mirage of 100% certainty: a decision backed by total certainty isn't a decision, just a logical consequence; and real intuition is not mysticism, but a mental NoSQL database processing unstructured patterns.

At the core of CPS, bothism serves as an antidote to monochrome thinking and the cognitive collapse triggered by panic over sensemaking. Analyzing complex systems demands tolerating simultaneous tensions without retreating into cozy dogmas or sterile feuds like Freud versus Jung. Anyone who genuinely adopts this stance accepts its social tax from day one: on polarized topics, non-tribal reasoning gets hammered by both extremes and mocked by people who confuse rigor with "making things complicated." Yet it remains the only way to operate once the chainsaw of data runs out of gas.
keyInsights: Bothism is not lukewarm fence-sitting: it means extracting the operational strength of competing approaches without swallowing either side's full ideological package.
Data almost never delivers absolute certainty; trained intuition functions like a NoSQL database spotting anomalies long before standard metrics catch up.
Countless intellectual and corporate wars—like the split between Freud and Jung—drag on out of sheer stubbornness to climb down from a high horse, not true incompatibility.
"No non-tribal reasoning appealing to bothism goes unpunished": stepping out of a binary trench guarantees criticism from both flanks, yet dramatically sharpens your decisions.

threadExamples.title: From Bill Inmon in 1995 to the sword of NoSQL intuition
threadExamples.detail: With a data-centric pedigree stretching back to dBase III, Clipper, and Oracle alongside Bill Inmon, Recuenco rejects naive data fundamentalism and advocates carrying both the chainsaw of Big Data and the sword of expert intuition for when the fuel runs out.

threadExamples.title: Ayn Rand, Cristiano Ronaldo, and McChrystal's Afghanistan slide
threadExamples.detail: From his longtime rule of "not buying the whole pig if you only want pork chops" applied to polarizing figures like Ayn Rand or Cristiano Ronaldo, to the tribal backlash around the Israel–Palestine conflict or McChrystal's Afghanistan diagram, Javier shows nuance always infuriates the trenches.

quote.text: Not necessarily from a Pollyanna standpoint, but from the basic premise that you can leverage the strengths of each—and doing without one of them means failing to capitalize fully on the solution.
quote.sourceTitle: The classic divide in Marketing between creativity and strategy

reflectionQuestions: Which false "either-or" dilemma—data versus judgment, short term versus long term, product versus brand—is impoverishing your strategy right now?
Are you rejecting a valuable idea or tool solely because it comes from a person, discipline, or school of thought whose entire package you dislike?
Do you have the nerve to defend a nuanced synthesis inside your organization even when it makes you unpopular with both simplifying camps?

transicion-obligada.short: Nobody changes on their own initiative: people change when the environment forces their hand—and even then, refusing remains an option.
transicion-obligada.analogy: Nobody replaces a mattress until their back genuinely hurts: present comfort almost always beats future improvement.
transicion-obligada.howToApply: If you need to drive change, make the real cost of standing still unmistakable and engineer the transition before a crisis forces you with zero margin left.
transicion-obligada.antiPattern: Expecting a comfortable organization to transform out of pure inspiration from a pep talk while everything still looks fine on paper.
paragraphs: "Nobody, nobody, nobody changes of their own accord," Recuenco writes: the environment nudges the change, and the option not to change is always still on the table. The reason is that the brain aims to conserve energy and prefers repeating what it has already automated. He illustrates this by comparing how Real Madrid and FC Barcelona managed the generational turnover of their squads.

deepDive.thesis: Nobody changes by sheer willpower: we move only when the environment corners us—and even then, the brain's drive to save energy can push us to stay put.
essay: Recuenco states the law of forced transition without sugarcoating: nobody, ever, changes of their own accord. The environment does not enforce change automatically; it suggests it under mounting pressure, always leaving open the suicidal option to stand still. The root cause is strictly biological and ties back to Kahneman and Tversky: the brain is an energy guzzler built to automate routines into repeatable mental "macros." Any disruption to the mechanics of a process that once brought success triggers fierce resistance, because thinking anew burns fuel.

The vital nuance unpacked in this thread (turra) is that decay does not arrive solely from external blunders, but from the very life cycle of systems: every organism or organization passes through birth, growth, maturity, and death, and the exact same internal mechanism that propelled your early rise eventually drives your decline. From that vantage point, Javier also rescues Eric Ries from corporate caricature: Lean Startup is not about throwing spaghetti at the wall without strategy, but about building a rapid-pivoting discipline engineered precisely to overcome our natural cognitive inertia.

Within the CPS framework, accepting forced transition transforms how innovation and strategy are practiced. Waiting for an executive committee to reinvent itself out of voluntary enlightenment while the legacy model still prints revenue is naive wishful thinking doomed to fail. Anyone who masters this principle learns to read early signs of metal fatigue before the window of opportunity slams shut, designing protocols that force the system to dismantle its own macros before the market executes the transition the hard way.
keyInsights: The environment never physically forces you to transform: it hands you the bill and lets you choose between steering the transition or sinking while clinging to your autopilot routines.
Cognitive biases and mental "macros" do not stem from stupidity, but from the brain's evolutionary programming to minimize energy burn.
In every complex system, the very internal formula that fuels the initial climb turns over time into the engine of rigidity and decline.
The real point of pivoting in Eric Ries's work isn't aimless improvisation—it is breaking biological and organizational resistance to change.

threadExamples.title: The Messi case: Real Madrid's handover versus Barça's gridlock
threadExamples.detail: Despite declaring himself a die-hard Real Madrid fan, Recuenco dissects Messi's 2020 exit crisis as a systemic lesson: Real Madrid accepted the wear on its winning cycle and managed its generational handover before inertia paralyzed it, while Barcelona stalled the transition until collapse.

threadExamples.title: Eric Ries misunderstood: pivoting is not throwing spaghetti at the wall
threadExamples.detail: Countering the superficial startup reading that confuses agility with having no strategy, Recuenco argues Eric Ries's framework was built to neutralize the mental macros that make entire teams dig in their heels after the environment has already turned.

quote.text: Nobody, nobody, nobody changes of their own accord. You change because the environment forces you to change. Or rather, it suggests it. You always still have the option not to change.
quote.sourceTitle: On opportunities, doors that open and close

reflectionQuestions: Which successful "macro" from five years ago still governs your decisions today even though the environment is screaming that its cycle is over?
If your business or career lost its current momentum tomorrow, do you already have the next door open—or are you quietly choosing not to change?
Are you using experiments and pivots to defeat your internal resistance, or just running aimless tests to mimic motion?

xavier-o-magneto.short: The classic X-Men dilemma applied to neurodivergence and extreme talent: patiently integrate into a hostile system, or rebel against it.
xavier-o-magneto.analogy: The perennial question facing atypical talent in a rigid system: do you patiently build bridges from within, or flip the table from the outside?
xavier-o-magneto.howToApply: Build environments where intellectual difference and neurodivergence have real purpose and coexistence, avoiding both submission and isolation.
xavier-o-magneto.antiPattern: Forcing singular talent to choose between hiding who they are to fit in or marginalizing themselves at war with the world.
paragraphs: Using Marvel's mutants, Recuenco examines the tension experienced by many gifted or neurodivergent people inside schools and companies engineered for the statistical average.

The CPS approach rejects both passive resignation and sterile resentment: it aims to design environments, educational bridges, and spaces of real coexistence where distinct minds can flourish without mutilating themselves or declaring war on everyone else.
xavier-o-magneto.origin: Series on education, neurodivergence, and pop culture in El Turrero Post (2026).

deepDive.thesis: The rift between Xavier and Magneto is no longer just a comic book: it decides whether we integrate neurodivergence through educational reform or spark a cognitive war.
essay: Recuenco adopts the classic rivalry between Charles Xavier and Magneto in X-Men as the sharpest allegory for the modern clash over neurodivergence and extreme talent. Both start from the same diagnosis—an industrial-standard society that fears, sidelines, and traumatizes people who think differently—yet prescribe irreconcilable cures. Xavier believes the root cause is ignorance and bets on schools, dialogue, and coexistence; Magneto concludes the root is human nature itself and answers with tribal separation, claims of superiority, and an aggressive bid for technological and economic power.

What makes Javier's analysis compelling is his refusal to romanticize his own side. Although he plants his flag squarely in Xavier's corner—as a "Xavier without the mansion" who survived bullying and feeling like a circus sideshow on his own—contrasting it with the Magneto path he attributes to Peter Thiel and Alex Karp at Palantir, he warns bluntly that neither choice is innocent: Xavier breeds internal betrayals, while Magneto breeds wars. He even admits the human temptation to feel "Magneto was right" whenever a hypocritical chorus lectures against meritocracy or technical progress.

Within CPS, this dilemma is resolved by moving from theory to real institutional engineering: walk the talk. For Recuenco, lingering in self-pity breeds cynicism and pushes brilliant minds toward Magneto-style payback in a world where legacy hierarchies promote a mediocre political fixer ahead of an Alan Turing. That is why he translates the Xavier bet into tangible projects like Colegio Balder—a working prototype where neurodivergent and neurotypical kids coexist without any child having to lead a double life or submit just to survive.
keyInsights: Xavier diagnoses ignorance and prescribes education and coexistence; Magneto diagnoses incurable human hostility and prescribes power, separation, and dominance.
Neither path comes without a tragic price: Xavier's route invites internal betrayal and attrition, while Magneto's inevitably spirals into social warfare.
When schools and companies force atypical kids and adults to live "double lives" built on submission, they are actively manufacturing future Magnetos.
A CPSer's integrity demands "chaining the muses to the earth": if you champion Xavier's path, you have to build real institutions, not just post tweets.

threadExamples.title: Palantir's manifesto versus "Xavier without the mansion"
threadExamples.detail: Recuenco contrasts the Magneto stance of Peter Thiel and Alex Karp—illustrated by Palantir's controversial 22 theses and framing neurodivergence as an evolutionary weapon of dominance—with his own reformist push to avoid a world where Santos Cerdán climbs higher than Alan Turing.

threadExamples.title: Jose's son and the real-world prototype at Colegio Balder
threadExamples.detail: Starting from the story of a seven-year-old boy whose first "shitty year" at school forced him into submission and a double life, Javier explains his hands-on involvement in Colegio Balder to build a genuine environment where gifted and neurotypical students coexist.

quote.text: The history of the X-Men shows that neither stance is innocent: Xavier breeds internal betrayals; Magneto breeds wars. Neurodivergence today is replaying that exact same tension.
quote.sourceTitle: Xavier or Magneto: neurodivergence, education, and power

reflectionQuestions: Is your school, team, or company building real bridges for cognitive coexistence—or wearing down its sharpest minds until they drift toward resentment and rupture?
How many valuable people around you are leading "double lives" today because only outside the office or classroom can they experiment, question, and fail without punishment?
If you advocate an integrative alternative to talent polarization, what are you tangibly building beyond good intentions?

zona-de-desarrollo-proximo.short: The gap between what someone can learn on their own and what they can reach with a mentor's guidance.
zona-de-desarrollo-proximo.analogy: Learning to ride a bike with someone holding the saddle: alone you still fall, with an attentive guide you clear the leap you couldn't make.
zona-de-desarrollo-proximo.howToApply: Place each person on challenges one rung above their current level, paired with a mentor who gradually steps back support.
zona-de-desarrollo-proximo.antiPattern: Leaving people stuck on boring tasks they have already mastered—or throwing them without a safety net into chasms that trigger only panic and shutdown.
