abrochador-liminal.antiPattern: Falling in love with a brilliant technology five years before the market is ready to figure out what it's actually good for.
paragraphs: The image is a snap fastener clicking shut with a crisp "snap." The liminal fastener (abrochador liminal) doesn't get starry-eyed over a technology's abstract potential; they build the product that makes it indispensable: VisiCalc for the Apple II, Akio Morita's Walkman, or the video game that sells the console. Recuenco believes most historic aha moments come from right there—and that its arch-enemy is the hack.

deepDive.thesis: Historic innovation doesn't come from technique in isolation; it comes from the hybrid operator who snaps a technological stimulus together with the zeitgeist via a decisive killer app.
essay: Recuenco coins an image as physical as it is exact: pressing a snap fastener shut and hearing that clean "snap" confirming two separate pieces have locked securely into place. The liminal fastener is the figure who triggers that click by connecting a technological stimulus to the prevailing zeitgeist through a killer app—a product desirable enough on its own to justify buying expensive hardware or infrastructure. Most industry-altering aha moments don't hatch inside an isolated lab; they come from that fertile friction on the border where technique and cultural pulse finally make contact.

The classic trap this thread dismantles is falling in love with abstract potential and mistaking the means for the end. Holding top-grade graphene or a promising blockchain network is like owning half a buckle: without a killer app, "no cookie for you." Worse still, the fastener faces a mortal enemy—its wolfsbane: the methodological hack armed with a couple of Design Thinking, Agile, or Osterwalder handbooks trying to invent value propositions while understanding neither the tech nor the business. Left on a blind date, the engineer writes off the finance suit as a bonehead and the finance suit sees the engineer as a head-in-the-clouds dreamer.

Within the architecture of CPS, the liminal fastener embodies the operational power of liminality and cross-disciplinary translation. Recuenco prefers this term over "liminal cook" because it spotlights the exact click where stimulus, historical moment, and breakthrough product converge—noting too that fighting the zeitgeist, as the U.S. did in Vietnam at the height of the Age of Aquarius, guarantees defeat regardless of material superiority. Mastering this role means building enough technical rigor to talk shop with engineers without getting laughed out of the room, and enough business instinct to spot where and when the dots connect.
keyInsights: A liminal fastener produces the historic "snap" by locking three inseparable pieces together: a real technological stimulus, the prevailing zeitgeist, and a concrete killer app.
Getting excited about what a console or material "could someday do" means falling into the potential trap; without an irreplaceable use case, brilliant technology is worth zero.
Innovation's greatest saboteur is the methodological hack reciting trendy frameworks without grasping either of the two worlds they claim to bridge.
A blind date between engineering and business almost always ends in mutual contempt unless a hybrid translator steps in with enough credibility to speak both languages.

threadExamples.title: VisiCalc on the Apple II, Star Raiders, and Akio Morita's Walkman
threadExamples.detail: Recuenco gathers three textbook cases of liminal fastening: VisiCalc made professionals buy the Apple II purely for the spreadsheet; Star Raiders proved on Atari 8-bit that the console is only the delivery vehicle for the game; and in 1979 Akio Morita snapped audio miniaturization together with the urban craze for street music to create the Walkman.

threadExamples.title: Graphene without a killer app vs. the Jobs-Wozniak tandem
threadExamples.detail: Starting from Samuel Gil's skepticism toward any startup with "graphene" in its pitch, Recuenco admits he has direct access to high-quality, well-priced graphene that remains useless without a fastener—just like blockchain. His counterexample is Apple: a supernatural engineer rescued from HP (Wozniak) paired with a business translator holding just enough technical judgment (Jobs).

quote.text: When you get excited about the console's possibilities, you're falling into the potential trap. When you ship a killer-app video game, you're being a liminal fastener.
quote.sourceTitle: A liminal fastener turns a technological stimulus into progress with the zeitgeist in play

reflectionQuestions: In the tech project you're championing right now, are you pitching a killer app that answers a concrete desire of the zeitgeist, or just the abstract potential of the "console"?
Who actually serves as a credible translator between tech and business on your team—or have you left both sides stuck on a blind date full of mutual prejudice?
Are you doing rigorous liminal boundary work, or improvising like a hack armed only with trendy templates and workshop jargon?

capitalismo-de-vigilancia.short: A digital business model that harvests behavioral data at scale to profile and bombard users, mistaking statistical spying for genuine personalization.
capitalismo-de-vigilancia.analogy: A salesperson trailing you secretly through the mall, jotting down everything you glance at, then shouting offers through a bullhorn every fifteen feet.
capitalismo-de-vigilancia.howToApply: Replace intrusive stalking with consent, real context, and genuine usefulness: treat attention as the scarcest resource on the table.
capitalismo-de-vigilancia.antiPattern: Assuming that hoarding more personal data automatically means knowing the customer better or earning their trust.
paragraphs: Popularized by Shoshana Zuboff, this is the model Recuenco squares off against with Personotecnia. For two decades, the adtech industry promised relevance and delivered cookie stalking and invasive interruption.

The outcome wasn't sharper marketing—it was generational immunity and attention fatigue: people now tune out anything that smells like an automated funnel, opening the door to ethical, context-aware personalization grounded in respect and real intelligence.
capitalismo-de-vigilancia.origin: Shoshana Zuboff; core pillar of the Personotecnia and PersonotecnIA arc (2025–2026).

deepDive.thesis: For two decades, platforms disguised statistical espionage and ad-data reselling as personalization—burning out human attention and turning marketing into hostile noise.
essay: In his macro-arc on Personotecnia, Recuenco situates surveillance capitalism—Shoshana Zuboff's term—inside a long genealogy of control: from Jeremy Bentham's panopticon and Foucault's internalized self-policing to the state-level machinery of the Stasi and the NSA, culminating in the 2013 watershed revealed by Edward Snowden with PRISM. From that inflection point on, power no longer has to build the entire surveillance apparatus alone; it rents or co-builds it alongside the platforms mediating everyday life, harvesting behavioral exhaust at scale to resell across the adtech ecosystem.

The great paradox Recuenco dismantles is that those twenty years were "the lost decades of personalization." By violating relevance theory and bombarding people with empty ostentation, the industry triggered automatic defensive immunity: today human attention slams shut the instant anything smells like an automated funnel, turning conventional advertising into corporate comedy. Far from course-correcting, the sector doubles down on what Giorgio Nardone calls an "ineffective attempted solution"—and now threatens to degrade AI under Eric Seufert's old axiom: everything eventually becomes an ad network.

Within the Complex Problem Solving system, diagnosing surveillance capitalism clears the ground for its constructive antithesis: Personotecnia. Against statistical extractivism and cartoonish buyer personas, it demands modeling real people, singular contexts, and processes under three iron rules: every shortcut is paid for in inaccuracy, intimate data requires reciprocal value, and every context shifts. Anyone who grasps this break ditches intrusive cookie stalking and learns to earn attention through genuine relevance—knowing that wherever real pertinence shows up, human beings still pause and listen.
keyInsights: After Snowden and PRISM, mass surveillance ceased to be a state monopoly and became infrastructure co-built with the private platforms mediating daily life.
Confusing indiscriminate data hoarding with personalization wrecked the industry's credibility and wired an automatic cognitive defense against empty ostentation.
The adtech industry suffers from a textbook "ineffective attempted solution": instead of fixing the model, it is priming AI to become the next channel for "everything is an ad network."
The Personotecnia alternative rests on reciprocity and context: the more intimate the data, the more tangible the returned value must be to avoid crossing into extractivism.

threadExamples.title: From Bentham's panopticon and the Stasi to the Snowden leaks
threadExamples.detail: Recuenco traces the historical lineage of surveillance—18th-century Bentham, Foucault's Discipline and Punish, East Germany's Stasi, the NSA, and the PRISM program exposed in 2013—to show that today's platform model caps centuries of control by outsourcing mass metadata capture to private corporations.

threadExamples.title: "Everything is an ad network" and the exhaustion of adtech
threadExamples.detail: Drawing on Eric Seufert and Giorgio Nardone's "ineffective attempted solution," Recuenco exposes how the obsession with turning every interface into ad inventory bred public immunity—and now threatens to squander AI's potential to finally deliver respectful personalization.

quote.text: My critique of the past two decades is structural. What the major platforms sold as personalization largely consisted of vacuuming up random data and reselling it to the advertising industry.
quote.sourceTitle: Personotecnia and the attention economy: relevance, context, and immunity

reflectionQuestions: When your company asks for personal data or tracks a customer, does it return tangible, reciprocal relevance—or practice extractivism dressed up as personalization?
Are your campaigns still running an "ineffective attempted solution"—more impressions, more retargeting, more noise—at an audience that has already developed automatic immunity?
Are your models treating people as static segments and statistical shortcuts, or accounting for the shifting singularity of their real context?

roguelike-de-mazos.short: A playful metaphor for CPS: every run changes the rules and the map, so you survive by building a versatile deck of mental tools.
roguelike-de-mazos.analogy: A card game where the labyrinth reshuffles every run: you win by how you combine disciplines and discard dead weight, not by memorizing one magic trick.
roguelike-de-mazos.howToApply: Build your personal "deck" by mixing frameworks from strategy, complexity, psychology, and tech—and adapt which cards you play to each challenge.
roguelike-de-mazos.antiPattern: Playing every run with the exact same pet card ("I throw Scrum or Design Thinking at everything") even when the boss is immune to it.
paragraphs: In games like Slay the Spire or Balatro, no single move wins every run. Each expedition spawns different enemies and constraints, and the skill lies in combining cards—mental models, disciplines, lived experience—into unexpected synergies.

Recuenco uses video games and comics as cognitive laboratories: a sharp solver doesn't memorize a fixed script, they collect combinable pieces and know when to drop the card that no longer pulls its weight.
roguelike-de-mazos.origin: Series of long-form threads (turras) on CPS training and gaming culture (2024).

deepDive.thesis: Complex Problem Solving isn't an isolated skill or a closed framework—it's a deckbuilding roguelike where you survive by orchestrating shifting synergies on every run.
essay: To clear up confusion after #CPSLive2024, Recuenco turns to deckbuilding roguelike video games—like Slay the Spire or Monster Train—and maps their three core loops onto the real work of a complex problem solver. Building the deck equals cognitive orchestration: selecting, combining, and pruning cards to spark synergies without bricking your hand. Exploring the procedural dungeon embodies uncertainty management, where every node reshapes the risk-reward map. And combat mirrors contextual tool management: solving unrepeatable situations by chaining effects inside a live, unforgiving environment.

The metaphor first clears away two conceptual traps by elimination. CPS is not just another "skill"—a confusion the World Economic Forum spread starting in 2016 before dropping it from its 2025 list—nor a tech framework fated to suffer the burnout cycle Pablo Grueso summed up as "what killed ITIL will kill Agile." Neither is it aimless chaos: while Recuenco celebrates the heterodox freshness of Bill Watterson's Calvinball and the Nintendo Wii over Taylorist spreadsheets, he insists that CPS harnesses creativity to the disciplined focus of hypotheses.

Adopting this lens within the wider architecture of CPS transforms how you train and make decisions. Instead of memorizing a rigid script or lying on a therapist's couch to nurse traumas from failed methodologies, practitioners collect combinable pieces from diverse disciplines and master something far harder: ruthlessly discarding the card that worked yesterday but clogs your hand today. Those who learn the game discover the power of sidestepping—dodging head-on collisions to open unexpected flanks—and turn every new problem into a strategic expedition where thinking better beats hitting harder.
keyInsights: CPS is neither a corporate checklist soft skill nor a new tech framework doomed to repeat the historical burnout of ITIL or Agile.
The deckbuilder roguelike analogy breaks CPS down into three inseparable mechanics: cognitive orchestration (the deck), uncertainty (the shifting dungeon), and contextual management (combat).
Unlike pure improvised chaos, the heterodox spirit of CPS pairs the creative freedom of Calvinball with disciplined focus on generating hypotheses.
Playing well isn't about hoarding tools indiscriminately or charging headfirst with brute force; it's about building synergies, pruning obsolete cards, and applying strategic sidestepping.

threadExamples.title: Slay the Spire, Monster Train, and the triple mechanics of CPS
threadExamples.detail: Recuenco ties designer Marvin Seo's breakdown on the Nerdlab Podcast to his own practice: in these games every run reshuffles the map, forcing you to balance synergies, exploratory risk, and tactical combat choices—just as complex problem solving demands.

threadExamples.title: Marshall Law in Tekken 3, Calvinball, and the Nintendo Wii
threadExamples.detail: Recalling his Tekken 3 matches against an ex-girlfriend's younger brother, Recuenco singles out Marshall Law—a tricky fighter who isn't the heaviest hitter yet wins through sidestepping and evasion—pairing him with Calvin and Hobbes's Calvinball and the Wii as emblems of heterodox creativity against Taylorist rigidity.

quote.text: It's CPS versus spreadsheets and rigid consulting—with the twist that CPS isn't chaotic when hunting for hypotheses, and knows that creativity needs focus.
quote.sourceTitle: Disruptive strategies and creativity in business and video games

reflectionQuestions: In your current professional repertoire, are you building a versatile deck of combinable mental models, or still trying to win every run with the same memorized play?
Which methodological "card" that served you well in the past are you clinging to out of pure attachment even though it blocks your synergies today?
Facing a bigger competitor or a deadlocked problem, are you insisting on a brute-force frontal clash, or looking for a sidestepping move that opens an unexpected flank?
